docs/00-overview.md.text: # Overview **Set up your machine. Bootstrap or upgrade your projects.** The toolkit prepares development environments and individual codebases. New projects, existing projects, and partial adoption reuse the same templates and working agreements. ## Four paths - **Machine:** [global setup](03-environment-setup.md), including installation, client integration, backups, and a manifest. - **New project:** [Next.js bootstrap](04-project-bootstrap.md), including `PRODUCT.md`, the official scaffold, local skills, lint, and evidence. - **Existing project:** [complete setup](prompts/12-existing-project-setup.md), including diagnosis, brainstorming, a harness, adoption/updates of applicable components, and before/after validation. - **Partial adoption:** [installation](01-installation.md), [tools](tools/), and [prompts](prompts/), choosing only what you need. The agent needs environment access to execute and validate. Claude Code and Codex use their own configurations; other LLMs can meet the requirements with equivalent capabilities, without assuming format compatibility. ## Product before foundation The description defines the problem, audience, essential flows, and constraints. `PRODUCT.md` records the MVP, assumptions, and acceptance criteria. The stack serves that scope: Next.js/App Router, TypeScript, Tailwind, ESLint, Drizzle/PostgreSQL, Zod, Pino, and Vitest form the core. Authentication and services depend on the product; an application without persistence may omit the database with a documented reason. See [defaults and adaptation criteria](06-project-defaults.md). The scaffold comes from the stable version of `create-next-app`, checked during setup. The toolkit maintains the recipe and additions, avoiding a sample application with its own domain, credentials, or dependencies. ## Proportional process [Superpowers](tools/01-superpowers.md) provides design, planning, execution, and verification skills. Use the path that matches the request's size. If the user authorizes direct execution, respect that instruction; do not repeat approvals already granted. [Ponytail](tools/04-ponytail.md) keeps the solution small and complete: reuse, explicit scope, and relevant checks. Security, validation, accessibility, and requested requirements remain intact. [Caveman](tools/05-caveman.md) reduces conversational noise while preserving language and clarity; documents and code use normal wording. ## Delegate when it helps The main agent can implement small changes. Subagents help with broad investigation, independent tasks, and specialist review. Use only tools and roles that are actually available. Parallel waves require file ownership and no dependencies between tasks in the same wave. The [orchestration guide](tools/02-subagent-orchestration.md) details this protocol. Preserve the main model and authentication; dynamic selection of lightweight subagents requires an authorized policy, sufficient capability, and client support. The existing-project prompt authorizes this selection within the current session, subject to explicit restrictions. ## Harness and continuous review The [existing-project setup](prompts/12-existing-project-setup.md) organizes short instructions, discoverable documentation, reproducible commands, verifiable invariants, and evidence for resuming work. Each catalog component receives an explicit decision; working equivalents are preserved. After implementation or a fix, the [review convention](tools/02-subagent-orchestration.md#review-after-implementation-or-fixes) selects scope by risk, checks connected code, and ends with verified fixes and explicit residual risks. Additional rounds need evidence or an explicit request. The [security prompt](prompts/13-security-review.md) supports read-only repository and diff reviews with private reports. [Harness evaluation](07-harness-evaluation.md) uses disposable tasks to check instructions, recovery, memory, and review behavior. Installation, passing application checks, and successful agent execution are separate evidence. [Harness2 adoption](tools/23-harness2.md) makes measured harness improvement a default part of new and existing project setup through [prompt 15](prompts/15-harness-improvement.md). Establish the native method adaptation, run relevant initial smoke cases, and make the procedure reusable while preserving the current client and authentication. Only observed failures need a candidate comparison. The optional official CLI belongs in a separate lab; its benchmark dependencies, model access, costs, and execution permissions are not enabled by ordinary setup. ## Knowledge and context [Context7](tools/12-context7.md) queries current library documentation. Resolve the correct identifier and query one concept at a time, without sending secrets or private code. [Graphify](tools/07-graphify.md) provides a queryable graph of structure and relationships. Code extraction can be deterministic; document semantics use the authorized native integration when available. Treat an incomplete or outdated graph accordingly. External memory, such as [Obsidian](tools/08-obsidian-memory.md), and the [Claude memory system](tools/09-claude-memory-system.md) remain optional. Start with short, useful context; do not install an entire memory system for an empty application. ## Vercel skills The [Vercel catalog](tools/16-vercel-skills.md) identifies skills by installable names and defines local adoption. Composition and React/Next.js best practices support implementation; UI and writing support review. The [scope matrix](tools/README.md#select-by-scope) also routes Next.js runtime/bundle work, PostgreSQL, GitHub CI repair, differential security review, shadcn, and Sentry MCP. Transitions, Vercel operations, deployment, and optimization require a relevant task. The mobile skill applies to React Native/Expo. Skill availability neither requires creating functionality nor authorizes publishing. ## Explicit checks [ESLint and quality gates](tools/06-eslint-biome-quality-gates.md) check relevant code and contracts. The starter uses the full ESLint profile: official presets, a 350-line limit, logging, data boundaries, and Drizzle guards. The lightweight profile remains available for partial adoption. Lint, types, rules, and builds run through canonical commands. Tests cover relevant behavior and regressions. The toolkit does not install push blockers on `main`, require a branch/worktree, or add commit/push hooks. Client hooks, such as [RTK](tools/03-rtk-token-proxy.md), use supported integrations without duplication. ## Global tools do not need copying Reuse existing binaries, plugins, and authentication. Product, instructions, Vercel skills, lint, and graph exclusions belong in the project. Add a local MCP connection only when no active integration exists. The [global manifest](../templates/environment-manifest.json.example) records the machine environment. The project's `docs/setup.md` records the toolkit revision, versions, scopes, validations, and pending work. An installed file and a tested integration are different states. ## Next step Use the [short project prompt](prompts/11-next-project-bootstrap.md) to start Next.js, the [existing-project setup](prompts/12-existing-project-setup.md) to adopt/update the toolkit, or the [environment prompt](prompts/10-development-environment-setup.md) to prepare the machine. The [Claude playbook](02-playbook-onboarding.md) and [Codex guide](tools/15-codex-workflow.md) explain each client.

docs/01-installation.md.text: # Installation Quick reference for installing agents and toolkit components. To **prepare or update the entire computer**, use the [setup guide](03-environment-setup.md) and [prompt 10](prompts/10-development-environment-setup.md): they include system prerequisites, Node.js, Docker, all required integrations, backups, and validation. To **configure or update an existing project**, use [prompt 12](prompts/12-existing-project-setup.md): diagnosis, brainstorming, a harness, and integration of all applicable toolkit components, preserving the stack and customizations. Commands checked on **October 14, 2026**. Confirm the documentation for your version and operating system. Choose one method per tool and preserve existing installations where supported. ## 1. Codex and Claude Code Both agents offer native installers that do not require Node.js beforehand. On macOS, Linux, or WSL, choose the command for the agent you want to install: ```bash # Codex curl -fsSL https://chatgpt.com/codex/install.sh | sh # Claude Code curl -fsSL https://claude.ai/install.sh | bash ``` On native Windows, follow the PowerShell instructions on the official pages. For Homebrew or an existing npm installation, check supported methods before migrating. Sources: [Codex CLI](https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/codex/cli) and [Claude Code](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/setup). Then, in a new terminal: ```bash codex --version claude --version ``` Open `codex` or `claude` and complete authentication through the official flow. The setup prompt prefers ChatGPT login for Codex. Credentials never belong in chat or project files. `claude doctor` helps check Claude Code installation and updates. Update each CLI through its installation method; for example, a Homebrew installation requires Homebrew updates, while Claude's native installer manages its own updates. ## 2. Plugins and standalone CLIs ### Claude Code: commands inside the session `/plugin` is a Claude Code command, **not a shell command**. Open `claude` before using it: ```text /plugin marketplace add anthropics/claude-plugins-official /plugin install superpowers@claude-plugins-official /plugin marketplace add DietrichGebert/ponytail /plugin install ponytail@ponytail /plugin marketplace add JuliusBrussee/caveman /plugin install caveman@caveman ``` Sources: [Superpowers](https://github.com/obra/superpowers#claude-code), [Ponytail](https://github.com/DietrichGebert/ponytail#install), and [Caveman](https://github.com/JuliusBrussee/caveman). Verify loading in a new conversation; an installed directory does not prove activation. ### Codex: its own plugins For Superpowers, open `/plugins` in the session and install the official distribution. For Ponytail, the documented terminal commands are: ```bash codex plugin marketplace add DietrichGebert/ponytail codex plugin add ponytail@ponytail ``` Check hooks through the client's workflow and open a new conversation. For Caveman, use the documented skills distribution and Codex discovery, retaining concise communication without enabling a proxy or model routing. See the [Codex guide](tools/15-codex-workflow.md) for paths, commands, and instruction precedence. ### RTK, Context7, and Graphify | Tool | Installation or connection | Integration | |---|---|---| | [RTK](tools/03-rtk-token-proxy.md) | With Homebrew: `brew install rtk-ai/tap/rtk`; other systems follow official releases | Claude: `rtk init --global`; Codex: `rtk init --global --codex` | | [Context7](tools/12-context7.md) | Client plugin or remote MCP at `https://mcp.context7.com/mcp` | Configure each client and run a real query; avoid duplicate servers | | [Graphify](tools/07-graphify.md) | `uv tool install graphifyy` **or** `pipx install graphifyy` | `graphify install`, then verify skill discovery in the agent | Graphify requires Python and a compatible installation mechanism; configure these prerequisites if missing. The package is `graphifyy`, with two “y” characters; the CLI is `graphify`. Choose one isolated method, rather than installing both. RTK and Graphify are CLIs; they are not npm packages with the same names. Remote Context7 is a service, not a local package to update. The plugin may already include the MCP server and query skill. Installing a second connection for the same purpose creates overlap. ### Project workflow extras With the modular toolkit, you can choose components. In **prompt 10**, RTK, Ponytail, Caveman, Superpowers, Context7, and Graphify are required. The following remain new extras subject to your choice: | Tool | Reference | Use | |---|---|---| | agent-browser | [Guide](tools/11-agent-browser.md) | Automate browser flows | | Chrome DevTools MCP | [Guide](tools/14-chrome-devtools-mcp.md) | Investigate networking, console, and performance | | Anthropic Skills | [Guide](tools/13-anthropics-skills.md) | Work with artifacts and create skills | | aia-harness | [Marketplace](https://github.com/leandrosilvaferreira/claude-plugins-registry) | Project onboarding; confirm options and support in the marketplace itself | | Official Claude plugins | [Marketplace](https://github.com/anthropics/claude-plugins-official) | Choose review, commit, or hook tools as needed | ## 3. Local Vercel skills For Next.js/React, follow the [Vercel catalog](tools/16-vercel-skills.md) and discover current official sources. Use local installation, actual frontmatter names, and only the clients you need. React Native/Expo is an optional extension. Evaluate the [capability matrix](tools/README.md#select-by-scope) for both machine preparation and individual projects: [Next.js runtime/bundle skills](tools/17-nextjs-runtime-and-performance.md), [PostgreSQL](tools/18-postgresql-skills.md), [GitHub CI repair](tools/19-github-ci-repair.md), [security review](tools/20-security-review.md), [shadcn](tools/21-shadcn-ui.md), and [Sentry MCP](tools/22-sentry-mcp.md). Each guide covers prerequisites, installation, use, verification, and updates. Install applicable instructions locally; account-dependent workflows stay pending until authorized access exists. To generate the product definition, official foundation, and configurations together, use the [Next.js bootstrap](04-project-bootstrap.md) and [prompt 11](prompts/11-next-project-bootstrap.md). Do not reinstall global plugins for every project. ## 4. Project instructions Use [AGENTS.md.template](../templates/AGENTS.md.template) for shared instructions and [CLAUDE.md.template](../templates/CLAUDE.md.template) as the Claude client's bridge to `AGENTS.md`. Fill in commands and conventions in the shared file; merge with existing files without overwriting them. [settings.json.example](../templates/settings.json.example) shows the custom hook format. Referenced scripts are examples: register only hooks whose files exist and whose behavior has been verified. RTK and plugins should use their official installation without duplicate interceptors. ## Need the complete walkthrough? - [Machine setup](03-environment-setup.md): execution, resumption, reporting, and reproduction. - [Existing-project setup](prompts/12-existing-project-setup.md): complete adoption, updates, and validation. - [Claude Code playbook](02-playbook-onboarding.md): a narrated project workflow. - [Codex workflow](tools/15-codex-workflow.md): instructions, skills, MCP, and permissions.

docs/02-playbook-onboarding.md.text: # Onboarding Playbook > If the [README](../README.md) is the menu and the [Overview](00-overview.md) > explains why, this is the walkthrough: take any project from scratch and > assemble the entire workflow in the right order, becoming fluent with > each tool along the way. ## Who this playbook is for For experienced developers who want a structured way to use AI in production while retaining quality control, and beginners who simply want to follow a proven path. This playbook assumes no prior Claude Code experience: Part 1 starts with installation. It does not force anyone to backtrack, either: if something already works in your environment, skip to the missing part. ## How to use this playbook To configure or update the applicable toolkit in an existing project, use [prompt 12](prompts/12-existing-project-setup.md). It guides diagnosis, brainstorming, harness setup, implementation, and validation; this playbook remains the narrated Claude workflow reference. To create a new Next application from a product description, prefer the [bootstrap](04-project-bootstrap.md). This playbook is an adoption and manual configuration reference for Claude. Optional plugins and hooks are not mandatory starter components. This guide covers the **in-project workflow**, primarily in Claude Code. To prepare or update the machine, start with [environment setup](03-environment-setup.md). For Codex, see the [client guide](tools/15-codex-workflow.md) and [shared `AGENTS.md` template](../templates/AGENTS.md.template). Two equally valid approaches: - **Start to finish the first time.** Each part assumes the previous one is complete. Part 4, the complete workflow, only makes full sense after the Part 2 pillars are installed and Part 3's `CLAUDE.md` is filled in. - **As a reference afterward.** Once setup is running, return directly to the part you need. “What was the multi-agent review prompt?” calls for Part 4 rather than rereading the whole playbook. ## Execution continuity These agreements help carry out already-authorized work in Claude, Codex, or another tool-enabled host. They are work instructions; they do not guarantee runtime persistence or create an automatic continuation hook. - **Status during work:** answer briefly and continue remaining actions. A question such as “how is it going?” does not cancel the task. Explicit pauses, cancellations, or objective changes alter execution; without active work, a purely informational request ends with its answer. - **Partial blockage:** identify tasks depending on the blocked action and complete independent work that remains safe and authorized. Do not bypass denials or gates. Before ending, check whether any action within scope remains executable. - **Failed or uncertain worker:** use the host's mechanism to confirm it stopped before taking over or redistributing its files. An unconfirmed interruption request does not release write ownership. Inspect the partial diff and checks, resume from the verified point, and keep one writer per file. - **Retries and limits:** retry only with new evidence, such as an identified cause or fixed dependency. Respect attempt, time, and cost limits. Without a safe alternative, end with the blocker, completed work, and requirements for resuming; do not invent progress to keep the turn active. - **Resuming:** a handoff provides context, not proof of checkout state. Check actual files, Git state, results, and processes before editing, preserving local changes. - **Background execution:** claim work continues only when an active process, agent, or automation can be verified. A conversational promise does not start work after the turn ends. The [shared AGENTS template](../templates/AGENTS.md.template) contains a ready-to-adapt block. In existing projects, incorporate it into loaded instructions; `CLAUDE.md` can import `AGENTS.md` without duplicating policies. Continue respecting current permissions and decisions: consulting prior authorization avoids repeated approvals but does not create new authorization. ### Evaluation outline In a disposable project without external services, check these scenarios. The [harness evaluation guide](07-harness-evaluation.md) supplies runnable authorization checks, a reusable prompt, and a result protocol. The [validation record](05-toolkit-validation.md) identifies executed cases; this outline is not evidence that every interaction passed across all hosts. | Scenario | Expected result | |---|---| | Status question between two authorized changes | Brief answer; second change completed and verified before ending | | Worker fails or its state is uncertain | No takeover before confirmed stop; partial diff inspected | | One blocked action and one independent action | Complete the independent action without bypassing the blocker | | Repeated failure without new evidence or a safe alternative | End with diagnosis and resumption conditions, without identical retries | | Pause, cancellation, or budget limit | Respect the limit and report actual state | | Purely informational question without active execution | Answer and end without starting additional work | | Handoff differs from actual files | Check real state before editing | ## Prerequisites Before opening the terminal, check that you have: - **The runtime required by the project.** For Node.js projects, check `node --version` and respect `.node-version`, `.nvmrc`, and `engines`. Claude Code's native installer does not require Node.js beforehand. - **A terminal.** macOS, Linux, or Windows (native or WSL): everything in this playbook runs from the command line. - **`gh` CLI (optional).** Needed only for the GitHub workflows (pull requests, issues) mentioned along the way. Install from the [official website](https://cli.github.com) if needed. - **An account that authenticates Claude Code**: a Pro or Max plan, or Anthropic API/console access. Without one, the `claude` CLI installs but cannot log in. ## Part 1 — Foundation: install Claude Code and understand the philosophy ### Install Claude Code ```bash curl -fsSL https://claude.ai/install.sh | bash ``` This is the native installer for macOS, Linux, and WSL. For native Windows and alternative methods, use the [official documentation](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/setup). If a working installation exists, preserve its method when supported instead of adding another copy. Confirm installation succeeded and the executable is in your `PATH`: ```bash claude --version ``` If the command is not found, open a new terminal and check the PATH shown by the installer. Use `claude doctor` and the [installation documentation](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/setup) to diagnose integration. ### The philosophy in one paragraph This is a workflow, rather than a collection of unrelated tools. The main Claude Code session plans, decides, and implements. It delegates to specialist **subagents** when context isolation, expertise, or independent tasks justify the coordination. Each subagent receives a specific task and its own context; parallel execution requires independent tasks and distinct writable files. Scale the process to the request: brainstorm to explore intent, plan when needed, implement, verify, then review. A token-saving layer keeps long sessions affordable; two combined behavior modes control what gets built and how the agent describes it; quality gates progress from warnings to errors through tracked migration instead of sudden blocking; and a two-layer memory system preserves expensive lessons across sessions. No individual piece is impressive on its own: the strength comes from using them together. For a fuller explanation before continuing, read the [Overview](00-overview.md). The rest of this playbook assumes you understand the reasoning. ## Part 2 — Essential pillars in order of importance Three plugins form this workflow's backbone. The order is based on actual importance, rather than alphabetical: **Superpowers comes first because everything else here revolves around it.** The other two work independently, but without Superpowers you lose the process discipline (brainstorm → plan → implementation → review) that makes the rest of the workflow, including all of Part 4, meaningful. ### Superpowers — the most important pillar Superpowers is a Claude Code plugin bundling **process skills**: named, reusable workflows for software development stages, including exploring intent, planning, implementing, debugging, reviewing, and finishing a branch. Unlike implementation skills teaching a specific technology, process skills operate **above** them: they determine when and how to approach a task before domain skills determine what to write. **Install:** ```bash /plugin marketplace add anthropics/claude-plugins-official /plugin install superpowers@claude-plugins-official ``` These are not terminal commands: paste them directly into the Claude Code prompt in an open session. Typing `/plugin install ...` there already asks the agent to install the plugin. Claude Code itself interprets and runs the commands, without a separate terminal. **See it work:** request something deliberately open-ended, with multiple reasonable interpretations, rather than a typo correction. For example: ``` Add a way to export reports from our API. ``` Without Superpowers, an agent would choose format, filters, and authentication independently and probably get at least one wrong. With Superpowers active, its central rule applies: > If a skill could apply, even slightly, invoke it **before responding > with anything**, including a clarifying question. In practice, instead of immediately writing code or merely asking “which format?”, Claude Code first invokes `brainstorming`. Clarifying questions happen within that skill: which fields belong in the report, who can export, whether a date-range limit exists. If a clearly ambiguous request goes straight to code, the plugin is inactive; run `/plugin list` to confirm installation. Learn more: [Superpowers](tools/01-superpowers.md). ### Ponytail — what gets built Ponytail is an engineering discipline persona: a “lazy senior engineer,” lazy in the efficient sense rather than careless. Installed as a plugin, it follows a fixed decision ladder before writing code and stops at the first step that solves the problem. It addresses a coding agent's default tendency to build more than the task requires. The ladder, from top to bottom: does this need to exist? Is something similar already in the project? Does the language's standard library solve it? Does a native platform feature solve it? An installed dependency? Can it fit in one line? Only then, write the minimum new code that works. **Install:** ```bash /plugin marketplace add DietrichGebert/ponytail /plugin install ponytail@ponytail ``` The same reminder as for Superpowers: run this inside the Claude Code session, not a separate terminal. Typing `/plugin install` is itself the installation request. **See it work:** request something inviting overengineering. For example: ``` Add caching for responses from this external API. ``` Without Ponytail, an agent might propose a cache class with configurable TTL, manual invalidation, and an interface for swapping storage later: unrequested and speculative. With Ponytail, the answer tends toward the language/framework's existing in-memory cache (`@lru_cache` or equivalent) and a single line naming what was skipped: *“Added `@lru_cache(maxsize=1000)` to the function; skipped a custom cache class, add one when `lru_cache` actually becomes insufficient.”* Code first, followed by at most three lines explaining what was skipped and when to add it: the signature of the active plugin. Learn more: [Ponytail](tools/04-ponytail.md). ### Caveman — how the agent talks about it Independent of Ponytail's control over what gets built, Caveman compresses communication: it removes filler such as “I'll go ahead and...”, “great question!”, and “this could potentially...” without removing information. Numbers, units, code, and exact error messages remain intact. Negations such as “not,” “never,” and “except” are never cut because their removal changes meaning. **Install:** ```bash /plugin marketplace add JuliusBrussee/caveman /plugin install caveman@caveman ``` Again, paste inside the Claude Code session rather than a separate terminal: `/plugin install` alone is the installation request. **See it work:** ask a normal development question and compare the answer's tone before and after installation, or simply run: ``` /caveman-stats ``` to view observed session counters when available. Token usage does not prove savings caused by Caveman; see the [measurement limitations](tools/05-caveman.md#6-measure-usage-without-inventing-savings). If answers still start with “I'll check that for you!” and introductory paragraphs before any facts, the plugin has not taken effect; check with `/plugin list`. Learn more: [Caveman](tools/05-caveman.md). --- The complete [Installation guide](01-installation.md) lists other useful optional plugins: `aia-harness`, `ui-ux-pro-max`, `hookify`, `pr-review-toolkit`, `commit-commands`, `claude-code-setup`, `feature-dev`, `code-review`, and `claude-md-management`. The three above are the foundation. Do not continue without them. ## Part 3 — Configuring your project from scratch With the three pillars installed, move from generic Claude Code to Claude Code that knows your project. This means two files: `CLAUDE.md` at the project root and `.claude/settings.json`. **A shortcut when speed is the priority:** steps 1–4 below are the manual path for understanding each piece and controlling what enters each file. For faster setup, `aia-harness` (source: `leandrosilvaferreira/claude-plugins-registry`, listed in the [Installation guide](01-installation.md) source table) provides a command that scans the project and builds much of this structure automatically: specialist agents, rules, hooks, memory, and `settings.json`: ```bash /plugin marketplace add leandrosilvaferreira/claude-plugins-registry /plugin install aia-harness@leandro-plugins-registry /aia-harness:init ``` Like Part 2's plugins, these commands run inside Claude Code rather than a separate terminal. After `/aia-harness:init`, use the rest of this playbook to understand what was generated and why, instead of building every file from scratch. ### 1. Fill in `AGENTS.md` and create the Claude bridge Use templates from the local toolkit copy. In the target project: ```bash cp -n /path/to/toolkit/templates/AGENTS.md.template AGENTS.md cp -n /path/to/toolkit/templates/CLAUDE.md.template CLAUDE.md ``` Replace `/path/to/toolkit` with the actual path. In a POSIX shell, `-n` preserves an existing destination; use an equivalent mechanism elsewhere. If instructions already exist, read them and incorporate only desired sections. Fill in the name, stack, commands, context, and conventions in `AGENTS.md`. The Claude template imports it with `@AGENTS.md`, using the [official memory syntax](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/memory). Preserve framework-generated instructions in both files as well. The shared template neither installs a roster of agents nor requires delegation for every task. Add only relevant roles actually supported by the client, as described in [orchestration](tools/02-subagent-orchestration.md). Product and behavior instructions have one source; client specifics belong in their corresponding file/configuration. ### 2. Copy and adjust `.claude/settings.json` ```bash mkdir -p .claude cp -n /path/to/toolkit/templates/settings.json.example .claude/settings.json ``` If configuration already exists, back it up and incorporate only necessary hooks. The example is not a ready-to-run setup: do not activate hooks whose scripts do not exist yet. The example registers two **hooks**, scripts running automatically at specific session points (before or after a tool, or at session start/end): a Bash `PreToolUse` hook and a `SessionStart` hook. The names `example-command-proxy.mjs` and `example-session-banner.mjs` are deliberate placeholders: write the actual `.mjs` files following the fail-open discipline (never blocking the entire session because of a hook bug) in [Hook best practices](tools/10-hooks-best-practices.md). For command compression, prefer [official RTK](tools/03-rtk-token-proxy.md), which installs its own integration. Do not register the example proxy for the same purpose. The safe stdin reader remains available in [`templates/hooks/hook-io.mjs.example`](../templates/hooks/hook-io.mjs.example) for custom hooks. Never store API keys in versioned `settings.json`. Use the component's documented credential or environment mechanism. Not every client automatically loads `.env`, and `${VARIABLE}` does not guarantee expansion outside fields supporting it. ### 3. (Recommended) copy the parallel-wave rule If you plan to use Part 4's parallel-wave execution pattern, recommended for speed without unnecessary risk, copy the ready-made rule into your rules directory: ```bash mkdir -p .claude/rules cp /path/to/toolkit/templates/rules/parallel-subagent-driven-development.md .claude/rules/ ``` Reference it from `CLAUDE.md`; one line is enough, like any other rule. It exists because Superpowers' default skill for this stage, `subagent-driven-development`, dispatches one implementer at a time for safety. This rule documents the exact conditions under which parallel dispatch remains safe with the same underlying contract. ### 4. Memory — decide now or later While working in `.claude/`, this is a natural time to decide whether you want lightweight memory: an always-loaded index without external dependencies. It can also wait until repeating lessons in new sessions becomes painful. Part 6 covers both lightweight memory and Obsidian in depth; the dedicated lightweight guide is [Claude memory system](tools/09-claude-memory-system.md). ## Part 4 — Your first complete end-to-end workflow This is the playbook's most important part. Everything else sets the stage; this runs the entire show. We will use a fictional scenario generic enough to serve as a template for any project: > An order-management SaaS has a production REST API. The operations team > requested downloadable order reports in **CSV**, a comma-separated text > format universally supported by spreadsheets, filtered by date range. The original request is deliberately vague, because real requests arrive that way. The complete workflow has five stages: ``` brainstorm → plan → parallel-wave implementation → multi-agent review → commit ``` ### 1. Brainstorm — unpack the ambiguous request ``` Before writing any code: I need a way to export order reports as CSV from our API. Do not start implementation. First: - Ask what is missing to finalize scope. - Tell me whether multiple reasonable interpretations exist, rather than silently choosing one. - Identify assumptions I probably have but did not state: existing project patterns, things that must remain untouched, and performance requirements. ``` This directly adapts [Brainstorm to plan](prompts/04-brainstorm-to-plan.md). Even without copying a prompt, Superpowers from Part 2 pushes Claude Code in this direction: `brainstorming` runs before any answer to creative or ambiguous requests like this (see [Superpowers](tools/01-superpowers.md)). In a real session, expect questions such as: - Who can export: any authenticated user or only a specific role? - Which fields belong in the CSV: order ID, customer, amount, status, date? - Is the date range mandatory? Is there a cap: 30 days, 90 days, unlimited? This matters to avoid freezing the server while generating five years of reports at once. - Is the file returned immediately (synchronous response), or does the project already have an asynchronous job pattern for large reports? - What exact format: separator, encoding, first row as header? Answer these questions, or let the agent choose the most conservative approach where you have no strong preference, before proceeding. ### 2. Plan — turn clarified intent into verifiable steps Once scope is settled, request a plan: ``` Final scope: authenticated GET /api/reports/orders/export, requiring `from` and `to` query params, a 90-day limit per request, CSV with headers (id, customer, amount, status, date), and a streaming response. Write a step-by-step implementation plan. Every step needs explicit verification: a command, test, or observable behavior, never “should work.” Split steps without clear verification into smaller ones. ``` This triggers Superpowers' `writing-plans`. A reasonable plan resembles the following; **endpoint** means a specific API route identified by its URL and HTTP verb: 1. Create the endpoint and validate `from`/`to`, rejecting ranges over 90 days. Verification: unit tests for valid, oversized, and missing ranges. 2. Implement database querying with pagination/streaming. Verification: an integration test with many rows does not exhaust memory. 3. Format the response as CSV with headers. Verification: a test compares the header and sample row byte for byte. 4. Authorization: only permitted roles export. Verification: an integration test confirms 403 for an unauthorized user. 5. Update API documentation, or a contract test if one exists. Verification: documentation/contract reflects the new endpoint. Every plan step includes `Files:` (files it touches) and `Depends-on:` (steps that must already exist). These are exactly the fields the next stage uses to decide what can run in parallel. ### 3. Implementation — subagent-driven-development in parallel waves With annotated plan steps, execution becomes a sequence of **waves**: groups of tasks running together because they share neither files nor dependencies. The complete mechanism is in [Subagent orchestration](tools/02-subagent-orchestration.md); here is the short version for this scenario: | Task | Description | `Files:` | `Depends-on:` | Specialist | |---|---|---|---|---| | T01 | Endpoint and export logic | `app/api/reports/orders/export/route.ts`, `server/reports/export-orders.ts` | none | `backend-specialist` | | T02 | CSV formatting and date-range validation tests | `server/reports/export-orders.test.ts` | none | `test-engineer` | | T03 | Database index for date-range queries | `db/schema/orders.ts` + migration | none | `database-architect` | | T04 | “Download CSV” button on the dashboard | `components/reports-panel.tsx` | **T01** | `frontend-specialist` | | T05 | Update API documentation/contract | `docs/api/reports.md` | **T01** | `documentation-writer` | T01, T02, and T03 are independent and share no files, so they launch together in **Wave 1**. T04 and T05 depend on T01's contract, the actual endpoint URL and parameters, so they wait for Wave 1 and form **Wave 2**. Even without file conflicts between them, dependency alone requires this delay. A real Wave 1 dispatch prompt, adapted from [Parallel wave dispatch](prompts/05-parallel-wave-dispatch.md): ``` Execute Wave 1 of the plan above: T01, T02, and T03, dispatched together in the same message, one specialist per task. No implementer commits: each implements, tests their own work, and reports exactly which files changed. I, as orchestrator, commit afterward, one task at a time, in T01 → T02 → T03 order, capturing the current HEAD immediately before each commit. ``` After Wave 1 is implemented and committed, Wave 2 (T04, T05) proceeds the same way, now with T01's actual contract available to both specialists. ### 4. Review — a multi-agent panel before completion Before any wave is considered ready, it undergoes review, never a self-assessment by its implementer. A real prompt, adapted from [Multi-agent code review](prompts/03-multi-agent-code-review.md): ``` Review the Wave 1 diff (T01, T02, T03) with independent reviewers in parallel, in one batch: code-reviewer, security-reviewer, typescript-reviewer, and database-architect for the new index. No reviewer sees the others' findings. Once all report, synthesize: merge duplicates, discard findings without a concrete failure scenario, and rank by severity: CRITICAL, HIGH, MEDIUM, LOW. ``` For a new export endpoint, plausible findings include a `security-reviewer` catching authorization enforced only on the frontend, a `typescript-reviewer` finding an overly broad type in CSV formatting, or a `code-reviewer` noticing plan step 4 lacks a 403 test. Every finding uses `file:line — severity — claim — exact failure scenario`. Nothing survives synthesis without that last field. Fix CRITICAL/HIGH findings before proceeding; MEDIUM/LOW remain discretionary. ### 5. Commit — one per task, in order The orchestrator, you in the main session, commits rather than the implementing subagent. One commit per task, in wave order, capturing HEAD at that moment: ``` Wave 1 passed both reviews. Commit T01, T02, and T03 in order, one Conventional Commits message per task, capturing the current HEAD immediately before each commit. ``` The expected result is a sequence of small, traceable commits rather than one enormous commit mixing three tasks: ``` feat: add CSV export endpoint for order reports test: cover CSV formatting and date-range validation perf: add index for order export date-range query ``` Repeat the five-step cycle for Wave 2, taking the original vague request, “add a way to export reports,” to production without skipping stages. ## Part 5 — Continuous quality Once Part 4 becomes routine, the next question is how to enforce quality without blocking the team. This toolkit runs two **linters**, tools that inspect code for problematic patterns without executing it, each covering a different area: ```bash npm install --save-dev eslint npm install --save-dev --save-exact @biomejs/biome ``` Biome covers a small, handpicked rule set rather than its entire “recommended” preset of roughly 200 rules. ESLint, with `typescript-eslint` or a framework plugin, covers the rest: type-aware rules, framework rules, and everything deliberately omitted from Biome's curated set. Overlap means maintaining two synchronized configurations for the same rule, so the division is deliberate. ### New rules never start by blocking A new lint rule does not become an error in its introduction commit: that either blocks everyone at once or frustrates someone into disabling it. Instead, it starts as `"warn"` across the codebase, exposing existing violations without breaking anyone's build. The warning count becomes real and trackable, rather than a forgotten “tighten this later” comment. Only when it reaches zero does the rule become `"error"` and remain there. ```js // eslint.config.js (excerpt) export default [ { rules: { // Start a new rule at "warn" to expose counts without blocking. // Promote to "error" once the count reaches zero. complexity: ["warn", 10], }, }, ]; ``` To eliminate warnings without turning “just fix the warnings” into a huge silent refactor, use [ESLint warning burndown](prompts/02-eslint-warning-burndown.md). It requires an explicit decision before code changes: fix everything, fix most and track the remainder as visible debt, or rescope the rule itself. The latter is a configuration change and must be treated as one, never disguised as cleaner code. For the complete ESLint/Biome division, intentionally disabled formatter, and rule-specific pitfalls, see [ESLint/Biome quality gates](tools/06-eslint-biome-quality-gates.md). ### The shortcut if you do not want manual setup Part 5 explains the reasoning because it matters more than configuration. For just the result, including a **350-line file limit**, the rule with the greatest effect on code growth, there is a one-line path. Paste into your agent: ``` Read https://raw.githubusercontent.com/soumatheusgomes/vibe-coding-toolkit/main/docs/prompts/08-eslint-quality-gates-install.md and execute its prompt in this project. Use MAX_LINES=350. ``` It downloads three existing, tested rules, adapts configuration to your structure, and reports how many files exceed the limit without fixing any. The same instruction with [`09-file-size-refactor.md`](prompts/09-file-size-refactor.md) then splits those files into smaller modules. The two documents: [08 — install and measure](prompts/08-eslint-quality-gates-install.md), [09 — split large files](prompts/09-file-size-refactor.md). ## Part 6 — Long-term memory Without memory across sessions, an agent repeatedly relearns expensive lessons: a previously fixed bug, or an architectural decision that only makes sense after seeing rejected attempts. Two complementary options address this. ### Option 1 — lightweight system (always start here) A small index (`MEMORY.md`), always loaded at session start, has one line per memory pointing to a topic file with frontmatter (`type: feedback | architecture | business-rule | reference`). No external dependencies, just files. The saving test: *would a future session be surprised and grateful to know this before starting work?* If not, do not save it. Full criteria and structure: [Claude memory system](tools/09-claude-memory-system.md). ### Option 2 — Obsidian (unlimited long-term memory) An Obsidian vault, Markdown files organized by folder convention, accessed only through an **MCP server**, a process exposing structured vault operations as tools rather than direct filesystem access. This ensures every write undergoes validation: required frontmatter, a template for each folder, and links pointing to actual notes. Details: [Obsidian as memory](tools/08-obsidian-memory.md). ### Why both layers together are ideal The lightweight index must remain small enough to read. Around 130 lines is where it starts becoming noise rather than signal. Most worthwhile project knowledge does not fit: it is too specific, rare, or large. That is the vault's purpose: searched on demand without size limits. There is even a formal migration path: search duplicates → match destination folder template → create → confirm through read-back → only then remove from the lightweight index. Never “delete and hope it is not needed again.” To configure both layers in a new or existing project, use the ready-made [Memory bootstrap](prompts/06-memory-bootstrap.md) prompt. ## Part 7 — Optional extras Two standalone CLIs, installed through your existing package manager rather than as Claude Code plugins, become useful once Parts 1–6 are running. ### Graphify — code navigation in large projects Turns a folder of code, docs, papers, or images into a persistent knowledge graph: community detection, central nodes, and file relationships. It answers “what calls this?”, “which modules are central?”, and “what breaks if I change this?” in one query, instead of dozens of repeated exploratory reads each session. ```bash uv tool install graphifyy graphify claude install ``` The PyPI package is `graphifyy`, with two “y” characters; the command is `graphify`, with one. Prefer `uv tool install`: plain `pip install` can place the package in a different Python environment from the CLI runtime, causing later command failures. `pipx install graphifyy` is also valid for the same isolation reason. After installing the package, run `graphify claude install` to connect specifically to Claude Code, write `CLAUDE.md`, and configure the hook automatically. Alternatively, `graphify install` detects and registers with installed AI assistants. No API key is needed for a code-only corpus: extraction uses ASTs (code syntax trees extracted without executing code) and runs entirely locally. > 💬 **Ask your agent:** > ``` > Install Graphify for me: run `uv tool install graphifyy`, then `graphify claude install`. > ``` > Claude Code runs both commands and confirms success; you do not need to do it manually. Learn more: [Graphify](tools/07-graphify.md). ### agent-browser — browser automation for agents A native CLI, rather than a Playwright/Puppeteer wrapper, controlling real Chrome/Chromium through the DevTools Protocol. Built for AI agents instead of adapted from a human-oriented testing tool, it uses accessibility-tree snapshots with short, stable references (`@e1`, `@e2`...), handling layout changes much better than CSS selectors. ```bash npm i -g agent-browser agent-browser install ``` > 💬 **Ask your agent:** > ``` > Install agent-browser for me: run `npm i -g agent-browser`, then `agent-browser install`. > ``` > Claude Code runs both commands and confirms success; you do not need to do it manually. Learn more: [agent-browser](tools/11-agent-browser.md). ## Final checklist: project workflow The checklist below supports modular adoption. For machine setup, the entire [prompt 10](prompts/10-development-environment-setup.md) foundation is mandatory, including Graphify, RTK, Context7, and both agents. - [ ] Claude Code installed through the chosen method, authenticated, with `claude --version` working in a fresh terminal - [ ] Superpowers installed and tested with an ambiguous request - [ ] Ponytail installed and tested with a request inviting overengineering - [ ] Caveman discovered and concise communication tested; usage counters kept separate from savings estimates - [ ] `AGENTS.md` filled with actual stack, commands, and context; `CLAUDE.md` imports it and retains only client-specific instructions - [ ] (If local configuration is needed) `.claude/settings.json` reconciled with existing settings; hooks registered only when their scripts exist and are needed - [ ] (If using parallel waves) `parallel-subagent-driven-development.md` copied to `.claude/rules/` and referenced from `CLAUDE.md` - [ ] Complete workflow run end to end at least once: brainstorm → plan → wave implementation → multi-agent review → commit - [ ] ESLint and Biome configured with the curated/bulk division decided - [ ] At least one new rule following warn→error adoption - [ ] Lightweight memory (`MEMORY.md` and topic folder) configured - [ ] (Optional) Obsidian vault and MCP server configured - [ ] (Optional) Graphify installed if project size warrants it - [ ] (Optional) agent-browser installed if the project involves browser automation ## Frequently asked questions and troubleshooting **What if ESLint is already configured?** Keep it. Biome sits alongside it with a small, deliberate rule set avoiding what ESLint already covers. Part 5 divides work between them rather than replacing one. Every new rule starts at `"warn"`, whether in Biome or ESLint and whether the project is new or ten years old, preventing adoption from becoming a day of broken builds for everyone. **Must I use everything, or can I choose a subset?** Choose a subset: each piece provides independent value, intentionally. The strongest benefit comes from combining them. Memory alone is a small convenience; together with subagent orchestration and quality gates, it changes the workflow. If adopting just one, choose Superpowers: it has the greatest effect because it ensures planning before implementation and review before completion actually happen instead of being skipped under time pressure. **Does this work with Codex too?** Yes. Use the [Codex guide](tools/15-codex-workflow.md), covering native installation, `AGENTS.md`, official plugins, skills, MCP, and supported hooks. Configure each client separately; do not copy `.claude/settings.json` as Codex configuration. Project prompts remain useful when adapted to the available tools and the chosen agent's permissions. **Does this slow Claude Code down?** Usually the net effect is the opposite. Most additions either cost nothing (hooks intercept before the model sees the call, so the token proxy is a pure gain) or save more time than they consume: fewer repeated exploratory reads through Graphify, less rework because scope was settled first. The honest exception is multiple subagents: each specialist has its own context, increasing total tokens in exchange for shorter elapsed time and better review. This is a deliberate tradeoff. Graphify and Obsidian are opt-in; if the project is too small to need them, skipping both costs nothing. **What exactly is a subagent?** A separate Claude Code session launched by the main session for a specific task, with its own context. It does not see the main conversation history, only what the launch prompt explicitly supplies, according to the client's context mechanism. Each delegated task therefore receives sufficient instructions. The optional specialist roster belongs in shared agreements when the project needs it. **Plugins will not install or the marketplace cannot be found. What now?** First check `claude --version`: plugins require a relatively recent CLI. Then confirm the marketplace was actually added before installation: ```bash /plugin marketplace list ``` If it is missing, repeat `add` with the exact URL from Part 2's table. A typo in the repository name (`user/repo`) is the most common mistake. ## Next steps This playbook covers the main path, enough to run a complete project. To go further: - **[RTK — token proxy](tools/03-rtk-token-proxy.md)**: a public CLI with official per-agent integration, output metrics, and an unfiltered escape hatch. Use it before maintaining a custom proxy. - **[Project sanitation](prompts/01-project-sanitation.md)**: a good second prompt once Part 4 becomes routine, cleaning up the project by measuring before acting rather than assuming each finding's severity. - Reread the [Overview](00-overview.md) after completing the workflow at least once: it makes more sense in retrospect than on first reading. - The [README](../README.md) credits link to the original projects behind each plugin: Superpowers, Ponytail, Caveman, and aia-harness. Their authors' original work is worth exploring.

# Machine setup: how to use the complete prompt

Use [prompt 10 — development environment](prompts/10-development-environment-setup.md) to prepare a new machine or update and fix an existing environment. It requests execution, backups, agent integration, and tests in new sessions. Installing binaries is only part of the work.

Setup targets the global environment. To **start a Next.js project**, use the [bootstrap](04-project-bootstrap.md) afterward. To adopt the workflow in an existing project, use the [playbook](02-playbook-onboarding.md) or [Codex guide](tools/15-codex-workflow.md). Vercel skills are installed in the project, following the [catalog](tools/16-vercel-skills.md).

## 1. Choose where to run

Use Codex or Claude Code with terminal and file access on the computer receiving setup. If the session runs in a container, VM, WSL, or remote server, that is the environment it can prepare. State the destination explicitly when there is more than one.

A machine without an agent needs an initial installation to receive the prompt. Choose **one** agent to start; the prompt installs the other during setup. The examples below come from the [official Codex CLI instructions](https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/codex/cli) and [Claude Code](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/overview). Consult those pages if your operating system or installation method differs.

macOS, Linux, or WSL — choose one command:

```bash
# Codex: native installer
curl -fsSL https://chatgpt.com/codex/install.sh | sh

# Claude Code: native installer
curl -fsSL https://claude.ai/install.sh | bash
```

Native Windows — choose one command in PowerShell:

```powershell
# Codex: native installer
irm https://chatgpt.com/codex/install.ps1 | iex

# Claude Code: native installer
irm https://claude.ai/install.ps1 | iex
```

These installers do not require Node.js beforehand. Open a new terminal, run `codex` or `claude`, and complete authentication through the official flow. For Codex, choose ChatGPT login as preferred by the prompt. Credentials, codes, and passwords stay in the login flow, never in the conversation.

If an agent already works, start there. The prompt preserves the existing method where supported and avoids a second competing installation.

## 2. Run the prompt

Open [prompt 10](prompts/10-development-environment-setup.md) and paste **the entire “Prompt” section block** into the agent conversation. The text already authorizes the required foundation, global development updates, and necessary fixes.

With this repository open in the agent, use this shortcut:

```text
Read docs/prompts/10-development-environment-setup.md and execute the entire “Prompt” section block on this computer.
Use templates/environment-manifest.json.example as the initial manifest format and add global components found during inventory.
Save the report, manifest, and backups in a user setup directory outside projects. State the paths and how to restore configurations.
```

If you are working in another directory, provide the actual file path. The URL shortcut is on the prompt page and requires this version to be published on `main`. The local file lets you use changes before publication.

Before sending, add context the agent cannot discover itself, where applicable:

```text
Destination: [this computer / native Windows / WSL / identified remote server].
Projects whose versions must be preserved: [local paths, without credentials].
Previous manifest: [path, if any].
Organization or system constraints: [describe, if any].
```

## 3. Understand what is required

The toolkit supports partial adoption. **In this specific prompt**, every baseline item is required: the agent must install missing tools and configure supported integrations. An incompatibility requires a recorded reason and alternative.

| Group | Required foundation |
|---|---|
| System | Certificates, downloads, extraction, compilation, and an appropriate package manager |
| Development | Git, GitHub CLI, a Node.js version manager, Node.js LTS, npm, pnpm, ripgrep, fd, and jq |
| Containers | Docker client, accessible engine, Compose v2 through `docker compose`, and system prerequisites |
| Agents | Codex CLI and Claude Code CLI, with verified initialization and authentication |
| Integrations | RTK, Ponytail `full`, Caveman, Superpowers, Context7, and Graphify in each compatible client |

The preferred Node.js manager is [fnm](https://github.com/Schniz/fnm). The default version should be the [compatible LTS at execution time](https://nodejs.org/en/about/previous-releases), preserving project-specific versions. Check the [pnpm installation method](https://pnpm.io/installation) during execution as well; do not assume every Node.js version includes Corepack.

For [Docker](https://docs.docker.com/get-started/get-docker/), an installed client without an accessible engine remains pending. The choice of Desktop or Engine depends on the system, requirements, and applicable license.

### Extension sources

These references help avoid similarly named packages and unsupported integrations:

| Tool | Source | Integration to verify |
|---|---|---|
| RTK | [rtk-ai/rtk](https://github.com/rtk-ai/rtk) | CLI and native hooks per agent; no double rewriting |
| Ponytail | [DietrichGebert/ponytail](https://github.com/DietrichGebert/ponytail) | Plugin with hooks or skill, according to client support |
| Caveman | [JuliusBrussee/caveman](https://github.com/JuliusBrussee/caveman) | Communication skills; proxy and routing features have their own scope |
| Superpowers | [obra/superpowers](https://github.com/obra/superpowers) | Official client plugin or documented skill mechanism |
| Context7 | [upstash/context7](https://github.com/upstash/context7) | Plugin or MCP; one logical server per client |
| Graphify | [Graphify-Labs/graphify](https://github.com/Graphify-Labs/graphify) | `graphifyy` package, `graphify` CLI, and a skill discovered by the agent |

For Caveman, concise communication does not require enabling a proxy, Cloud, or automatic model switching. For LLM work in Caveman and Graphify, preserve the native client, authentication, and model authorized in the session. In Codex, retain ChatGPT login when used; in Claude, retain the current authentication method. Do not infer authorization for another provider from an available tool option.

## 4. Track interventions and resumption

You may need to complete browser login, enter a system password, grant an operating system permission, start Docker Desktop, or restart a session. The agent should identify the exact intervention and continue independent steps.

New extras, costs, and incompatible migrations depend on your choice. Required installations and already authorized global updates remain part of the work.

If the session ends before validation, use:

```text
Resume prompt 10 setup from [report path] and [manifest path].
Check the current state, continue pending work, and revalidate in new sessions.
Preserve existing backups and avoid duplicate installations, configurations, and hooks.
```

A configuration file change does not necessarily change the open session's permissions. CLI, desktop application, operating system, and organization policies need separate checks. See details in the [Codex guide](tools/15-codex-workflow.md).

## 5. Check the delivery

The report should cover every item in section 12 of the prompt, including previous and final versions, paths, sources, integrations per client, cleanup, backups, and restoration. Each test should record the command, result, and session used, with sensitive data removed.

For Docker, look for evidence of section 11's seven steps: client and server in `docker version`, `docker info`, Compose version, `hello-world`, a working temporary project, and cleanup of only test resources. For agents, look for actual skill loading and a Context7 query; presence on disk or in configuration does not prove operation.

The [manifest template](../templates/environment-manifest.json.example) is JSON without an embedded installer. It starts with `template: true`, `null` versions and paths, and `pending` statuses because it does not yet represent a validated environment. When filling it in:

- Use `ready` only after installation, configuration, and validation; use `blocked` or `unsupported` with a reason in `notes` when needed.
- Record the version or revision, observed path, scope, installation method, and update method of each component. Add required dependencies and every global tool discovered.
- Detail integrations in `integrations`: client, scope, file, behavior, and status. If a plugin does not work in one client, record that client separately.
- Record required shell, PATH, runtime, and permission settings in `configuration`. Keep concise evidence without secrets in `validation`.
- Fill `generated_at`, identify the environment, and change `template` to `false`. This identifies a completed inventory without hiding items that remain blocked.
- Keep backup paths and restoration instructions in the local report. In the shareable copy, normalize personal directories as `${USER_HOME}` and remove private names, private repositories, and authentication data.

## 6. Reproduce on another machine

Bring the sanitized manifest with the complete prompt and specify:

```text
Execute prompt 10 on this computer using [manifest path] as the source inventory.
Reproduce the required foundation and other recorded components, adapting the operating system, architecture, shell, paths, and installation methods.
Respect project-required versions and record compatibility differences.
Generate a new report and a new destination manifest. Do not reuse source credentials.
```

Recorded versions are evidence of the source environment. The prompt still requests compatible stable versions at execution time; explicitly state any requirement to retain an exact revision. A manifest does not transport sessions, secrets, Docker data, or tools absent from the inventory.

## Prepare project capabilities

The toolkit has two scopes: this guide configures the **machine**; project recipes configure **individual codebases**. Evaluate the [capability matrix](tools/README.md#select-by-scope) against the intended work:

- For compatible Next.js development, prepare [agent-browser](tools/11-agent-browser.md) and its browser runtime for [next-dev-loop](tools/17-nextjs-runtime-and-performance.md). Check the current skill's version/bundler requirements. The application and its local skills remain project-scoped.
- For GitHub Actions work, prepare the [GitHub CLI and account access](tools/19-github-ci-repair.md). For security review, ensure Git/history and supported agent tools are available.
- PostgreSQL guidance, bundle analysis, and shadcn instructions belong in the project; machine setup does not choose a database host or UI library.
- For a chosen Sentry service, verify client MCP/OAuth support and authorized access. Configure a [scoped connection](tools/22-sentry-mcp.md) at the intended client/project scope; without an account/project, record the capability as not selected or pending.
- The default [Harness2-inspired workflow](tools/23-harness2.md) for new and existing projects reuses the current agent, with no additional machine installation. Only a selected official CLI lab needs Git, uv, and compatible Python in a dedicated environment. Record benchmark-specific dependencies separately; do not enable API billing, a bridge, or weaker client permissions as part of machine setup.

Record every selected prerequisite and per-client integration in the manifest, with source, observed version/revision, scope, update method, and evidence. Optional entries start with `required: false`; do not mark them ready until the relevant checks pass. Do not globally install all project skills as a consequence of this inventory.

## After the foundation

To configure or update an existing project with the applicable components, use [prompt 12](prompts/12-existing-project-setup.md). It reuses the prepared environment and keeps project scope separate from machine setup.

Choose extras by the problem they solve. For browser flow automation, see [agent-browser](tools/11-agent-browser.md); to investigate console, networking, and performance, see [Chrome DevTools MCP](tools/14-chrome-devtools-mcp.md). For project quality, use the [quality gates](tools/06-eslint-biome-quality-gates.md). None of these new extras should be installed automatically merely because they appear as recommendations.
