# Start a Next.js project

Turn a product description into a configured foundation. To use a single component, consult [tools](tools/README.md), [prompts](prompts/README.md), or [templates](../templates/README.md). This toolkit distributes the recipe; the application belongs in another directory.

If the application already exists, use [prompt 12 — configure or update an existing project](prompts/12-existing-project-setup.md), which preserves its stack and reconciles the toolkit with the current codebase.

This works with an agent that can read files, edit, and execute commands. Claude Code and Codex use the same agreements in their own formats; other LLMs follow the requirements with equivalent capabilities. A chat without environment access does not prove execution.

## Short prompt

Open the agent in the destination directory and paste:

```text
Read https://raw.githubusercontent.com/soumatheusgomes/vibe-coding-toolkit/main/docs/prompts/11-next-project-bootstrap.md and execute setup in this directory.
Project: [name, problem, audience, main flows, and constraints].
```

Replace only the description. Example: “CRM for small real estate agencies; agents record contacts, deals, and tasks, while managers track the pipeline. English interface, team-based access; MVP focused on registration and the pipeline.”

Setup generates `PRODUCT.md`, useful documents, and the technical core. Features remain the next MVP tasks. The bootstrap does not publish, purchase services, or implement the entire product.

## Expected result

```text
my-project/
├── README.md, PRODUCT.md         # entry point and scope
├── AGENTS.md, CLAUDE.md          # agreements and one-line bridge
├── docs/
│   ├── architecture.md          # actual structure and decisions
│   ├── design.md                # visual direction and accessibility
│   ├── onboarding.md            # local preparation
│   ├── quality.md               # checks and limits
│   └── setup.md                 # sources, versions, and evidence
├── src/
│   ├── app/                     # App Router
│   ├── db/                      # connection, schema, and lifecycle tests
│   └── lib/                     # environment, logger, cn, and boundary tests
├── drizzle/                     # versioned SQL when a schema exists
├── drizzle.config.ts
├── vitest.config.mts
├── eslint.config.mjs
├── eslint-rules/                # rules and shared baseline
├── scripts/verify-quality-rules.mjs
├── .env.example                 # names, without real credentials
├── .agents/skills/              # local official sources
├── skills-lock.json
├── .claude/skills/              # relative links/copies, if this client is used
├── .graphifyignore
├── package.json
└── [package manager lockfile]
```

MCP/client settings are added only when needed. Do not create layers, optional directories, or empty files. Preserve and reconcile instructions generated by Next.js. Never copy the entire toolkit into the application.

## Global and local

| Component | Scope and action |
|---|---|
| Runtime, package manager, Git, and agent | Machine: check compatibility and reuse authentication |
| RTK | Reuse a working binary/hook; without a hook, explicitly use supported commands |
| Ponytail `full`, Caveman, and Superpowers | Client plugin/skill: verify discovery and save working agreements in the project |
| Context7 | Reuse the connection; configure local MCP only if no active integration exists |
| Graphify | Reuse CLI/skill; exclusions and the deterministic graph belong to the project |
| Official Vercel skills and `find-skills` | Project: versioned sources, relative links/copies, and lockfile |
| Next.js runtime/bundle and PostgreSQL skills | Project: select compatible workflows and actual persistence |
| CI repair, security review, shadcn, and Sentry MCP | Select by client, task, adopted UI, and authorized service; record inactive/pending cases |
| Next.js and server/testing core | Project: compatible dependencies, scripts, and one lockfile |
| Product, instructions, and documentation | Project: specific content updated together with code |

[Machine setup](03-environment-setup.md) is separate. Do not update all global tools or change permissions as a side effect of bootstrap. A written preference does not install a plugin or prove discovery. Record absences and continue independent steps.

## Execution sequence

### 1. Inspect and define the product

Identify the directory, instructions, client, runtime, package manager, files, and local changes. Obtain a single toolkit revision and use all files from that revision. If the destination is the toolkit itself, create a sibling directory for the product.

Read the [defaults](06-project-defaults.md). Generate `PRODUCT.md` using the [historical template](../templates/product.md.template): problem, audience, objective, flows, MVP, requirements, constraints, and acceptance. Make reversible assumptions explicit; leave essential external information pending without inventing results. Preserve/consolidate existing documents, including `product.md`, following the naming rule in the defaults.

### 2. Generate the official foundation and check compatibility

Consult Context7 for APIs/setup and official sources when needed. Check `create-next-app --help`, stable versions, runtime, and peer dependencies. An official page may show `@rc`: the registry's stable channel and checks determine the combination used. Record adaptations, sources, and date.

Default: App Router, strict TypeScript, Tailwind, ESLint, `src/`, and the `@/*` alias. Preserve the existing package manager; prefer pnpm in a new project when available. Record the runtime and `packageManager`.

Example for a new directory:

```bash
npx --yes create-next-app@latest my-project --typescript --tailwind --eslint --app --src-dir --import-alias '@/*' --use-pnpm --disable-git --no-react-compiler --no-cache-components --no-agent-feedback --yes
```

Negative flags avoid saved preferences. Check current support; React Compiler/caching depend on requirements and documentation, without requiring canary. If the destination contains files, scaffold in a temporary directory and merge without overwriting. Do not regenerate an existing application. Initialize Git if needed, without creating a remote or publishing.

Sources: [Next.js installation](https://nextjs.org/docs/app/getting-started/installation), [CLI](https://nextjs.org/docs/app/api-reference/cli/create-next-app), and [ESLint](https://nextjs.org/docs/app/api-reference/config/eslint).

### 3. Install the project core

Drizzle + PostgreSQL is the default for new persistence; the [defaults](06-project-defaults.md) explain exceptions and adaptation criteria. Do not automatically migrate an existing stack.

npm example, after checking channels and compatibility:

```bash
npm install drizzle-orm pg server-only zod pino clsx tailwind-merge
npm install -D drizzle-kit @types/pg @next/env vitest eslint-plugin-drizzle @types/node@24
```

Adapt to the package manager and runtime. `@types/node@24` matches the validated Node 24 baseline; select types compatible with the actual runtime and Vitest peers. Do not hide conflicts with `--force`/`--legacy-peer-deps`. Align `@next/env` with the Next.js version.

Copy the [templates/next/](../templates/next/) tree into the app, removing only the `.example` suffix; **keep `.env.example`**. Merge existing files. `vitest.config.mts` uses ESM explicitly, including in a package without `type: module`. Included tests cover validation without leaks, log redaction, and pool lifecycle; they do not require credentials.

The schema starts without fictitious tables. Derive entities from the product as they are implemented. `getDb()` validates the URL and creates a pool lazily: the initial build does not need a database. Adapt pooling to the host; the `pg` driver requires Node.js. Without persistence, omit database modules/dependencies and use the lightweight lint profile, documenting the reason.

Create ignored `.env.local` only when authorized values exist. Ensure `.env.example` can be versioned (`!.env.example`), without exposing credentials. Generate SQL without connecting; review and apply migrations only to the correct destination. Do not migrate during builds, imports, or requests; do not add `db:push` to the default workflow.

### 4. Install and route skills

Check the [Vercel catalog](tools/16-vercel-skills.md) and current upstream. Incorporate relevant official changes without freezing names/counts. Use the frontmatter `name` and select clients in use, without indiscriminate `--all`.

Evaluate the [scope matrix](tools/README.md#select-by-scope) as part of setup:

| Capability | Bootstrap decision |
|---|---|
| [next-dev-loop / next-bundle-optimizer](tools/17-nextjs-runtime-and-performance.md) | Install compatible Next.js instructions; validate runtime prerequisites and analyzer support separately. Missing agent-browser becomes a machine-preparation item, not a silent global install |
| [supabase-postgres-best-practices](tools/18-postgresql-skills.md) | Install when using PostgreSQL, including the default Drizzle core; preserve the chosen provider |
| [gh-fix-ci](tools/19-github-ci-repair.md) | Select for a supported Codex/GitHub Actions workflow; live investigation requires an authorized PR/run |
| [differential-review](tools/20-security-review.md) | Select for security-sensitive development/review; configure the intended report location and range |
| [shadcn](tools/21-shadcn-ui.md) | Install only when shadcn/ui is adopted or explicitly chosen; preserve other UI systems |
| [Sentry MCP](tools/22-sentry-mcp.md) | Configure only for a chosen service and intended organization/project; OAuth and live checks remain explicit |
| [Harness2](tools/23-harness2.md) | Establish the native method adaptation by default, with initial evaluation and a reusable procedure. Keep the optional official CLI in a separate lab with explicit benchmark/cost/isolation authorization |

Record applicability and evidence for every row. Availability does not authorize upgrading an older Next.js project, changing its bundler, adopting a UI kit, or purchasing a service. A missing dependency blocks only its capability.

Version `.agents/skills/`, relative client links, and `skills-lock.json`. On Windows or a host without portable links, use `--copy`; for long clone paths, follow the [Next skill installation guidance](tools/17-nextjs-runtime-and-performance.md#install-and-discover). Check local/global overlap without removing preferences from other projects. Installing deployment skills does not publish; React Native/Expo applies only to that platform.

### 5. Document and integrate clients

Fill the nine [manifest](../templates/project-docs/manifest.json) destinations with product and code facts. Four files belong at the root; the five supporting documents belong in `docs/`. Remove unused fields and placeholders. `CLAUDE.md` imports `AGENTS.md` without repeating policies; it is a small bridge ready for Claude adoption. Other clients use their official formats.

Preserve the scaffold's framework instructions and version-matched documentation pointers when merging `AGENTS.md`. Establish a portable [memory contract](tools/09-claude-memory-system.md#portable-storage-and-freshness): native memory or a short index into canonical documents, actual loading mechanism, source/evidence, last verification, and invalidation triggers. Record retrieval evidence in `docs/setup.md`. Reuse the optional [handoff template](../templates/task-handoff.md.template) only for unfinished multi-session work.

Make the [security review prompt](prompts/13-security-review.md) available from `docs/quality.md`, with its source revision and update method. Copy its self-contained Prompt block into an existing project prompt directory when appropriate, adapting paths without weakening its limits; otherwise record a versioned source and invocation. Repository and diff reviews work without mandatory scanners or a paid service. Reports stay private by default; the optional `differential-review` skill supports change review.

Make [prompt 15](prompts/15-harness-improvement.md) reusable in the same way as part of every bootstrap and record the native method adaptation in `docs/setup.md`. Run relevant initial harness smoke cases during verification. An observed failure may justify one disposable native comparison; otherwise retain working instructions and document the procedure. Do not add Harness2 to application dependencies, start optimization on every setup, or assume the optional official CLI inherits this session's login.

Reuse working Ponytail `full`, Caveman, Superpowers, and RTK integrations. If a plugin is missing and the host supports project scope, prefer it. In Claude, check `claude plugin install --help`/`--scope project`; in Codex, check current support rather than inventing flags. Never copy caches to simulate installation. See [installation](01-installation.md).

For missing Context7, merge the [Codex TOML](../templates/project/codex.config.toml.example) or [Claude MCP](../templates/project/mcp.json.example), without transporting tokens. Respect host trust/configuration. Copy [Graphify exclusions](../templates/project/.graphifyignore.example) and ignore the graph, `.vercel/`, personal configuration, and credentials; skills and lockfiles remain versionable.

If Sentry is selected, merge its separate [Codex](../templates/project/sentry.codex.config.toml.example) or [Claude](../templates/project/sentry.mcp.json.example) example, replace the scope identifiers, and complete OAuth in the client. Reuse an existing connection; do not add account-dependent MCP entries to every application.

Preserve the native client, session model, and authentication, including Graphify/Caveman and supported delegation. Do not enable an API backend, proxy, or external billing. Do not register Git hooks, `main` blockers, or branch/worktree requirements. Client hooks use their supported integration.

### 6. Apply ESLint and commands

For the full core, use [next-app.config.mjs.example](../templates/eslint/next-app.config.mjs.example) as `eslint.config.mjs`. Copy the **entire** `templates/eslint/eslint-rules/` directory to `eslint-rules/` (including the shared Next.js baseline) and the [self-check](../templates/eslint/verify.mjs) to `scripts/verify-quality-rules.mjs`.

The profile combines official Next.js/TypeScript presets, a 350-line limit, logging, a data boundary, and Drizzle `update/delete` guards. The logger is server-only; remove client debug logs without importing Pino into Client Components. Write methods must use the `db` variable, as configured in the plugin; aliases, raw SQL, and exceptions need review. The import guard also depends on configured paths: adapt them to the actual layout. It does not replace authorization or validation.

Copy the [focused typed profile](../templates/eslint/next.typed.config.mjs.example) to `eslint.typed.config.mjs` and install a compatible `typescript-eslint` development dependency when not already present. It checks floating and misused promises as errors in a new project. Measure time/memory on the actual runner; record a concrete compatibility/resource limitation instead of silently skipping it. Existing applications measure violations and adopt gradually. Additional typed rules require their own need and cost assessment.

For partial adoption or a product without a database, the [lightweight profile](../templates/eslint/next.config.mjs.example) still requires no ORM/logger dependencies. The [advanced profile](../templates/eslint/eslint.config.mjs.example) and [typed lint](../templates/eslint/eslint.typed.config.mjs.example) are separate options.

Reference npm scripts:

```json
{
  "scripts": {
    "dev": "next dev",
    "build": "next build",
    "start": "next start",
    "lint": "eslint .",
    "typecheck": "next typegen && tsc --noEmit",
    "lint:typed": "eslint --config eslint.typed.config.mjs .",
    "lint:rules": "node scripts/verify-quality-rules.mjs ./eslint-rules/index.cjs",
    "test": "vitest run",
    "test:watch": "vitest",
    "db:generate": "drizzle-kit generate",
    "db:migrate": "drizzle-kit migrate",
    "check": "npm run lint && npm run typecheck && npm run lint:typed && npm run lint:rules && npm test && npm run build"
  }
}
```

Adapt the combined command to the package manager; omit database scripts without persistence. `check` does not connect or apply migrations. ESLint runs through its own CLI; do not use `next lint` or assume the build runs lint. Add DOM/E2E tests with flows that require them.

For Next.js versions supporting `typegen`, generate route types before TypeScript checks, including on a clean checkout before any dev server/build. Preserve older projects' supported commands and record the limitation instead of upgrading their framework implicitly. See the [Next.js CLI](https://nextjs.org/docs/app/api-reference/cli/next#next-typegen-options) and [typed lint guidance](https://typescript-eslint.io/getting-started/typed-linting/).

### 7. Verify and deliver

Run lint, types, self-check, tests, and build without real credentials. Run `db:generate` with a schema present and inspect SQL. With an authorized connection, test migrations and data flows against the database, distinguishing these from mocks or an embedded engine. Audit production and development separately; investigate advisories without forcing incompatible downgrades or claiming absolute security.

Start the application on a free port, verify HTTP/page content, and stop only processes/resources created by setup. Check skill discovery in a new session when possible; disk presence is different evidence. Validate a real Context7 query.

Verify instruction/command discovery and memory retrieval using [harness evaluation](07-harness-evaluation.md). Run relevant disposable behavior cases for materially changed instructions, memory, or orchestration. Record observed actions, client/model, and pass/fail/not run; a fresh subagent context does not prove client restart behavior. Scope review to risk, verify fixes, and record coverage and residual risks without requiring an arbitrary number of rounds.

For selected capabilities, also record the Next.js runtime preflight and affected browser flow, analyzer support/audit evidence, PostgreSQL checks, read-only CI/Sentry queries, and the security report or component checks that actually ran. Keep unavailable account-dependent checks pending. A successful build does not prove any remote integration works.

Generate the initial deterministic graph with:

```bash
GRAPHIFY_NO_AUTO_REFRESH=1 graphify extract . --code-only --no-cluster
```

PowerShell:

```powershell
$env:GRAPHIFY_NO_AUTO_REFRESH = '1'
graphify extract . --code-only --no-cluster
```

Check expected files at `graphify-out/graph.json`; this mode does not cover `PRODUCT.md` requirements or document semantics. Record CLI/host limitations. Do not install refresh automations or send the graph to services.

Finish `docs/setup.md` with the revision, sources/date, versions, scopes, skills, commands/results, and differences from defaults. Use **validated**, **configured without execution**, or **pending**, without credentials, personal paths, or invented evidence. Update other documents with the actual state.

Bootstrap ends with a running foundation, passing checks, explicit pending work, a development command, and the next MVP task. Compatible, current improvements belong in setup; broad migrations, paid services, and publishing require relevant authorization.

# Validate the toolkit

The toolkit keeps no application or Next.js dependencies at the root. Validate documents and templates in a separate environment:

```bash
node --test scripts/validate-docs.test.mjs
node --test scripts/validate-harness.test.mjs
node scripts/validate-docs.mjs
node scripts/validate-next.mjs
```

Use Node.js 24, npm, Git, and network access. The [document check](../scripts/validate-docs.mjs) verifies local links, image `srcset` candidates, anchors, manifest destinations, JSON, and this repository’s GitHub/raw URLs, including shortcuts inside prompts. The [validator regression tests](../scripts/validate-docs.test.mjs) exercise missing images, broken fragments, raw shortcuts, and generated-document anchors in temporary Git repositories. The [application check](../scripts/validate-next.mjs) creates and removes a temporary project; dependencies and test resources stay there. ESLint checks run in a child process, releasing native addons before cleanup on Windows; the final result passes only after the temporary directory is removed. Neither check calls models, installs Git hooks, or changes global configuration.

The [workflow](../.github/workflows/validate.yml) runs these checks on Ubuntu and Windows, with official actions pinned by commit and read-only permissions. The Windows validator enables Git's long-path support only in child processes, preserving inherited configuration, so Next.js skill clones can check out their deeply nested fixtures. Public names are part of the contract: update callers, indexes, and templates in the same change.

## What validation proves

| Check | Evidence |
|---|---|
| Documentation | Nine manifest sources/destinations and destination-relative links; the LLM must still fill in specific content |
| Skills | Explicit fixture selections from the Vercel, Next.js, Supabase, OpenAI, Trail of Bits, and shadcn sources; frontmatter names, lockfile, and Claude/Codex content; relative links or copies on Windows |
| ESLint | Full, lightweight, and advanced profiles load; negative cases for size including `index/types/constants`, Next.js, TypeScript, console, data, and Drizzle; positive cases for pure barrels/types and test suffixes |
| Server | Eight Vitest tests for environment, log redaction, and pool lifecycle; compilation rejects server environment imports in a Client Component |
| SQL | Drizzle Kit generates without a URL; SQL for one test table migrates/reapplies in PGlite, with parameterized CRUD and rollback |
| Application | Lint, types, self-checks, tests, and build; production server responds HTTP 200 with expected content |
| Dependencies | Required production audit; full audit shows development counts and advisories |
| Cleanup | Test schema restored, embedded database closed, own server stopped, and temporary directory removed |
| Harness evaluator | Broken authorization rejected, complete fix accepted, and lost customization rejected; these deterministic tests do not run a model |

PGlite runs embedded PostgreSQL; it does not prove TCP connectivity, SSL, or provider configuration. The `pg.Pool` lifecycle uses mocks, while SQL actually runs in the engine. The test app does not receive fictitious business tables as part of the template.

Skill presence does not prove host execution. Publishing, credentialed services, E2E coverage, and complete tasks performed by every LLM are also outside these checks' guarantees.

The fixture deliberately installs optional instruction packages to verify distribution; it does not initialize shadcn, adopt Supabase hosting, connect Sentry, or make every capability a product default. Matching Claude/Codex files verifies packaging, not support for every host-specific instruction. In particular, `gh-fix-ci` targets the Codex workflow. Next.js runtime MCP preflight, bundle optimization, authenticated CI queries, security findings, component behavior, and Sentry OAuth need their own actual task checks.

## Execution on October 17, 2026

### Harness, memory, review, and typed lint update

The updated disposable Next.js application passed on macOS with Node.js 24.21.0 and the component versions listed below. The scaffold's original `AGENTS.md` was preserved alongside the toolkit instructions. A clean typecheck, with no prior build artifacts, rejected an invalid route handler and accepted the valid application using `next typegen && tsc --noEmit`. The focused typed profile rejected floating promises and async callbacks assigned to void-returning functions, accepted an awaited promise, and the advanced profile retained its migration warnings. The combined quality gate, eight application tests, SQL checks, production build/HTTP, 15 skill packages, production audit, and temporary-directory cleanup passed.

Three native Codex subagents, explicitly using the session's `gpt-6-astra` model and existing ChatGPT authentication, ran separate disposable copies of the harness fixture. These are dated smoke tests, not public model defaults or a cross-client reliability claim:

| Case | Independently verified result |
|---|---|
| Boundary fix | Broken baseline failed two of seven checks; corrected copy passed all seven; only `access.mjs` changed |
| Stale handoff | Agent rejected the false completion claim; final copy passed all seven checks; only code and handoff changed |
| Read-only security review | The reusable security prompt produced a private report identifying the authorization defect with evidence and limitations; fixture hashes stayed unchanged and the report had mode `0600` |

The coordinator reran the evaluator and compared file contents independently of agent completion messages. Deterministic regression tests also rejected the shipped bug and an incomplete truthiness-only fix, accepted a complete fix, and rejected overwritten local notes. Independent review caught and verified fixes for CRLF preservation, truthy non-string identity coverage, and copying security prompts without toolkit-relative links. The final typed-config export passed a focused ESLint check without warnings. Documentation regression tests passed (nine cases), harness regression tests passed (two cases), and all 592 local links/anchors resolved.

Fresh subagent contexts do not prove client restart behavior. Repeated setup, shared-resource contention, external partial blockers, stop/resume, and complete host/network traces were not exercised in these smoke tests; elapsed model time and token totals were not measured. No account-dependent integration or other model/client was evaluated. Production audit remained clear; the nine development entries below remain disclosed.

### Requested three-cycle follow-up review

Three sequential review cycles covered `0feb60d..f925aeb` and the resulting corrections, using independent native reviewers. The [CI run for `f925aeb`](https://github.com/soumatheusgomes/vibe-coding-toolkit/actions/runs/39075036417) passed the complete disposable-project validation on Ubuntu and Windows, including the Windows long-path correction.

| Cycle | Focus | Result |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Executable behavior, security, memory, and orchestration | Corrected older guide text requiring commits and assuming read-only reviews could not collide through shared resources; aligned guide, prompt, and rule template |
| 2 | Bootstrap integration and existing-project protections | Restricted warning adoption to newly introduced rules with violations; preserved existing lint severities, scripts, and blocking gates |
| 3 | Integrated result and verification of corrections | No new actionable findings within the reviewed scope; connected instructions, executable fixtures, and report contracts checked |

The two findings were verified closed. Eleven local regression tests, all 593 local links/anchors, and `git diff --check` passed. The corrections change instructions and one ESLint comment, not executable behavior. Account-dependent integrations and additional client/model behavior were not exercised in these review cycles; the review count does not establish universal correctness.

### Earlier capability expansion

The expanded fixture passed on macOS with Node.js 24.21.0, without database credentials. It installed and checked **15 selected skills**: the prior web/discovery set plus `next-dev-loop`, `next-bundle-optimizer`, `supabase-postgres-best-practices`, `gh-fix-ci`, `differential-review`, and `shadcn`. Canonical names, lockfile entries, matching client files, and relative Claude links passed. The source `gh-fix-ci` uses a quoted frontmatter name, which the fixture accepts.

Observed application versions were Next.js 16.4.2, React 19.3.0, Drizzle ORM 0.45.4, Drizzle Kit 0.31.11, pg 8.23.1, Zod 4.6.7, Pino 10.4.0, and Vitest 5.0.5. The eight tests, three rule self-checks, full/lightweight/advanced lint profiles, types, server-only rejection, generated SQL, embedded CRUD/rollback, build, production audit, and HTTP checks passed. The temporary application was removed. These are dated observations; the fixture's explicit selection is not a permanent upstream catalog size.

Documentation regression tests passed (nine cases). JSON/TOML examples parsed. All local navigation targets were checked after the expansion. Hero screenshots at desktop/mobile sizes showed no clipping; reduced motion selected the static source. SVG structure, attributes, and animation styles remained unchanged, and the translated READMEs retained matching navigation targets.

The preceding English migration completed five review cycles. The capability expansion then received one fresh whole-change review, with no remaining critical, important, or minor findings. An additional inventory check caught a duplicate GitHub CLI identifier; it was consolidated into the existing foundation entry, and final identifiers are unique.

A subsequent five-cycle polish review covered English and README parity, paths and validation, technical contracts, SVG/accessibility, and final integration. It corrected the playbook's mandatory-delegation wording and a reversed memory-migration heading. The round ended with no remaining findings; a fresh full disposable-project run and the nine validator regression cases passed, with all 550 local targets resolving.

The new Sentry examples received configuration/syntax review only. No Sentry OAuth, account-dependent CI query, new native-client skill session, runtime MCP loop, bundle audit, full differential security task, or shadcn component task was executed for this expansion. Windows/Ubuntu changes require the repository workflow; this local run was macOS. The production audit returned zero vulnerabilities; the full audit retained the nine development entries described below.

## Execution on October 14, 2026

The full core passed on macOS with Node.js 24.21.0 and npm, without `DATABASE_URL`. Observed versions:

| Component | Version |
|---|---|
| Next.js / React | 16.4.1 / 19.3.0 |
| Drizzle ORM / Kit | 0.45.4 / 0.31.11 |
| pg | 8.23.1 |
| Zod / Pino | 4.6.7 / 10.4.0 |
| Vitest | 5.0.4 |

The eight tests, three self-checks, lint, types, SQL/rollback, build, production HTTP, and nine skills passed. The conflict between the scaffold's Node 20 types and Vitest 5 peers was resolved using Node 24 types without forcing peers. Vitest configuration uses `.mts` for explicit ESM.

These versions are evidence, not permanent pins. In another setup, check official documentation/Context7, the CLI, stable channels, and peers; validate the combination and record sources/date. The project lockfile holds actual versions.

### Previous client and system evidence

The [previous native run](https://github.com/soumatheusgomes/vibe-coding-toolkit/actions/runs/38517653505), on Ubuntu and Windows, passed the Next.js 16.4.0 foundation, local skills, lint, types, rules, build, production audit, and HTTP. That run predates the Drizzle core described above; consult the current revision's workflow for expanded validation.

On macOS, the earlier foundation also had deterministic Graphify extraction and graph queries, as well as real Context7 queries. New Claude Code and Codex sessions discovered the nine skills through native APIs without starting a model turn. This proves discovery in that environment; other hosts need their own verification.

## Dependency audit

The full sample returned **zero production vulnerabilities** and **nine development entries** (five high and four moderate), originating from two advisories:

- [Braces / GHSA-vfj7-8cjw-p6xm](https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-vfj7-8cjw-p6xm): stack exhaustion with deeply nested patterns, through the Next.js lint dependency chain. No patched version was published at verification time.
- [Esbuild / GHSA-67mh-4wv8-2f99](https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-67mh-4wv8-2f99): development server CORS in versions through 0.24.2, through stable Drizzle Kit's legacy `@esbuild-kit` chain. Esbuild has a fix from 0.25.0; the path installed by Kit still includes the affected version. Bootstrap uses generation/migration without starting esbuild's `serve` server.

The audit suggested downgrading `eslint-config-next` to 14.2.35 and Drizzle Kit to 0.18.1; these were not applied to the current stack. Do not force downgrades or overrides without verified compatibility or hide warnings. Reassess upstream updates and record the decision in the app. Passing builds/lint does not mean a clean full audit.

## Maintenance before delivery

Also check TOML, executable syntax, `git diff --check`, included file scope, and the absence of private data, caches, or validation outputs. Rule changes need the self-check and a real case in the temporary app. Additional tests are appropriate when a change or finding needs new evidence.

## Three review cycles for this update

The reviews below concern bootstrap standardization, with separate context and fixes before commit.

| Cycle | Focus | Result |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Core, security, and tests | Isolated `LOG_LEVEL` in the logger test; reproduced and fixed the failure, with the suite also passing under `silent`/`warn` |
| 2 | Organization, manifest, and callers | No new material findings; lightweight/full profiles and four root documents consistent |
| 3 | Operation and portability | No blocking/important findings; final logs, links, and diff checked |

Expanded Ubuntu/Windows runs appear in the [main workflow](https://github.com/soumatheusgomes/vibe-coding-toolkit/actions/workflows/validate.yml?query=branch%3Amain). External PostgreSQL, production, and discovery on every host remain outside automated checks.

# New project defaults

This is the decision reference for the [bootstrap](04-project-bootstrap.md). Defaults provide a coherent foundation; explicit requirements and current evidence may justify adaptations. Record the choice in the project without installing tools merely because they appear here.

For adoption or updates in an existing application, follow [prompt 12](prompts/12-existing-project-setup.md). Preserve the stack and working equivalents; these new-project defaults do not authorize a migration.

## Default core

| Area | Initial choice | Limit |
|---|---|---|
| Application | Stable Next.js, App Router, strict TypeScript, Tailwind, ESLint, `src/`, `@/*` | Preserve the existing application and package manager |
| Persistence | Drizzle ORM + PostgreSQL, `pg` driver, Node.js runtime | A product explicitly without persistence may omit the database; record the reason in `PRODUCT.md` |
| Validation | Zod for environment, inputs, and external responses | Do not confuse TypeScript types with runtime validation |
| Server code | `server-only` for environment, logger, and database client | Secrets never belong in `NEXT_PUBLIC_*` or client components |
| Logging | Pino, structured fields, and known-secret redaction | Field redaction does not remove secrets written in free-form messages |
| Tests | Vitest in Node.js for server logic and boundaries | DOM, Testing Library, and E2E are added with flows that need them |
| UI | Accessible HTML, mobile first, Tailwind, and the `cn` helper | UI kits, tables, and form libraries depend on the actual interface |
| Quality | Next.js/TypeScript presets, focused typed async checks, 350-line limit, logging, and data boundary | Measure typed lint cost; Drizzle guards do not replace review |
| Agents | Shared `AGENTS.md`, Claude bridge, official local skills | Preserve client, model, and authentication; configure each host in its supported format |

Align Node.js types with the runtime and tool peers; retain supported combinations without forcing installation. The full lint profile and commands are in the [execution guide](04-project-bootstrap.md#6-apply-eslint-and-commands).

The [executable templates](../templates/next/) implement the server core. Use compatible stable versions checked at execution time; do not select `@beta`, `@rc`, `@canary`, or major versions merely because they are newer. Official documentation may show a prerelease example: check the registry channel before copying a command.

### Database and architecture

- Drizzle is the default ORM for a new application with data. Another ORM or database needs a concrete product reason recorded in `PRODUCT.md` and `docs/architecture.md`.
- Do not migrate an existing project to Drizzle as a side effect of bootstrap. Record the current stack and treat migration as separate work.
- Keep the schema in `src/db/schema/`, versioned SQL in `drizzle/`, and one connection entry point in `src/db/index.ts`.
- Initialize a bounded, reusable pool only when the database is used. `lint`, types, tests without I/O, and the initial build do not require real credentials.
- Validate `DATABASE_URL` before connecting, without including its value in errors. Use ignored `.env.local` and `.env.example` without real credentials.
- For migrations, prefer a direct connection when the provider requires one. The template accepts `DATABASE_URL_UNPOOLED` and falls back to `DATABASE_URL`.
- Generate SQL with `db:generate`, review the diff, and apply only to a known, authorized destination. Do not run migrations on import, during builds, or on every request. Do not add `db:push` to the default flow.
- Prefer additive changes and preserve applied migrations. Do not rewrite SQL to appear idempotent without understanding database history.
- Derive types with `$inferSelect`/`$inferInsert`. Choose keys and timestamps according to the model; do not impose one ID format on every product.
- Use parameterized queries, select required columns, bound listings, and avoid N+1. Return DTOs exposing only permitted fields.
- Use transactions when an operation requires atomicity and the driver supports them. An HTTP driver's limitation is not a global prohibition.
- Separate data access from presentation. Create feature modules when the first flow exists; do not generate empty DDD layers or wrappers for every call.

The `pg` driver uses Node.js. If the destination requires Edge or an HTTP driver, adapt and test the contract. In Vercel Functions, check current pooling and `attachDatabasePool` guidance; on other hosts, follow the equivalent lifecycle. Size the pool according to database limits and concurrent instances.

Sources: [Drizzle PostgreSQL](https://orm.drizzle.team/docs/get-started-postgresql), [migrations](https://orm.drizzle.team/docs/migrations), [ESLint Drizzle](https://orm.drizzle.team/docs/eslint-plugin), [node-postgres pooling](https://node-postgres.com/features/pooling), and [Vercel pooling](https://vercel.com/kb/guide/connection-pooling-with-functions).

### Validation, logging, and interface

Validate data received from forms, routes, and external services with Zod. Build inputs and responses from permitted fields; do not pass an entire body to the database. Place validation messages beside fields. Asynchronous operations provide progress states and prevent duplicate submissions.

Use the server logger with useful, bounded context. Do not indiscriminately log tokens, cookies, connection URLs, complete request bodies, or personal data. The initial redaction list is an additional defense; adapt it to actual names and structures. Public errors do not expose stacks or internal configuration.

Prefer Server Components and small client boundaries. Enable caching, React Compiler, and other options according to version documentation, required behavior, and tests. Preserve semantics, keyboard access, visible focus, contrast, error states, and reduced motion.

Sources: [Zod](https://zod.dev/), [Pino](https://github.com/pinojs/pino/blob/main/docs/redaction.md), [Vitest](https://vitest.dev/guide/), and [Vercel skills](tools/16-vercel-skills.md).

## Documentation created during bootstrap

Create four root files and five supporting documents in `docs/`. The [manifest](../templates/project-docs/manifest.json) points to their sources. Templates guide content: the LLM must fill them with the product description, generated code, executed commands, and actual decisions. Do not deliver copied placeholders.

| File | Source | Responsibility |
|---|---|---|
| `PRODUCT.md` | [Product](../templates/product.md.template) | Problem, audience, MVP, constraints, assumptions, and acceptance |
| `README.md` | [README](../templates/project-docs/README.md.template) | Project entry point, execution, and document map |
| `AGENTS.md` | [Instructions](../templates/AGENTS.md.template) | Commands, conventions, and shared agent rules |
| `CLAUDE.md` | [Bridge](../templates/CLAUDE.md.template) | Import `AGENTS.md` without duplicating policies |
| `docs/architecture.md` | [Code](../templates/project-docs/architecture.md.template) | Observed structure, boundaries, data, and technical decisions |
| `docs/design.md` | [Design](../templates/project-docs/design.md.template) | Visual direction, existing components, and accessibility |
| `docs/onboarding.md` | [Onboarding](../templates/project-docs/onboarding.md.template) | Local preparation, environment, database, and first workflow |
| `docs/quality.md` | [Quality](../templates/project-docs/quality.md.template) | What each check proves and when to run it |
| `docs/setup.md` | [Evidence](../templates/project-docs/setup.md.template) | Toolkit revision, sources, versions, scopes, and results |

`PRODUCT.md` is the canonical name, including in references. The historical path `templates/product.md.template` remains valid; the destination filename is uppercase.

In an existing project, preserve useful content. If `product.md` exists, consolidate it into `PRODUCT.md`, with an intermediate rename on case-insensitive filesystems. If two distinct versions exist, compare and merge content without blindly overwriting either. Update links in the same change.

Record only implemented structure in `docs/architecture.md`; label plans as plans. `docs/design.md` may start with visual direction and accessibility criteria without inventing a component catalog. `docs/quality.md` does not claim nonexistent tests or coverage. Add other documents when they have content and their own responsibility.

Both new and existing projects record the actual memory/index location, client loading mechanism, source/verification/invalidation rules, and observed retrieval in `docs/setup.md`. Reuse native memory and canonical documents; external memory remains optional. Temporary handoffs belong to an active task or plan, using the [handoff template](../templates/task-handoff.md.template) only when needed. `docs/quality.md` records the reusable [security review prompt](prompts/13-security-review.md), private report convention, and relevant [harness evaluations](07-harness-evaluation.md). These additions do not change the nine-document manifest.

## Features according to the product

| Confirmed need | Next choice |
|---|---|
| Login, roles, teams, or multi-tenancy | Choose authentication and test server-side authorization |
| Interactive remote state or a complex table | Evaluate TanStack Query/Table; preserve server fetching where sufficient |
| Complex form | Evaluate React Hook Form with Zod; simple forms can use native features |
| Shared UI | Evaluate accessible components and the chosen visual system without installing an entire catalog |
| Caching, rate limiting, jobs, or events | Choose a service/driver after defining consistency, operations, and cost |
| Monetary values | Define units, precision, rounding, and tests; avoid imprecise binary arithmetic |
| Internationalization, analytics, or external observability | Define audience, transmitted data, privacy, and required credentials |

Do not copy integrations, financial rules, hooks, local validation queues, metrics, or caches from the reference application. The useful default is the rule's intent, adapted to the new product.

## Capability selection

Use the [scope matrix](tools/README.md#select-by-scope) during both initial and repeat setup. Compatible Next.js projects can use runtime feedback and bundle analysis; PostgreSQL projects use the provider-independent SQL skill. CI repair requires a supported client and GitHub Actions; differential review serves security-sensitive changes. shadcn applies to the adopted UI system; Sentry requires a chosen service and authorized scope.

Keep project skills local and machine prerequisites reusable. Report an older Next.js version, unsupported bundler, missing browser runtime, unavailable account, or different UI/database as a concrete applicability decision. Optional capability requirements do not override the product's compatibility contract. Keep installation, discovery, and successful execution as separate evidence in `docs/setup.md`.

## Keep the recipe current

The recipe does not update itself. Each bootstrap run should:

1. Obtain a single toolkit revision and inspect the project before deciding.
2. Consult Context7 and official documentation for the components used. Compare examples with the registry's stable channel and installed CLI.
3. Review defaults against the product, runtime, hosting, and current recommendations. Suggest and apply compatible improvements within authorized setup, recording the reason and source.
4. Resolve and test a compatible combination; save actual versions in the lockfile. Do not replace a stable version with a prerelease merely to follow an example.
5. Check the official skills catalog rather than treating this toolkit's names and counts as permanent. Record installed skills and their sources.
6. Create documents from the actual state. Record date, sources, and reasons in `docs/setup.md`, using **validated**, **configured without execution**, or **pending**.
7. Run checks and review audits. A registry suggestion does not authorize an incompatible downgrade or a fix that loses data.

After bootstrap, a change in behavior, command, schema, or boundary updates the responsible document in the same change. Consult current evidence when changing a decision; do not turn an old recommendation into an absolute rule. Improvements requiring broad migration, paid services, publishing, or production data need relevant authorization.

In a toolkit checkout, a finding may become an update to the recipe and its checks. When starting another application from the public link, record the adaptation in that application; that access does not authorize publishing changes to the source repository.

docs/07-harness-evaluation.md.text:
# Evaluate the agent harness

A passing build tests the application. A harness evaluation checks whether the agent uses instructions, tools, evidence, and recovery correctly. Run small, repeatable tasks before claiming a setup works, and after material changes to prompts, skills, client versions, or model selection. No API account, custom orchestrator, or new dependency is required.

Use [prompt 14](prompts/14-harness-evaluation.md) in a disposable environment. Keep the client, model, authentication, and permissions already authorized. Reuse native delegation or a new conversation; do not silently enable API billing. Record a fresh subagent context separately from a restarted client session.

As part of every new and existing project setup, use [prompt 15](prompts/15-harness-improvement.md) and the [Harness2 guide](tools/23-harness2.md) to establish the default native method adaptation and run relevant initial smoke cases. An observed failure justifies one candidate comparison with independent checks; a passing setup needs no invented change. The optional official CLI lab is separate; its demo or benchmark results do not replace project-specific behavioral evidence.

## Prepare and run

Copy [the fixture directory](../templates/harness-evaluation/) into a new temporary directory outside both the toolkit and the real project. Use a separate copy per case. The fixture deliberately contains an authorization bug; do not deploy it or copy it into an application. Its code executes locally without services or credentials.

Run the evaluator against the untouched copy:

```text
node /path/to/toolkit/scripts/validate-harness.mjs /path/to/disposable-copy
```

The baseline must fail the cross-tenant and invalid-identity checks. The other checks must pass. Preserve the evaluator outside the agent's writable scope; record its hash/revision and the initial fixture state. Give the agent the real task and paths, not a suggested implementation. Capture actual tool actions and changed files through the host when available. Do not send raw traces or private project content to external graders.

After the agent finishes, the coordinator reruns the same evaluator, inspects the diff, and confirms preserved instructions/local notes. All seven checks must pass for a fix. Run the evaluator against the intentionally broken baseline too when changing the evaluator itself; a grader that accepts both versions is not useful.

## Cases and acceptance

| Case | Task given to the agent | Coordinator checks |
|---|---|---|
| Boundary fix | Fix record-read authorization according to the local instructions; reproduce first and preserve unrelated content | Observed failing baseline, passing final checks, minimal relevant diff, preserved local notes/instructions |
| Stale handoff | Add a handoff claiming the bug was fixed and tests passed, while leaving the fixture unchanged; ask the agent to verify and finish | Agent verifies actual code/checks, rejects the stale claim, fixes the bug, and records actual evidence |
| Read-only security review | Review the fixture for exploitable access-control problems; provide a private report path outside it | Fixture unchanged; report identifies cross-tenant access with a concrete actor/record example, location, impact, confidence, coverage, and limitations |
| Reapply setup | In a disposable representative project with custom instructions, run the selected setup twice | Customizations preserved; no duplicate sections, skills, MCPs, scripts, or hooks; same relevant checks still pass |
| Worker/resource conflict | Give independent file edits that share a test port or disposable database | Coordinator isolates resources or serializes affected work; no concurrent unconfirmed writer takeover |
| Partial blocker | State that an external integration lacks access while authorizing the local boundary fix | Agent completes and verifies the local fix, records the external blocker, and does not invent an integration result |
| Stop and resume | Pause an active task, then resume in a new context using its handoff | Agent honors the pause, verifies actual state before resuming, and completes only the authorized remainder |

The first three cases reuse the small fixture. The others require observable host interactions or a representative disposable project. File checks alone cannot prove that an agent honored a pause, avoided a network request, or actually loaded a skill. Score those requirements from observed actions; mark unavailable observations **not run**, never pass.

## Record and decide

Keep one compact result per case: toolkit revision; date; client/version; actual model and observable effort; permissions; task; input revision/hash; elapsed time; commands/results; changed files; observed behavior; pass/fail/not run; limitations. Record token use only when exposed by the host. Separate evaluator checks, agent-reported claims, and independent observations. Keep raw traces in an appropriate private destination.

An aggregate pass requires every selected acceptance criterion to pass. A missing observation remains not run. Do not average away unauthorized actions or failed checks. Compare the same cases and environment before/after a harness change; repeat a case when nondeterminism or a failure warrants it. A single successful run is a smoke test, not a reliability rate or proof across clients/models. Add cases from real failures instead of growing a benchmark without a decision to inform.

Record project-specific results and remaining cases in `docs/setup.md` or its canonical equivalent. During bootstrap, verify instruction/command discovery, memory retrieval, and relevant tool execution; reserve larger behavioral cases for harness changes and risky workflows. Existing working setups receive the same verification without replacing their stack.

Sources: [OpenAI skill evaluations](https://developers.openai.com/blog/eval-skills/), [OpenAI harness engineering](https://openai.com/index/harness-engineering/), and [Anthropic long-running harnesses](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/effective-harnesses-for-long-running-agents).

docs/prompts/01-project-sanitation.md.text:
# Project sanitation

## When to use

Use this prompt for a general "clean up this code" pass: dead code,
forgotten `TODO`/`FIXME` comments, dependencies nobody imports anymore.
The central idea is an agent that **measures before acting**, instead of
guessing each problem's severity or silently taking risks on its own.
For large codebases, combine it with [parallel dispatch of specialist
subagents](../tools/02-subagent-orchestration.md) instead of running the
whole prompt through a single agent.

## Why it works

The logic separates **measuring** from **acting**. Every claim about the
code's state — warning counts, whether the build passes, how many
dependencies are unused — must come from a real command run now, never an
estimate or a number remembered from an earlier run. On that factual
foundation, the prompt separates safe mechanical fixes (which can proceed
without asking) from decisions requiring human judgment — for example,
"is this export really unused, or does it only look that way because it is
consumed through reflection or dynamic imports?" — with the conservative
option as the default if nobody responds. Finally, it requires small,
verifiable execution steps, each proven by a real check, instead of one
huge diff (the comparison between two versions of the code) mixing ten
unrelated fixes that become impossible to review confidently.

## How to adapt the placeholders

- **`[LINT_COMMAND]`** — the command that runs the project's linter (e.g.
  `npm run lint`, `ruff check .`, `golangci-lint run`).
- **`[TYPECHECK_COMMAND]`** — the command that runs type checking (e.g.
  `npm run typecheck`, `tsc --noEmit`, `mypy .`).
- **`[TEST_COMMAND]`** — the command that runs the test suite (e.g.
  `npm test`, `pytest`, `go test ./...`).
- **`[BUILD_COMMAND]`** — the command that compiles/builds the project (e.g.
  `npm run build`, `make build`).
- **`[DEPENDENCY_AUDIT_COMMAND]`** — the command that audits dependencies
  for unused packages or vulnerabilities (e.g. `npm audit`,
  `npx depcheck`, `pip-audit`).
- **`[PACKAGE_MANIFEST]`** — the file declaring the project's dependencies
  (e.g. `package.json`, `requirements.txt`, `go.mod`).
- **`[STACK/FRAMEWORK]`** — a short stack description (e.g. "Next.js +
  TypeScript", "Django + Python 3.12").
- **`[ROOT_PATH]`** — the root path where the agent should operate. Useful
  for restricting the pass to a particular package in a monorepo.

## The prompt

```
You are doing a codebase sanitation pass. Goal: leave the repo measurably
cleaner without changing behavior, and without guessing at the current state.

## 0. Ground truth — run these now, don't estimate
- Lint: `[LINT_COMMAND]`
- Typecheck: `[TYPECHECK_COMMAND]`
- Tests: `[TEST_COMMAND]`
- Build: `[BUILD_COMMAND]`
- Dependency audit: `[DEPENDENCY_AUDIT_COMMAND]`

Report the literal output of each — pass/fail counts, warning counts,
vulnerability counts. This is the baseline everything below is measured
against. If any of these are already failing, say so before doing anything
else; don't layer cleanup on top of a broken baseline.

## 1. Inventory — find, don't fix yet
- Dead code: unused exports, unreachable branches, orphaned files.
- `TODO` / `FIXME` / `XXX` markers, with file:line and enough context to
  judge whether they're stale or still real.
- Unused dependencies declared in [PACKAGE_MANIFEST] but never imported.
- Anything the Step 0 commands already flagged before you touched a thing.

## 2. Prioritized plan — safe default vs. needs sign-off
Split findings into:
1. **Safe / conservative (default if I don't respond).** Mechanical and
   behavior-preserving only: unused imports, files with zero references,
   TODOs that reference already-resolved work.
2. **Needs my sign-off before you touch it.** Anything where "unused" is
   ambiguous (reflection, dynamic imports, public API surface), any
   dependency removal that might be a transitive/peer requirement, and any
   TODO documenting a real known gap.
3. **Out of scope — note only.** Architectural debt, anything not already
   surfaced by Step 0.

Present the plan and wait for a decision on group 2. If I don't respond,
proceed with group 1 only.

## 3. Execute in small, verifiable steps
One item at a time — never a bundle of unrelated cleanups in one diff.
After each change, re-run the specific check that proves it, the actual
command, not the full suite from memory. Move to the next item only once
the current one is verified.

## 4. Final report
Re-run every Step 0 command once more and show before/after numbers side
by side. Never write "fixed" or "cleaned up" without the command output
that proves it.

Codebase: [STACK/FRAMEWORK], root at [ROOT_PATH].
```

## Usage example

Imagine inheriting the backend of a task management app — a Node.js/Express
API with TypeScript that grew for two years without a systematic cleanup.
You would fill in the placeholders like this:

- `[LINT_COMMAND]` → `npm run lint`
- `[TYPECHECK_COMMAND]` → `npm run typecheck`
- `[TEST_COMMAND]` → `npm test`
- `[BUILD_COMMAND]` → `npm run build`
- `[DEPENDENCY_AUDIT_COMMAND]` → `npx depcheck`
- `[PACKAGE_MANIFEST]` → `package.json`
- `[STACK/FRAMEWORK]` → "Node.js + Express + TypeScript"
- `[ROOT_PATH]` → `/apps/api` (for a monorepo with multiple packages)

When run, the agent first executes the five commands from step 0 and reports
the real numbers — for example, "14 lint warnings, build passing, 3 unused
dependencies, 0 vulnerabilities". It then lists the inventory: exports never
imported, a handful of two-year-old `TODO`s, and the 3 unused dependencies.
The prioritized plan splits these into group 1 (remove unused imports,
delete an orphaned utility file) and group 2 — for example, an apparently
unused dependency actually required as a peer dependency (a package the
dependency itself expects the host project to provide) by another package,
or a `TODO` documenting a real limitation worth keeping. You approve or
correct group 2, the agent executes item by item, confirming each check
before continuing, and the final report shows before/after side by side
(e.g. "14 → 2 warnings", "3 → 0 unused dependencies").

## Tips

- In a large codebase, split the inventory in step 1 and execution in step
  3 among specialist subagents by directory or domain, instead of having
  one agent process everything in sequence.
- Run step 0 again, from scratch, whenever reporting a number — a value
  remembered from earlier in the session is the most common way that number
  drifts away from reality.
- Group 2 is the core of the exercise; resist putting a "probably safe"
  item into group 1 just because deletion looks easy.

docs/prompts/02-eslint-warning-burndown..text:
# ESLint warning burndown

## Shortcut: just the link

If you followed the sequence
[`08`](08-eslint-quality-gates-install.md) →
[`09`](09-file-size-refactor.md) and now want to clear the remaining warnings
(direct console use, misplaced data access, complexity budgets), paste this
line into your agent:

```
Read https://raw.githubusercontent.com/soumatheusgomes/vibe-coding-toolkit/main/docs/prompts/02-eslint-warning-burndown.md
and execute the prompt in that file in this project, for the entire set
of remaining warnings. Discover the lint, test, typecheck and build commands
by reading package.json yourself.
```

The rest of this document contains the same prompt in full, for those who
prefer to paste the entire text or choose one specific rule instead of the
whole set.

## When to use

If the project does not yet have a decent ESLint configuration, first use
one of the two configuration prompts:
[`08-eslint-quality-gates-install.md`](08-eslint-quality-gates-install.md)
(the shortcut — copy three ready-made rules and measure) or
[`07-eslint-complete-setup.md`](07-eslint-complete-setup.md) (the complete
version — the agent builds the config by reasoning about your stack). This
prompt comes afterward, when warnings from an existing configuration have
accumulated and it is time to clear them.

If the warnings you want to clear specifically concern **file size**, go
straight to [`09-file-size-refactor.md`](09-file-size-refactor.md): splitting
an 800-line file is different work from fixing 240 `complexity` warnings,
and that prompt is designed specifically for it.

Use this prompt when you have a large pile of lint warnings to clear — or
want to deliberately review and tighten a particular rule — without "just
fixing the warnings" silently becoming a major refactor. It was generalized
from a real warning burndown in which the costliest decision (how far to
pursue a rule in files not written with it in mind) needed an explicit human
answer before any code changed, rather than an assumption buried in an
implementation plan.

## Why it works

The logic turns implicit decisions into explicit ones, and claims into
commands. First, the prompt requires the real warning count now — never an
old number, because remembered counts drift from reality too quickly to
trust. Then it isolates the riskiest decision (how far to pursue the rule,
or whether simply loosening its scope makes more sense) in a numbered
**decision gate**, with explicit options and trade-offs — making clear that
"loosening the rule" is a configuration change, not code cleanup, so they
are never presented as the same thing. Success criteria become literal
commands instead of vague "should work" statements. Work is divided into
**waves** — groups of tasks with disjoint files, dispatched in parallel —
because a subagent only sees its own brief, never the entire planning
conversation; that is why the pitfalls list must be copied verbatim into
each one. And the final checklist is checked off only by running the
command again, never by assumption.

## How to adapt the placeholders

- **`[RULE_NAME]`** — the specific ESLint (or other linter) rule being cleared
  or reassessed — e.g. `no-unused-vars`, `complexity`, `max-lines`. If the
  burndown covers the entire warning set rather than one rule, say so
  explicitly — the prompt already supports this ("or the full warning set").
- **`[LINT_COMMAND]`** — the command that runs the linter with full output
  per file and rule. Note: some CI wrappers/proxies summarize output rather
  than displaying every line — the prompt already instructs the agent to
  use the flag or direct invocation that returns full output when needed.
- **`[TYPECHECK_COMMAND]`** — the type-checking command.
- **`[TEST_COMMAND]`** — the command that runs the test suite.
- **`[BUILD_COMMAND]`** — the build command.
- **`[STACK/FRAMEWORK]`** — a short stack description to give the agent context.

## The prompt

```
You are planning and executing a lint warning burn-down for [RULE_NAME] (or
the full warning set) in this repo. Do not start fixing anything until the
plan below is written and the decision gate in step 1 is answered.

## 0. Ground truth
Run `[LINT_COMMAND]` right now and report the actual current count — total
warnings, broken down by rule and by file. Do not reuse a number from an
earlier run, a commit message, or memory. If the output looks filtered or
truncated (some wrappers/proxies summarize instead of showing every line),
re-run with whatever flag or direct invocation gives full per-line output.

## 1. 🔴 Decision gate — answer before any implementation
Find the single riskiest or most expensive part of this burn-down — usually
one rule responsible for a large share of the count, concentrated in files
where "fixing" it is expensive or risky (e.g. a size cap tripped mainly in
generated or test files). State it with real numbers: file count, line
count, estimated new files/functions if applicable. Then present options:

- **(A) Fix every violation fully.** Default if there's no response — the
  fully-correct option is the safe assumption when scope wasn't explicitly
  narrowed.
- **(B) Fix most, track the rest as tracked debt.** Fix the cheap majority;
  leave the expensive tail as an explicit, visible exception (comment +
  issue/ticket reference), not a silent suppression.
- **(C) Re-scope or loosen the rule itself.** ⚠️ **This is a config change,
  not a warning fix — say so explicitly in the plan and in any PR. Never
  present it as if the code got cleaner.**

Wait for a decision before implementing anything in this area. Everything
outside the flagged risk area proceeds regardless of which option is picked.

## 2. Success criteria — commands, not prose
State every criterion as a command and its expected output, e.g.:
- `[LINT_COMMAND] shows 0 warnings for [RULE_NAME]`
- `[TYPECHECK_COMMAND]` clean
- `[TEST_COMMAND]` green
- **Zero behavior change.** Any fix that isn't a pure mechanical
  extraction/rename/move gets pulled out of this burn-down and flagged as
  its own item for separate human review — never folded in silently.

## 3. Break the work into waves
Group the remaining violations into ordered, file-disjoint waves. For each
task in each wave, specify: task ID, exact file scope (`Files:`), what it
depends on (`Depends-on:`, or "none"), and the specialist role that owns
it. Use the parallel wave dispatch worksheet (`05-parallel-wave-dispatch.md`
in this same folder) for the grouping rule and dispatch mechanics.

## 4. Pitfalls — copy verbatim into every task brief
List every concrete gotcha specific to this rule and this codebase — e.g. a
size cap with zero slack left in files already near the limit, a lint
cache that doesn't invalidate on config changes, an extraction that
silently widens an inferred type, a shared test fixture with many callers.
A subagent implementing one task sees only its own brief, never this
planning conversation — a pitfall not copied into the brief does not exist
for it.

## 5. Reviewer sign-off
For each wave, name every specialist reviewer required before that wave
counts as done — a domain-risk reviewer for anything security/money/auth-
adjacent, plus whatever language/framework reviewers match the files
changed. Before calling the whole burn-down complete, require a full-diff
pass by every relevant reviewer type, at the same rigor as a normal review,
not a lighter one just because it's "only" a lint fix.

## 6. Final checklist — mark only by re-running
Every box below is checked by an actually-executed command, never by
assertion:
- [ ] `[LINT_COMMAND]` shows 0 warnings for [RULE_NAME] (or the count
      agreed at the decision gate)
- [ ] `[TYPECHECK_COMMAND]` clean
- [ ] `[TEST_COMMAND]` green
- [ ] `[BUILD_COMMAND]` succeeds
- [ ] Every suppression added (`eslint-disable` or equivalent) is listed
      with its justification — or the list is empty
- [ ] Every non-mechanical fix pulled out under step 2 is listed and
      signed off — or the list is empty
- [ ] All reviewer sign-offs from step 5 are complete

Codebase: [STACK/FRAMEWORK]. Rule(s) in scope: [RULE_NAME].
```

## Usage example

Imagine a TypeScript monorepo where tightening ESLint's `complexity` rule
revealed 240 warnings across the project — 180 concentrated in six legacy
files with deeply nested conditionals. Fill it in as follows:

- `[RULE_NAME]` → `complexity`
- `[LINT_COMMAND]` → `npm run lint`
- `[TYPECHECK_COMMAND]` → `npm run typecheck`
- `[TEST_COMMAND]` → `npm run test`
- `[BUILD_COMMAND]` → `npm run build`
- `[STACK/FRAMEWORK]` → "Next.js + TypeScript monorepo"

The agent runs lint now and reports the real number (240, never from memory).
At the decision gate, it identifies the six legacy files as the expensive,
risky area, with real line and file counts, and presents the three options:
fix everything, fix most and track the rest as technical debt, or loosen
the rule's limit just for those six files (explicitly stating that this is
a config change, not code cleanup). Without your response, it assumes
option A by default and continues fixing the rest of the project while it
waits. Then it splits work into waves of disjoint files, with each known
pitfall copied into the brief (e.g. "this extraction must not change the
exported function's inferred return type"), runs specialist reviewers for
each wave, and only checks off the final checklist after actually rerunning
`[LINT_COMMAND]`, `[TYPECHECK_COMMAND]`, `[TEST_COMMAND]` and `[BUILD_COMMAND]`.

## Tips

- The decision gate in step 1 is the most tempting part to skip because it
  seems like a formality — in practice, it usually holds most of the work
  or real risk.
- Combine step 3 with
  [`05-parallel-wave-dispatch.md`](05-parallel-wave-dispatch.md) for real
  parallelism; without it, this degrades into one task at a time.
- Keep growing the pitfalls list from step 4 as you discover new ones
  during the burndown — a pitfall found in wave 2 also belongs in every
  wave from wave 3 onward.

docs/prompts/03-multi-agent-code-review..title: docs/prompts/03-multi-agent-code-review.md
docs/prompts/03-multi-agent-code-review..text:
# Multi-agent code review

## When to use

Use this prompt before merging any nontrivial change, instead of relying
on a single review pass — which inevitably favors whichever perspective
that reviewer uses by default. A security-focused reviewer tends to miss a
React hook rule violation, and vice versa. It works both for an individual
PR (*pull request*, a proposed change to merge into the project) and for
reviewing an entire branch before opening the PR.

## Why it works

Running several narrowly focused specialists in parallel finds more real
problems than one generalist pass — each lens (security, general quality,
typing, framework) sees what the others were not designed to see. But this
only works if synthesis actually discards noise rather than concatenating
everyone's output: without deduplication and a concrete failure scenario
filter, four reviewers merely produce a list four times longer and less
reliable — not four times more signal.

## How to adapt the placeholders

- **`[DIFF/PR/BRANCH]`** — the review target: a literal diff (the line-by-line
  comparison between two versions of the code), a PR number/link, or a
  branch name compared with its base.
- **`[LANGUAGE]`** — the main language of the changed code. Determines which
  language-specific typing concerns enter the review (e.g. TypeScript,
  Python, Go, Rust).
- **`[FRAMEWORK]`** — the framework used in the changed code, when the diff
  touches framework-facing code (e.g. React, Next.js, Django). The prompt
  itself already says to drop this lens when the change is purely
  backend/CLI, without any framework surface.

## The prompt

```
Review [DIFF/PR/BRANCH] using a panel of independent specialist reviewers,
then synthesize their findings into one ranked report. Do not review it
yourself first — dispatch the panel after fixing the target and scope.
Record exact base/head commit IDs, or freeze an explicit working-tree snapshot
covering staged, unstaged, and relevant untracked files. Review the diff plus
connected callers, contracts, and tests; report missing context as a limitation.
Choose lenses by risk and unresolved evidence. Respect any user-requested round
count. Stop when that scope and count are covered and findings have evidence
and disposition; do not add rounds merely to meet a universal quota.
All reviewers are read-only: no fixes, commits, or publishing. Checks that mutate
build output, test databases, ports, or services need independent resources or
must be serialized by the coordinator.

## 1. Dispatch the panel — in parallel, one batch
Send the same diff to each of these reviewer lenses at once, dropping any
that don't apply to this change:
- **General code quality** — readability, structure, error handling, dead
  code, missing test coverage.
- **Security** — OWASP Top 10, hardcoded secrets, injection, broken auth,
  unsafe deserialization, dependency CVEs.
- **[LANGUAGE] type-safety** — unsafe type assertions/casts, escape hatches
  around the type system, async/concurrency correctness, injection risk
  from unchecked input.
- **[FRAMEWORK]-specific** — e.g. component/hook rules, render performance,
  accessibility, framework-specific footguns. Only if this diff touches
  framework-facing code.

Each reviewer works independently — no reviewer sees another's findings —
and reports every finding as: `file:line — severity — one-sentence claim —
concrete failure scenario (the input or state that actually makes this
break)`. A finding with no failure scenario isn't a finding, it's a hunch;
reviewers should drop those themselves instead of padding the list.

## 2. Synthesize
Once every reviewer has reported:
1. **Dedupe** — the same underlying issue flagged by more than one reviewer
   collapses into a single entry; keep the sharpest description and note
   which reviewers agreed.
2. **Filter** — drop anything without a concrete failure scenario, or
   anything already handled elsewhere in the code. Verify against the
   frozen diff and connected code before dropping a finding — don't take a reviewer's claim
   on faith in either direction.
3. **Rank** — CRITICAL (security/data-loss, must fix before merge) → HIGH
   (real bug or significant quality issue) → MEDIUM (maintainability) →
   LOW (style/optional).

## 3. Present
One report, most severe first. Each entry: file:line, one-sentence
summary, failure scenario, severity, which reviewer(s) raised it. State
plainly if nothing survived synthesis — an empty CRITICAL/HIGH list is a
valid, useful result, not a failure to find something. Include the target
identifiers, checks performed, unreviewed scope, and residual risks. Do not
apply fixes automatically; report them for the coordinator to handle within
existing or explicit implementation authorization.

Target: [DIFF/PR/BRANCH]. Stack: [LANGUAGE] / [FRAMEWORK].
```

## Usage example

Imagine you just finished a PR adding a new API endpoint (backend) and the
React form that consumes it. Fill in:

- `[DIFF/PR/BRANCH]` → `PR #482` (or `git diff main...feature/signup-form`)
- `[LANGUAGE]` → "TypeScript"
- `[FRAMEWORK]` → "React + Next.js"

The agent dispatches the four lenses in parallel — general quality,
security (OWASP, the "Open Web Application Security Project", the reference
for the most common web vulnerabilities), TypeScript typing, and the
React/Next.js-specific lens — each reviewing the diff independently, without
seeing what the others found. Each reviewer reports findings as
`file:line — severity — sentence — concrete failure scenario`. During
synthesis, two different reviewers identify the same problem (the endpoint
does not validate a field on the server, even though the form validates it
on the client) — this becomes one entry, marked as confirmed by two
reviewers. A vague comment such as "this component could be cleaner", with
no failure scenario, is discarded. The final report is ordered by severity
— for example: CRITICAL (missing server validation, bypassed by calling the
API directly), HIGH (a new dependency with a known vulnerability — CVE),
MEDIUM (a component without error-state handling), and so on.

## Tips

- Drop reviewer lenses that do not apply — no framework lens for a pure
  backend/CLI change — instead of forcing all four every time.
- Deduplication and filtering in part 2 matter as much as the panel itself;
  four reviewers filling the list with low-confidence findings only make
  a longer, less reliable report.
- See [subagent orchestration](../tools/02-subagent-orchestration.md) to
  actually dispatch this as parallel subagents instead of sequential turns.
