# Brainstorm to plan

## When to use

Use this prompt whenever a request is open or vague enough that an agent
could reasonably build three different things from it — for example, "add
a notification system", without saying which channel (email? push? in-app?),
for whom, or when to trigger it. It works both for a raw request from a
stakeholder (the person or group interested in the outcome, inside or
outside the technical team) and an idea you sketched too quickly and have
not yet fleshed out.

## Why it works

The failure this prompt prevents is concrete: the agent reads an ambiguous
request, silently chooses the most plausible interpretation, and confidently
builds on it — the mismatch with what you really wanted appears only after
the work is finished, when undoing it costs far more than asking beforehand
would have. Separating "understanding intent", "planning" and "implementing"
into distinct phases, each with its own checkpoint, prevents ambiguity from
silently leaking from one phase into another. The first phase uses focused
Socratic questions (questions designed to help you uncover your own answer,
instead of the agent simply guessing) to establish what "done" means, what
is in and out of scope, and constraints you did not mention but probably
have; when the request allows more than one reasonable reading, the agent
presents the interpretations side by side instead of choosing one alone
and hoping to get it right. Requiring an executable verification check — a
command, a test, an observable behavior — for every plan step, instead of
"should work", prevents the agent from marking a step complete before
actually proving it.

## How to adapt the placeholders

- **`[DESCRIBE THE REQUEST HERE — as short or open-ended as it actually
  is]`** — replace with the request exactly as it reached you: a loose
  sentence, a requirement pasted straight from a conversation, or an idea
  that has not yet become a formal requirement. Do not refine the request
  before pasting it here — the more raw and ambiguous it is, the more value
  Step 1 (clarification questions) provides. If the request is already well
  defined, that is fine: the prompt itself tells the agent not to ask
  questions for their own sake when there is no real ambiguity.

## The prompt

```
Before writing any code for this request: [DESCRIBE THE REQUEST HERE — as
short or open-ended as it actually is].

Do not start implementing. Follow this sequence:

## 1. Clarify intent first
Ask a short set of pointed questions to pin down:
- What "done" actually looks like for this request.
- What's explicitly in scope vs. explicitly out of scope.
- Any constraints I haven't stated but probably have — existing patterns
  to follow, things not to touch, performance or compatibility needs.

If the request is genuinely ambiguous — more than one reasonable reading —
say so directly and lay out the interpretations side by side instead of
silently picking one and hoping it's right. Keep this round tight; don't
interrogate a request that's already clear.

## 2. Turn the clarified intent into a plan
Once scope is settled, write a step-by-step plan. Every step gets an
explicit verification check attached — a command to run, a test to pass, a
behavior to observe — never "should work." A step with no way to verify it
is a sign that step is too vague; break it down further.

## 3. Get a go-ahead
Show the plan and wait for a lightweight confirmation, or corrections,
before touching any code. A plan that changes after feedback is expected,
not a failure — re-confirm only the parts that changed.

## 4. Implement against the plan
Work through the plan in order. For each step, actually run its
verification check and show the result before checking it off — never
mark a step done because it "should" pass. If a step's verification
fails, stop and fix it before moving to the next step; don't build on an
unverified foundation.
```

## Usage example

Imagine someone casually made the following request — without saying
whether the coupon gives a fixed amount or percentage, whether multiple
coupons can be combined, or when it expires:

- `[DESCRIBE THE REQUEST HERE...]` → "add a discount coupon system to checkout."

In Step 1, the agent writes nothing — it responds with questions: "does the
coupon give a fixed amount, a percentage, or both?", "can multiple coupons
apply to the same order?", "does the coupon expire by date, usage count,
or both?" Since "fixed amount vs. percentage" is genuinely ambiguous, it
lays out both readings side by side instead of choosing on its own.

After you answer ("percentage, cannot be combined, expires only by date"),
the agent writes a plan in Step 2 with steps such as "create a coupons
table" → verification: the migration runs without errors; "validate the
coupon in the checkout endpoint" → verification: tests covering valid,
expired and nonexistent coupons pass; "apply the discount to the order
total" → verification: the calculation test passes.

In Step 3, it shows the plan and waits for your go-ahead — a simple "okay"
or a specific adjustment ("forget usage-based expiry, just the date") is
enough. Only in Step 4 does implementation begin, running and showing each
verification result before marking the step done. If the expired-coupon
test fails, it stops there, fixes it, and only then proceeds to the next
step — never building on a step it has not proven works.

## Tips

- Skip Step 1 questions when the request is already small and unambiguous —
  the prompt itself says this; do not force the ritual on a one-line fix.
- The Step 3 go-ahead should be lightweight — "go ahead" or a specific
  correction, not a full design review. Save the real scrutiny for the
  plan's verification checks.
- Combines directly with the brainstorm → plan → implementation → review
  skills in [superpowers](../tools/01-superpowers.md); this prompt is a
  portable, tool-independent version of the same discipline.

docs/prompts/05-parallel-wave-dispatch.m.text:
# Parallel wave dispatch

## When to use

Use this prompt when you already have a task list — from a plan, an epic
(a larger set of related tasks), or simply a batch of independent fixes —
and want to turn it into safe parallel execution waves (groups of tasks
running at the same time) instead of a single agent working through tasks
sequentially. It is the "fill in the blanks" version of the same pattern
in [subagent orchestration](../tools/02-subagent-orchestration.md) and the
[parallel dispatch rule template](../../templates/rules/parallel-subagent-driven-development.md).

## Why it works

Parallel waves require no cross-dependencies, disjoint writable files, and
independent mutable resources. Separate source files can still share a port,
build directory, test database, or service. Allocate independent resources or
serialize the affected work; this reduces known races, not every integration
risk. Implementers only edit and report changes. When commits are authorized,
the orchestrator alone commits, sequentially, capturing the current HEAD for
each task rather than reusing an earlier reference.

## How to adapt the placeholders

- **`[FEATURE/PLAN/TASK LIST]`** — appears twice: on the first line (what to
  split into waves) and the last ("Plan/task list:"). Paste your task list,
  plan or epic there; if it is long, repeat just a name or short summary
  the second time instead of the entire text.
- **`[BACKEND_ROLE]`, `[FRONTEND_ROLE]`, `[DB_ROLE]`, `[TEST_ROLE]`** — merely
  example roles/specialists for each task's `Owner:` field. Replace them
  with the actual specialist agent names in your project (if you use
  Claude Code with an agent table in `CLAUDE.md`, use exactly those names
  so `Owner:` already points to the right agent to dispatch). Add or remove
  roles as needed — the prompt itself says to use "whatever roles this
  project defines".

## The prompt

```
Break [FEATURE/PLAN/TASK LIST] into parallel execution waves. Follow this
exactly — the safety of running multiple agents at once depends on the
rules below, not on judgment calls made in the moment.

## 1. List every task
For each unit of work, write:
- **ID** — short and stable (T01, T02, ...).
- **Description** — one line.
- **Files:** — every path/glob this task will create or modify. Be exact;
  when in doubt, list more rather than fewer.
- **Resources:** — ports, build directories, test databases, and services
  used by implementation or checks; state isolation or `none`.
- **Depends-on:** — task IDs whose output this task needs, or `none`.
- **Owner:** — the specialist role responsible (e.g. [BACKEND_ROLE],
  [FRONTEND_ROLE], [DB_ROLE], [TEST_ROLE] — use whatever roles this
  project defines).

Any task where `Files:`, `Resources:`, or `Depends-on:` is uncertain gets `Depends-on:
everything already listed` — that's the safe default, not a shortcut to
skip filling it in.

## 2. Group into waves
Two tasks go in the **same wave** only if ALL hold:
1. Neither depends on the other, directly or transitively.
2. Their `Files:` sets are completely disjoint — zero overlap.
3. Mutable resources are independent or explicitly isolated.

If any condition fails or is uncertain, put the dependent (or file-colliding) task in a later
wave. A task with no valid same-wave partner is simply a wave of one —
that's correct, not a failure of the grouping.

Show the result as a table: wave number, task IDs in it, owner per task.

## 3. Execute each wave, in order
For every wave:
1. **Dispatch every implementer in the wave in a single batch** — this is
   what makes it parallel instead of a string of sequential turns.
2. **Implementers do not commit.** They implement, verify their own work,
   and report exactly which files changed — and stop there.
3. **When commits are authorized, the orchestrator commits**, one task at a time, in a fixed order:
   right before each commit, capture the current HEAD fresh (never reuse a
   HEAD captured earlier, never assume `HEAD~1`), stage that task's files,
   commit.
4. **That wave's reviewers run together, after all its commits exist** —
   dispatch them in one batch too, each reviewing their task's own
   before/after range and connected callers, contracts, and tests. Reviewers
   remain read-only; serialize checks sharing mutable resources. Without commit
   authorization, use recorded working-tree snapshots instead.
5. Only once every task in the wave is verified and reviewed (and committed
   when authorized), move to
   the next wave.

Plan/task list: [FEATURE/PLAN/TASK LIST].
```

## Usage example

Imagine a small project with four queued tasks. The
`[FEATURE/PLAN/TASK LIST]` placeholder becomes this list, and generic roles
(`[BACKEND_ROLE]`, `[FRONTEND_ROLE]`, `[DB_ROLE]`) become actual project agents:

- **T01** — create the `reports` database table (migration). `Files:`
  `src/db/schema/reports.ts`, `drizzle/*`. `Depends-on:` none.
  `Owner:` database-architect.
- **T02** — endpoint exporting reports as CSV, reading the `reports` table.
  `Files:` `src/app/api/reports/export/route.ts`.
  `Depends-on:` T01. `Owner:` backend-specialist.
- **T03** — "Export CSV" button on the reports screen calling the new
  endpoint. `Files:` `src/components/reports/ExportButton.tsx`.
  `Depends-on:` T02. `Owner:` frontend-specialist.
- **T04** — fix a typo in the login screen text, unrelated to the other
  three. `Files:` `src/components/auth/LoginForm.tsx`. `Depends-on:` none.
  `Owner:` frontend-specialist.

This example assumes commits are authorized; otherwise use reviewed working-tree
snapshots at the same boundaries, without committing.

In Step 2, the agent builds the waves table: T01 and T04 belong in the
**same wave**, because neither depends on the other and their files do not
overlap, assuming independent resources for their checks. The owner alone
does not establish independence. Record the concrete resource allocation in
each task brief before dispatch.
T02 can only enter a wave after T01 is committed (wave 2), and T03 only
after T02 (wave 3) — even though T03 and T04 share no files, T03 cannot enter
wave 1 because it depends on T02, which does not yet exist.

In Step 3, wave 1 dispatches the T01 and T04 implementers together in one
batch; neither commits on their own, they only report changes. The
orchestrator commits T01 and then T04 (fixed order), capturing HEAD again
before each commit. T01 and T04 reviewers then run together. Only afterward
does wave 2 (T02 alone) start — followed finally by wave 3 (T03 alone).

## Tips

- When scope or resources are uncertain, serialize the task and inspect them.
  An unrecognized dependency can still cause a race.
- A fixed commit order per wave (not "whoever finishes first") keeps HEAD
  easy to track — capture it immediately before that specific task's
  commit, never earlier.
- When two tasks genuinely cannot avoid touching the same files, take it
  as a signal to combine them into one task or isolate each in a separate
  worktree (a parallel repository copy in another folder, isolated from
  the main one) — do not force both into the same wave. Serial execution is
  also valid. Worktrees are optional and do not isolate ports, databases,
  or external services.

docs/prompts/06-memory-bootstrap.md.text:
# Memory bootstrap

## When to use

Use this prompt when starting a project from scratch — or adopting
persistent memory in an existing project — that has no memory system
between agent sessions yet. Without one, every new session relearns the
same expensive lesson an earlier session already paid to discover: a
subtle bug, an architecture decision that only makes sense with knowledge
of what was tried and rejected, or a business rule the code does not make
obvious. This is the prompt version of the pattern described in the
[Claude memory system](../tools/09-claude-memory-system.md) (the fast tier)
and [Obsidian as memory](../tools/08-obsidian-memory.md) (the long-term tier).

## Why it works

The prompt builds two tiers with different purposes. The first is a small
index automatically loaded in every session — so it must stay lean: if it
grows too large, it stops being read properly and becomes another large
file nobody opens. The second is an unlimited long-term store, consulted
on demand instead of always loaded. The "worth saving" criterion (Step 2)
is deliberately restrictive — the question is not "is this true about the
project?", but "would a future session be surprised and grateful to know
this before starting, instead of learning it the hard way?" — because the
biggest threat to a memory system is not forgetting something important,
but accumulating so much irrelevant material that nobody reads the index
anymore. The growth policy (Step 3) never lets an entry disappear without
confirmation: it is deleted from the index only after being created **and**
successfully read back from the long-term store — deleting before that
confirmation is data loss, not cleanup.

## How to adapt the placeholders

- **`[MEMORY_DIR]`** — appears three times; the folder for the fast
  (always-loaded) tier. In Claude Code, a common convention is
  `.claude/memory/` can be a custom folder — verify loading explicitly;
  prefer the active client's native memory or existing repository docs.
- **`[CONFIG_FILE]`** — the file your agent automatically loads at the start
  of every session, where memory's `INSTRUCTIONS.md` must be referenced to
  be read without asking. In Claude Code, this is usually the project's
  `CLAUDE.md`.
- **`[LINE_CAP]`** — the maximum number of nonblank lines the index may have
  before triggering the cleanup routine in Step 3. The prompt suggests
  130 as a starting point — adjust to your situation.
- **The entire conditional block in Step 4** (the bracketed paragraph
  beginning "If this project has a long-term vault/wiki already…") — this
  is not a simple blank to fill in, but a conditional instruction for the
  agent to decide by inspecting the project. If a long-term store already
  exists — a vault (a long-term notes repository such as Obsidian or
  Notion), wiki, or docs folder — replace the entire block with a direct
  sentence naming its location and access method, filling in what the
  prompt calls `[VAULT_TOOL/LOCATION]` (the store's name or location) and
  `[HOW — MCP tool, CLI, direct file edit]` (the access mechanism — an MCP
  server, short for "Model Context Protocol", the standard way an agent
  calls external tools; a CLI; or direct file editing). If none exists,
  leave the block unchanged — it already tells the agent to acknowledge
  that and deliver only tier 1, without inventing a destination the growth
  policy will eventually need.
- **`[PROJECT NAME/STACK]`** — the project name and technical stack, just
  for context (e.g. "Task management SaaS, Next.js + PostgreSQL").

## The prompt

````
Reuse the active client's native memory or existing repository docs first.
Do not add a vault, MCP server, or dependency. Verify how the client loads
the index; a folder name alone does not enable automatic memory.

Set up a two-tier memory system for this project: a small always-loaded
index for facts a session needs before it starts working, and a place for
everything else that doesn't need to load every time.

## 1. Tier one — the always-loaded index
Reuse existing equivalents; create only missing files:
- `[MEMORY_DIR]/INSTRUCTIONS.md` — the rules below, wired into whatever
  this project auto-loads at session start (e.g. [CONFIG_FILE]), so every
  session reads them without being asked.
- `[MEMORY_DIR]/MEMORY.md` — the index itself: one line per saved fact,
  linking to its own topic file.
- `[MEMORY_DIR]/` as a folder for individual topic files, each with
  frontmatter:
  ```
  ---
  name: kebab-case-slug
  description: one-line summary — used to judge relevance in a future session
  metadata:
    type: feedback | architecture | business-rule | reference
  source: path, decision record, or approved reference
  evidence: observation or check supporting the lesson
  last_verified: YYYY-MM-DD
  invalidate_when: change that would make the fact stale
  ---
  ```

## 2. What's worth saving — the narrow test
Save a memory only when the answer to this is yes: **would a future
session be surprised and grateful to know this before starting, rather
than discovering it the hard way?**

Concretely:
- Derivable by reading the code or git history → don't save it.
- A deadline, a motivation, or anything temporary to right now → don't
  save it.
- A debugging recipe that belongs in a commit message → don't save it.
- A mistake a session made that had to be corrected, an architecture
  pattern found only after failed attempts, a business rule invisible in
  the code, or where to find something outside the repo (a dashboard, a
  wiki, a channel) → save it.

Err toward not saving. A memory nobody needed is clutter; a lesson
relearned the hard way is expensive — but a small, high-signal index beats
a large, ignored one every time.

Keep temporary handoffs (objective, changed files, checks, blockers, next
step) in the task record, separate from durable memory. Promote only verified
lessons. Before using a memory, check its source and invalidation condition
against the current state; reverify or mark stale entries superseded. Never
invent evidence or verified dates, or store credentials and private dumps.

## 3. Growth policy — keep the index small forever
Before adding a new entry, count the index's non-blank lines. Past
[LINE_CAP] (e.g. 130), sanitize first:
1. Score every existing entry: recency × specificity × likelihood of
   preventing a real future mistake.
2. For each low-scoring entry, migrate it out — never just delete it —
   in this exact order:
   1. **Dedup** — search the long-term store (below) for the same topic;
      extend an existing note instead of creating a duplicate.
   2. **Match the target's template** — long-term notes may have their
      own required structure; follow it exactly.
   3. **Create** the note in the long-term store.
   4. **Confirm** — read the note back. No successful read, no deletion.
   5. **Only then** delete the entry from the index and its topic file.
3. Rewrite the index with only what's left.
4. Then add the new entry.

Deleting before the read-back confirms is data loss, not cleanup. If
unsure whether an entry still earns its place, leave it — migrating later
costs nothing.

## 4. Tier two — the long-term store
[If this project has a long-term vault/wiki already: name it explicitly —
e.g. "migrate low-value entries to [VAULT_TOOL/LOCATION], accessed via
[HOW — MCP tool, CLI, direct file edit]." If nothing like that exists yet,
say so and stop after tier one; don't invent a destination for entries the
cap will eventually need to shed.]

Project: [PROJECT NAME/STACK].
````

## Usage example

Imagine starting a task management SaaS from scratch — Next.js + PostgreSQL —
and the team already uses an internal Notion wiki for longer-term documentation:

- `[MEMORY_DIR]` → `.claude/memory`
- `[CONFIG_FILE]` → `CLAUDE.md`
- `[LINE_CAP]` → `130`
- Step 4 conditional block → "migrate low-value entries to the internal
  Notion wiki, accessed through the official integration"
- `[PROJECT NAME/STACK]` → "Task Tracker SaaS, Next.js + PostgreSQL"

The agent creates `.claude/memory/INSTRUCTIONS.md` (linked in the project's
`CLAUDE.md`), an empty `.claude/memory/MEMORY.md`, and prepares the
`.claude/memory/` folder for topic files. Two weeks later, during a session,
the agent discovers — after two failed attempts — that a race condition
(two processes competing for the same data simultaneously) only happens
because two routes write to the same table without a lock; it saves this
as an `architecture` entry in `.claude/memory/tasks-table-race-condition.md`
and adds an index line. Months later, the index exceeds 130 lines: before
adding the next entry, the agent scores the existing ones, chooses the
lowest-value entries (for example, a configuration detail now readily found
in the code), migrates each to the Notion wiki following dedup → template →
create → confirm by reading back, and only then deletes the corresponding
index entry — never the other way around.

## Tips

- The saving criterion in Step 2 is deliberately restrictive — most of what
  an agent learns during a session does not deserve permanent memory.
  Resist recording everything "just in case".
- The migrate-before-deleting order in Step 3 exists because an unconfirmed
  migration is data loss, not relocation — never skip straight to deleting
  the index entry.
- If no long-term store exists yet, deliver tier 1 only instead of inventing
  a destination — see [Obsidian as memory](../tools/08-obsidian-memory.md) for
  how to build one from scratch.

docs/prompts/07-eslint-complete-setup.md.text:
# Complete ESLint setup

## When to use

Use this prompt when you need to CONFIGURE ESLint from scratch, or review
and modernize an existing configuration with a comprehensive, opinionated
philosophy — not to clear accumulated warnings in a codebase with lint
already configured (that is [`02-eslint-warning-burndown.md`](02-eslint-warning-burndown.md),
a different, complementary prompt). Three typical scenarios: a new project
with no lint yet; a project with an old, inherited or messy configuration
needing a complete overhaul; or simply wanting this particular philosophy
(`error` for real bugs or anything always unsafe, `warn` for refactoring
pressure, custom rules for domain invariants no generic plugin covers) to
replace the existing configuration.

> [!TIP]
> If you want the result instead of the reasoning, there is a shorter path:
> [`08-eslint-quality-gates-install.md`](08-eslint-quality-gates-install.md)
> points the agent to three custom rules already written and tested in
> [`templates/eslint/`](../../templates/eslint/) — it copies instead of
> writing, so the result is always the same code. This prompt remains the
> right path when you want the agent to build the configuration by reasoning
> about your entire stack, including framework-specific rules that 08
> deliberately leaves out.

## Why it works

The core philosophy comes down to four decisions. First, there are only two
severity levels: `error` for anything always buggy or unsafe — never a
matter of taste — and `warn` for refactoring pressure and heuristics with a
real false-positive rate, which should never block a commit or fail CI.
Second, formatting stays entirely outside ESLint — quotes, semicolons and
line breaks belong to a separate formatter (Prettier, Biome, dprint), never
duplicated here. Third, type-aware linting uses a separate, focused async-safety
gate for new projects and a measured warning migration for existing code —
powerful but costly enough to exhaust memory on a constrained CI runner. Fourth, a small
number of custom rules cover architecture or domain invariants that no
off-the-shelf rule expresses — always as a last resort, only after
confirming no published plugin already solves the case.

## How to adapt the placeholders

- **`[BUILD_OUTPUT_DIRS]` / `[GENERATED_CODE_DIRS]` / `[AI_HARNESS_DIRS]`** —
  project-specific folders to ignore: build output (`.next/**`, `dist/**`...),
  generated code (`drizzle/**`, `prisma/generated/**`...), and an in-repo AI
  harness folder (`.claude/**`), if any.
- **`[RAW_LIBRARY]` / `[YOUR_WRAPPER]`** — if your project bans a raw
  dependency in favor of its own wrapper (e.g. banning direct imports of a
  date library because the project has its own date module), the name of
  the banned library and its replacement wrapper.
- **`[YOUR_DB_CLIENT_NAME]`** — your Drizzle client name, if the project uses
  Drizzle (used in `enforce-delete-with-where` and `enforce-update-with-where`).
- **`[YOUR_REACT_MAJOR]`** — the React major version installed in the project.
- **`[BOOTSTRAP_FILES]`** — files deliberately exempted from a custom rule,
  typically the logging bootstrap (the only place allowed to use
  `console.*` directly).
- **`[UI_LAYER_GLOB]` / `[DB_CLIENT_ENTRYPOINT]`** — if your project has
  architecture boundaries to protect (e.g. UI cannot import the database
  client directly), the UI layer glob and the database client entry path.
- **`[YOUR_SWITCH_COMPONENT]`** — if the project uses its own design system,
  its switch/toggle component (used in `jsx-a11y/label-has-associated-control`).
- **`[FORMATTER]`** — which formatter the project uses: `prettier`, `biome`
  or `dprint`.

## The prompt

````
# ESLint Setup Prompt — Portable

> **How to use:** paste this whole document as an instruction to a coding agent in the
> target repo (Claude Code, Cursor, etc.). Anything in `[BRACKETS]` must be adapted to
> that specific project — ask the user if it's unclear. Everything else is meant to be
> applied close to verbatim.

## Goal

Set up ESLint 9 (flat config, `eslint.config.mjs`) matching this taste:

- **Strict (`error`) on things that are always a bug or always unsafe.**
- **Lenient (`warn`) on refactoring pressure** — complexity/size budgets and
  false-positive-prone heuristics should nudge, never block a commit or fail CI.
- A small number of **project-authored rules** encode architecture/domain invariants
  that no off-the-shelf rule expresses.
- **Formatting is not ESLint's job.** A separate formatter (Prettier/Biome/dprint) owns
  quote style, semicolons, `eqeqeq`-style stuff, line-wrapping. Don't duplicate that
  here.
- **Type-aware linting is a separate, focused tier** — it's powerful but too slow
  and memory-hungry to run on every commit at scale (see §8).

Prerequisite: ESLint ≥ 9, flat config only — no `.eslintrc*` anywhere.

These severities are defaults for newly introduced rules. Inventory and reuse
existing configuration, scripts, framework presets, and CI gates. Preserve
stronger existing protections; do not downgrade errors, remove checks, or replace
working script names merely to match these examples.

## Language scope

This targets the **JavaScript/TypeScript family** — `.js/.jsx/.mjs/.cjs` and
`.ts/.tsx`, including React JSX. That's ESLint's native, first-class target, and where
essentially every rule below (core, `typescript-eslint`, `react`, `security`,
`import-x`, and all of §7's custom rules) actually applies.

ESLint *can* also lint non-JS-family content through dedicated parser plugins — Vue
SFCs, Svelte, Astro, Markdown, YAML, JSON/JSONC, GraphQL, HTML, CSS-in-JS — but none of
that is covered here. Those need their own parser and rule set, and in particular the
§7 custom rules are written directly against JS/TS/JSX AST node types
(`ImportDeclaration`, `JSXElement`, `MemberExpression`, `TSInterfaceDeclaration`, …) —
they don't translate to a different AST shape without a rewrite, not just a
find-and-replace of names.

Within the JS/TS family this scales down cleanly: React/Next.js-specific rules are
already gated behind "only if" in §0, and a plain-JavaScript project (no TypeScript)
just drops the `typescript-eslint` layer — see §0.

## 0. Detect the stack first

Don't apply every section blindly. Check the target repo for:

- TypeScript, or plain JavaScript? Assume TypeScript unless proven otherwise. **Plain
  JS, no TypeScript:** drop `...tseslint.configs.strict` (§2) and every
  `@typescript-eslint/*` rule (§3, §8) — keep the ESLint-core rules (`no-var`,
  `complexity`, `max-depth`, `max-statements`, `max-params`, `max-lines-per-function`,
  `max-nested-callbacks`, …), none of those are TS-specific.
- Not a JS/TS-family target at all (Vue SFC, Svelte, Markdown, YAML, JSON, GraphQL,
  …)? → see "Language scope" above before going further — this document doesn't cover
  those.
- React? Next.js? → only then pull in `react` / `react-hooks` / `jsx-a11y` /
  `@next/eslint-plugin-next`
- An ORM with destructive statements (Drizzle, Prisma, Knex, …)? → only then add a
  delete/update-without-where guard
- A shared component library with its own text-input primitives? → only then add §7.5
- Does the project handle money/currency? → only then add §7.4
- A layered architecture (domain/application vs. infra vs. UI)? → only then add §6

Skip whatever doesn't apply instead of forcing it in.

## 2. Base composition skeleton (`eslint.config.mjs`)

Flat config as an ordered array — **later blocks win on the same file**, which is how
several of the overrides below (test-file relaxations, one-off exemptions) are meant to
work. Take each preset as a whole unit; don't hand-pick rules out of it.

```js
import js from "@eslint/js";
import { defineConfig, globalIgnores } from "eslint/config";
import tseslint from "typescript-eslint";
import security from "eslint-plugin-security";
import importX from "eslint-plugin-import-x";
import { createTypeScriptImportResolver } from "eslint-import-resolver-typescript";
// React/Next.js only:
// import reactPlugin from "eslint-plugin-react";
// import reactHooks from "eslint-plugin-react-hooks";

// import nextPlugin from "@next/eslint-plugin-next";
// Drizzle only:
// import drizzle from "eslint-plugin-drizzle";
// Your own local rules (see §7) — CommonJS, since the flat-config loader needs a
// synchronous require for rule modules in most setups:
// import local from "./eslint-rules/local.cjs";

const testFiles = [
  "**/*{.,-}{test,spec}.{js,jsx,ts,tsx,mjs,cjs,mts,cts}",
  "**/{__tests__,__mocks__,fixtures,mocks}/**/*.{js,jsx,ts,tsx,mjs,cjs,mts,cts}",
];

export default defineConfig([
  js.configs.recommended,
  ...tseslint.configs.strict, // not just "recommended" — drop to recommended only if

  // nextPlugin.configs["core-web-vitals"],

  { languageOptions: { parserOptions: { tsconfigRootDir: import.meta.dirname } } },

  // §3 — error-tier hygiene, every source file
  {
    files: ["**/*.{js,jsx,ts,tsx,mjs,cjs}"],
    rules: { /* no-var, prefer-const, no-empty, no-restricted-imports, ... */ },
  },

  // §3 — TypeScript-specific error tier + §5 size/complexity budget, production only
  {
    files: ["src/**/*.{ts,tsx}"], // adjust to your actual source root
    rules: { /* consistent-type-imports, no-unused-vars, complexity, max-depth, ... */ },
  },

  // §3 — ORM guard, if applicable

  // §3 — security heuristics
  { files: ["src/**/*.{ts,tsx}"], plugins: { security }, rules: { /* ... */ } },

  // §6 — architecture boundaries, if applicable
  {
    plugins: { "import-x": importX, "import-x-debt": importX },
    settings: { "import-x/resolver-next": [createTypeScriptImportResolver()] },
    rules: { "import-x/no-restricted-paths": [/* ... */], "import-x-debt/no-restricted-paths": [/* ... */] },
  },

  // §7 — local custom rules
  // { files: ["src/**/*.{ts,tsx}"], plugins: { local }, rules: { "local/max-file-lines": "error", ... } },

  // Your local-rules directory itself (CommonJS)
  // {
  //   files: ["eslint-rules/**/*.cjs"],

  //   rules: { "@typescript-eslint/no-require-imports": "off" },

## 3. Severity philosophy — the actual taste

Two tiers only. Nothing in between.

**`error`** — always a bug or always unsafe, never a matter of taste:

```js
"no-var": "error",
"prefer-const": "error",
"no-empty": ["error", { allowEmptyCatch: true }],

"@typescript-eslint/no-require-imports": "error",
"@typescript-eslint/consistent-type-imports": [
  "error",
  { prefer: "type-imports", fixStyle: "inline-type-imports" },
],
"@typescript-eslint/no-unused-vars": [
  "error",
  { argsIgnorePattern: "^_", varsIgnorePattern: "^_" }, // prefix-underscore opt-out,
                                                          // instead of disabling the rule
],

// A stray interface declared inside a function body is a smell — keep shapes at
// module scope or in a shared types module:
"no-restricted-syntax": [
  "error",
  {
    selector:
      ":matches(FunctionDeclaration, ArrowFunctionExpression, FunctionExpression) TSInterfaceDeclaration",
    message: "Declare interfaces outside functions or move exported shapes to a shared types module.",
  },
],

// Ban a raw dependency your project wraps with its own helper, e.g.:
"no-restricted-imports": [
  "error",
  { paths: [{ name: "[RAW_LIBRARY]", message: "Use [YOUR_WRAPPER] instead of importing [RAW_LIBRARY] directly." }] },
],

"security/detect-eval-with-expression": "error",
"security/detect-pseudoRandomBytes": "error",

"import-x/no-unresolved": "error",
"import-x/no-duplicates": "error",

// ORM destructive-without-where guard, if the ORM has one (Drizzle does):
"drizzle/enforce-delete-with-where": ["error", { drizzleObjectName: ["[YOUR_DB_CLIENT_NAME]"] }],
"drizzle/enforce-update-with-where": ["error", { drizzleObjectName: ["[YOUR_DB_CLIENT_NAME]"] }],
```

Explicitly re-disable from `tseslint.configs.strict` if they don't fit your taste
(this source config disables both, on purpose, not by oversight):

```js
"@typescript-eslint/no-non-null-assertion": "off", // pragmatic escape hatch, allowed
"@typescript-eslint/no-empty-object-type": "off",  // {} as a loose-shape placeholder, allowed
```

**`warn`** — refactoring pressure and heuristics with a real false-positive rate. Should
surface in the editor and in `npm run lint` output, but never fail CI or block a commit:

```js
// size/complexity budget — full table in §5, all "warn"

"security/detect-possible-timing-attacks": "warn",
"security/detect-unsafe-regex": "warn",
"security/detect-child-process": "warn",
// security/detect-object-injection: deliberately SKIPPED — flags ordinary bracket
// access, too noisy; if your TS config has noUncheckedIndexedAccess, that already
// covers the real risk here.

// React, if applicable — one exception below is a real bug class, not a heuristic:
"react/jsx-key": "warn",
"react/no-array-index-key": "warn",
"react/jsx-no-target-blank": "warn",
"react/no-danger": "warn",
"react/jsx-no-leaked-render": ["error", { validStrategies: ["ternary", "coerce"] }],
// ^ this one IS "error": `count && <Badge/>` silently renders the literal text "0"
// when count is 0 — a real runtime bug, not a style nit. Forces `count > 0 && ...`
// or a ternary instead.

// jsx-a11y, if applicable — all "warn", same reasoning (real value, real false positives):
"jsx-a11y/alt-text": "warn",
"jsx-a11y/aria-props": "warn",
"jsx-a11y/aria-proptypes": "warn",
"jsx-a11y/aria-role": ["warn", { ignoreNonDOM: true }],
"jsx-a11y/aria-unsupported-elements": "warn",
"jsx-a11y/role-has-required-aria-props": "warn",
"jsx-a11y/role-supports-aria-props": "warn",
"jsx-a11y/label-has-associated-control": ["warn", { controlComponents: ["[YOUR_SWITCH_COMPONENT]"] }],
"jsx-a11y/anchor-is-valid": "warn",
"jsx-a11y/anchor-has-content": "warn",
"jsx-a11y/heading-has-content": "warn",
"jsx-a11y/click-events-have-key-events": "warn",
"jsx-a11y/no-static-element-interactions": "warn",
```

**Formatting rules do not belong here at all** — no `eqeqeq`, quote style, semicolons,
line-wrapping. If your formatter (Prettier/Biome/dprint) already owns one of these,
leave a one-line comment saying so instead of just silently omitting it — otherwise
future-you wonders why an "obvious" rule is missing.

## 4. Ignores (baseline)

```js
globalIgnores([
  "node_modules/**",
  "[BUILD_OUTPUT_DIRS]",       // e.g. .next/**, dist/**, build/**, out/**
  "coverage/**",
  "[GENERATED_CODE_DIRS]",     // e.g. drizzle/**, src/generated/**, prisma/generated/**
  "**/*.tsbuildinfo",
  "package-lock.json",
  "[AI_HARNESS_DIRS]",         // e.g. .claude/** — if an AI coding harness lives
                                // in-repo, exclude its own tooling scripts, or nearly
                                // every reported error becomes no-undef noise from
                                // Node-runtime hook scripts that never declared Node
                                // globals, drowning out real findings
]),
```

Comment **why** each entry is there, not just what it is — an unexplained ignore invites
someone to "clean it up" later and reintroduce exactly the noise it was blocking.

## 5. Size & complexity budget — the core ask

Apply to production source only (e.g. `src/**/*.{ts,tsx}`), all at **`warn`** (§3 — this
is pressure, not a gate):

| Rule | Value | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `complexity` | `12` | cyclomatic complexity ceiling per function |
| `max-depth` | `4` | nesting ceiling |
| `max-statements` | `20` | statements per function |
| `max-params` | `4` | **stays on even for test files** — a 5-parameter test helper is still a smell |
| `max-lines-per-function` | `{ max: 150, skipBlankLines: true, skipComments: true }` | |
| `max-nested-callbacks` | `3` | |

Plus one project-authored rule that is **not** a vanilla ESLint rule and is deliberately
**`error`**, not `warn` — a whole-file line-count ceiling (§7.1). The asymmetry is
intentional: a function that's grown too complex is a nudge (`warn`); a file that's
grown too large is a hard stop (`error`) — file size is cheap to check, expensive to let
rot, and has no legitimate reason to be waived the way a gnarly function sometimes does.

**Test-file relaxation** — on the shared `testFiles` globs above (`.test`, `.spec`,
`-test`, `-spec`, including `.e2e-spec`, plus test/mock/fixture directories), turn fully **`off`** (not just relaxed): `max-statements`,
`max-lines-per-function`, `max-nested-callbacks`, `@typescript-eslint/no-non-null-assertion`,
and any architecture-boundary rule from §6. Leave `max-params` on, and leave the
file-line-count rule (§7.1) on too but downgraded to `warn` with an explicit
"include tests" flag — a giant test file is still worth flagging, just not as a hard
error.

## 6. Import/architecture boundaries

If the project has a layered architecture, encode the boundaries mechanically instead of
relying on code review to catch a stray import:

```js
"import-x/no-restricted-paths": [
  "error",
  {
    zones: [
      // one entry per invariant that must NEVER regress, e.g.:
      { target: "[UI_LAYER_GLOB]", from: "[DB_CLIENT_ENTRYPOINT]" },
    ],
  },
],
```

For boundaries you're still migrating **toward** — existing violations you haven't
cleaned up yet, but don't want to get worse — register the same plugin under a second
alias and set it to `warn` instead of `error`:

```js
plugins: { "import-x": importX, "import-x-debt": importX },
rules: {
  "import-x-debt/no-restricted-paths": [
    "warn",
    { zones: [ /* boundaries you're still cleaning up */ ] },
  ],
},
```

This lets you commit to a target architecture immediately — as a visible warning
everywhere it's already violated — without a big-bang refactor to reach `error`-clean
first. Promote a zone from the `-debt` list to the `error` list once it's actually clean.

## 7. Project-authored custom rules (patterns to replicate, not copy verbatim)

Rules with no off-the-shelf equivalent, written as a small local flat-config plugin (a
CommonJS `eslint-rules/` directory, imported into `eslint.config.mjs`). Implement
whichever apply to the target project's actual domain — adapt names/paths in
`[BRACKETS]`, don't hardcode a different project's own naming into this one.

### 7.1 File-length ceiling — `error` in production, `warn` on tests

Count lines in the file; report once if over a threshold (350 is what this taste uses —
tune to the codebase). Skip `.d.ts` and generated/vendor paths. Detect forwarding/type-only
modules by their AST: imports, ESM re-exports and TypeScript interface/type declarations
only. Never exempt `index.*`, `types.*` or `constants.*` by name: runtime initializers,
functions, classes and components still count, even alongside re-exports. On test/mock/fixture
globs: same rule, but `warn`, with an explicit opt-in flag to check them at all (tests
are allowed more slack before this becomes noise).

### 7.2 No direct low-level logging in application code — `error`, exempt tests + designated bootstrap files

Ban `console.log/error/warn/info/debug/...` (and friends: `trace`, `dir`, `table`,
`group*`, `count*`, `time*`, `assert`, `profile*`) outside test files, so a structured
logger is the only sanctioned path. Carve out an explicit exemption for the 1–2 files
that ARE the logging bootstrap itself (a migration runner, an operation-log writer) via
a later config block scoped to those exact paths, setting the rule back to `"off"`.

### 7.3 No direct data-layer access from the UI layer — `error`

If there's a repository/service layer between UI and the database, flag any import of
the raw DB client/handle from UI-layer files (pages, components) — forces routing
through the service layer. Detect via the import specifier (the DB client's module
path) plus which specifiers are pulled from it (default/namespace import, or a named
binding matching the client's conventional name).

### 7.4 No native arithmetic on money-shaped values — `error` — only if the project handles currency/money

Flag `+ - * / % **` (and compound-assignment forms), unary `+`/`-`,
`Number()`/`parseFloat()`/`parseInt()`, `Math.ceil/floor/round/trunc/max/min`,
`.toFixed()`, and `.toNumber()` on any identifier/property whose **name** looks like a
money/currency value — match by word segment (camelCase-split), not substring, so e.g.
`maxConcurrency` isn't a false positive for containing "cur". The point is forcing all
arithmetic on money through a dedicated decimal-safe helper module instead of native
floating point. Exempt test files and the money-math helper module itself.

### 7.5 UI input consistency — only if there's a shared component library

- Ban raw `<input>`/`<textarea>` outside the design system's own primitive components
  (exempt semantic non-text `type`s: `checkbox`, `radio`, `file`, `hidden`, `range`,
  `date`, etc. — those aren't "text entry" in the sense this rule cares about).
- Require a `maxLength` attribute (or a spread prop, trusted to carry one) on every use
  of the shared text-input components, same exemption list. Prevents an unbounded text
  field from shipping by omission. `off` on test files.

### 7.6 Require an auth/session gate on every sensitive server entry point — `error`

For server actions / API route handlers: collect every exported handler in files
matching the sensitive-entrypoint convention (e.g. a `"use server"` file under an
actions directory, or a route handler under an API directory), and verify each is
gated — directly, or transitively through a same-file helper resolved via real ESLint
scope analysis, not string matching — by a call to one of the project's known
auth/session-check functions. Keep that "known gate functions" list as a small config
object at the top of the rule, so adding a new gate helper is a one-line edit. Known
limitation worth keeping honest about: this only proves the gate was *called*, not that
a non-throwing gate's return value was actually checked by the caller — don't oversell
what it guarantees.

## 8. Two-tier lint: fast default + focused type-aware gate

Keep `eslint.config.mjs` fast and put type-aware rules in
`eslint.typed.config.mjs`, using the [focused Next profile](../../templates/eslint/next.typed.config.mjs.example).
Type information requires a TypeScript program; measure elapsed time and peak memory
on the actual repository before expanding the rule set. Do not enable a broad
`recommendedTypeChecked` or `strictTypeChecked` preset by default.

For greenfield TypeScript projects, enable these two rules as errors and include
`lint:typed` in the explicit `check`/CI sequence:

```js
import defaultConfig from "./eslint.config.mjs";

export default [
  ...defaultConfig,
  {
    files: ["src/**/*.{ts,tsx}"], // match files included by the project's tsconfig
    languageOptions: {
      parserOptions: { projectService: true, tsconfigRootDir: import.meta.dirname },
    },
    rules: {
      "@typescript-eslint/no-floating-promises": "error",
      "@typescript-eslint/no-misused-promises": "error",
    },
  },
];
```

In an existing codebase, preserve each rule's current severity and blocking gate.
Only newly introduced rules with existing violations may begin at `warn`: record
the count, scope, runtime, and reduction plan, then promote each rule once clean.
New rules without violations start at `error`. If the current gate requires zero
warnings, measure adoption separately without weakening that gate.
The separate [advanced typed profile](../../templates/eslint/eslint.typed.config.mjs.example)
retains the broader warning rules for measured adoption; preserve those checks
when already installed rather than replacing them with the focused profile.
Keep the migration command visible; do not describe warning-only execution as a
blocking async-safety gate. Add other typed rules only for a demonstrated need.
Keep this tier out of Git hooks; this setup does not install hooks.

## 9. package.json scripts

```json
"lint": "[FORMATTER] check . && eslint . --cache",
"lint:fix": "[FORMATTER] check --write . && eslint . --fix --cache",
"lint:typed": "eslint --config eslint.typed.config.mjs ."
```

If you have local custom rules (§7) and use `--cache`: ESLint's cache invalidates on
linted-file changes but **not** on changes to the custom rule's own implementation file.
Add a tiny pre-lint script that deletes `.eslintcache` whenever a file under the
local-rules directory is newer than the cache file, or you'll silently lint against a
stale rule after editing one.

## 10. Keep checks explicit; Git hooks are opt-in

Use the package.json scripts as explicit checks. Do not install pre-commit/pre-push hooks, a hook manager, branch restrictions or push blockers as part of this setup.

Preserve existing hooks and their configuration. Only add or change Git hooks when the user specifically requests that integration. If requested, use the project's existing mechanism and keep type-aware lint outside the fast hook path.

## 11. After generating the config

Run the lint command for real, read the actual output, and fix or consciously re-tune
(don't silently loosen) whatever it flags. Don't report this as done until it's been run.

---

## What's deliberately left out

- **No character-based line-length rule (`max-len`).** This taste enforces line *count*
  (file/function size — §5, §7.1), not line *width*. If the target project wants a
  character cap per line, that's an intentional addition on top of this, not something
  carried over from here.
- **No formatting rules of any kind** in ESLint — quote style, semicolons, `eqeqeq`,
  wrapping. That's a separate formatter's job (§3).
- **No broad type-aware preset** — the separate greenfield gate checks two async
  hazards; existing code adopts them through measured warnings (§8).
````

## Usage example

Imagine a new Next.js + TypeScript + Drizzle project that has never had
ESLint configured — only the default linter from `create-next-app`, never
customized. Fill in the placeholders roughly as follows:

- `[BUILD_OUTPUT_DIRS]` → `.next/**`
- `[GENERATED_CODE_DIRS]` → `drizzle/**`
- `[YOUR_DB_CLIENT_NAME]` → `db`
- `[YOUR_REACT_MAJOR]` → `19`
- `[FORMATTER]` → `biome`
- `[UI_LAYER_GLOB]` / `[DB_CLIENT_ENTRYPOINT]` → fill in only if the project
  already separates UI and data-access layers; otherwise skip all of §6

The agent detects the stack (§0: TypeScript + React/Next.js + Drizzle, so it
keeps the `typescript-eslint` layer, React/a11y plugins and Drizzle guard
rule), installs the right dependencies (§1), and builds a complete
`eslint.config.mjs` following §2's skeleton — with §3's two-tier philosophy,
§4's ignores, §5's complexity budget, and the custom rules in §7 that make
sense for the project (at least §7.1, the per-file line ceiling, and §7.2,
the direct `console.log` ban). Since the project uses Drizzle but has no
layer boundaries or custom text component yet, §6 and §7.5 are left out.
The expected result is an actually runnable `eslint.config.mjs` — not a
skeleton with `TODO`s — plus an `eslint.typed.config.mjs` with
§8's focused rules in a separate `lint:typed` script, included in greenfield
`check`/CI and measured before promotion in legacy code. Finally, the agent actually runs lint (§11) and reports the real
output rather than assuming it worked.

## Tips

- This is orthogonal to the [warning burndown prompt](02-eslint-warning-burndown.md)
  — use this first for a good configuration from the start, and that one
  later, when warnings accumulate and it is time to clear a specific rule.
- §0 ("Detect the stack first") prevents the agent from applying whole
  sections that do not fit the project — check that it really skipped what
  it should before accepting the result.
- The final section, "What's deliberately left out", is not a minor detail:
  it makes clear that omitting `max-len` and formatting rules is intentional,
  not an oversight — useful to point to if someone later asks "where is the
  line-length rule?".

docs/prompts/08-eslint-quality-gates-ins.text:
# Install ESLint quality gates (350-line ceiling)

## Shortcut: just the link

If you do not want to copy a prompt, paste this line into your agent. It
works with any agent that can read a URL — Claude Code, Codex, Cursor:

```
Read https://raw.githubusercontent.com/soumatheusgomes/vibe-coding-toolkit/main/docs/prompts/08-eslint-quality-gates-install.md
and execute the prompt in that file in this project. Use MAX_LINES=350
and the package manager you find in the repository.
```

The rest of this document contains the same prompt in full, for those who
prefer to paste the entire text or adapt it first.

## When to use

Use this prompt when you want the three lint rules this toolkit advocates
running in any JavaScript or TypeScript project — a file-size ceiling, a
ban on direct `console` calls, and a ban on the presentation layer importing
the database client — without reconstructing the reasoning behind them.

The difference from [`07-eslint-complete-setup.md`](07-eslint-complete-setup.md)
is scope. Prompt 07 evaluates the whole stack and reuses the relevant
profiles, including framework rules. This one focuses on three existing,
tested `.cjs` files to copy and connect. Use it when you want the 350-line
ceiling and local boundaries installed with a measured adoption baseline.

After installation, the natural next step is
[`09-file-size-refactor.md`](09-file-size-refactor.md) — it tells the agent
to split the files exceeding the ceiling.

## Why it works

The hard part of a custom lint rule is not the idea, but the code. A rule
written on the fly from a description fails silently: it exempts too many
or too few test files, does not know that the size of an `index.ts` that
only re-exports has no meaningful limit, and reports at the wrong position.
None of these errors looks like a failure — it looks like a rule that
"catches nothing" or "catches everything", and someone turns it off.

The ceiling identifies barrels through the AST, without exempting `index.*`,
`types.*` or `constants.*` by name. Imports, ESM re-exports and type
declarations with no logic of their own may be exempt; executable code
counts. The `.test`, `.spec`, `-test` and `-spec` suffixes (including
`.e2e-spec`) and test directories share the three rules' classification.
`includeTests` measures those tests with their own budget.

When updating an existing installation, recopy the three `.cjs` files from
the same revision, run the self-check and measure the baseline again:
modules with logic previously exempted by name may start appearing in the
report. Updating this toolkit does not change copies already installed in
other projects.

That is why the prompt does not ask the agent to write rules. It asks it to
copy. The agent decides only what actually depends on your project: where
the presentation layer lives, which module exports the database client,
which file is the log adapter, and which directories to ignore.

The final step is measuring, not fixing. The prompt tells the agent to run
the linter, count violations per rule, and choose severity from that count:
a rule with zero violations starts as `error`; a rule with violations starts
as `warn`, with the count recorded as a baseline. A gate that starts red
because of preexisting code is not a gate, but noise someone will disable
by the first Friday.

## How to adapt the placeholders

This prompt deliberately has few placeholders — step 1 tells the agent to
discover almost everything it needs by reading the project.

- **`[MAX_LINES]`** — the per-file line ceiling. The toolkit default is
  `350`. Below ~200, the rule constantly fights legitimate code; above
  ~500, it stops applying pressure.
- **`[PACKAGE_MANAGER]`** — `npm`, `pnpm`, `yarn` or `bun`. If unsure, leave
  `npm` and the agent will correct it after reading the project.
- **`[SOURCE_URL]`** — where the agent gets the files. If you cloned this
  repository, use the local path `templates/eslint`. Otherwise, use the
  GitHub raw URL already filled in the prompt.

## The prompt

```
Install this project's ESLint quality gates by COPYING pre-written rule
files, not by writing rules from scratch. The rules already exist and are
already tested; your job is to place them and adapt the configuration to
this project's real shape.

## 0. Get the files

Fetch these six files into a temporary location from the same revision of
[SOURCE_URL] (default:
https://raw.githubusercontent.com/soumatheusgomes/vibe-coding-toolkit/main/templates/eslint):

  eslint-rules/utils.cjs
  eslint-rules/core-rules.cjs
  eslint-rules/index.cjs
  eslint.config.mjs.example
  eslint.typed.config.mjs.example
  verify.mjs

After inspecting the project in step 1, place or merge them like this;
preserve existing configuration, scripts, and protections:

  ./eslint-rules/utils.cjs
  ./eslint-rules/core-rules.cjs
  ./eslint-rules/index.cjs
  ./eslint.config.mjs          (from eslint.config.mjs.example)
  ./eslint.typed.config.mjs    (from eslint.typed.config.mjs.example, TypeScript only)
  ./verify.mjs                 (temporary; delete after step 5)

Copy the .cjs files byte for byte. Do not reformat them, do not convert
them to ESM, do not merge them into one file, do not "improve" them. They
are CommonJS on purpose so ESLint loads them with no build step. If you
rewrite them, this prompt has failed.

## 1. Read the project before changing anything

Report what you found before continuing:

- package manager, existing lint script, existing ESLint version
- whether this is TypeScript, and what path aliases tsconfig.json defines
- the source root: src/, app/, lib/, or the repository root
- the presentation layer: which directories hold UI or route entrypoints
- the data module: which file exports the database/ORM client, and under
  what name
- the log adapter: the module the project already logs through, if any

If the project is on ESLint 8 or older, stop and say so. The config uses
defineConfig and globalIgnores from eslint/config, which do not exist
before ESLint 9.

If there is no data module, say so and remove the
quality/no-direct-data-access rule instead of inventing a boundary this
project does not have.

## 2. Install dependencies

  [PACKAGE_MANAGER] i -D eslint@^9 @eslint/js@^9
  # TypeScript projects:
  [PACKAGE_MANAGER] i -D typescript-eslint
  # Only if enforcing import boundaries:
  [PACKAGE_MANAGER] i -D eslint-plugin-import-x eslint-import-resolver-typescript

Pin @eslint/js to the same major as eslint. Unpinned, the installer picks
@eslint/js@10, whose peer range demands eslint@10, and the install fails
with ERESOLVE.

## 3. Adapt eslint.config.mjs

Every item here is a real edit against what step 1 found, not a review:

- the `files` globs, if the source root is not src/
- quality/max-lines: set `max` to [MAX_LINES]
- quality/no-direct-data-access: set `modules` to the real import
  specifiers of the data module, `bindings` to the real exported client
  name, `layers` to the real presentation directories, `extensions` to
  the component file extension (drop `extensions` entirely on a
  non-React project)
- the import-x zones: rewrite them for this project's real layers, or
  delete the whole import-x block if the project has no layering yet. If
  you delete it, also delete its two imports at the top of the file and
  its two entries in the test-file block, or ESLint fails on an unknown
  rule id
- the quality/no-direct-console "off" block: point it at the real log
  adapter, or delete the block if there is none
- the `globals` list: add what this project's runtime actually provides
- globalIgnores: add this project's build output directories

Two failure modes that are completely silent when you get them wrong.
First, a block that turns a rule `off` must come AFTER the block that
turns it on — for a file matched by both, flat config applies the later
block last, so an `off` placed earlier is overridden without any warning.
Second, `except` inside a no-restricted-paths zone is relative to `from`;
it carves files out of `from` and cannot exempt an importer. To exempt an
importer, narrow `target`.

## 4. Wire the scripts

  "lint": "eslint ."
  "lint:fix": "eslint . --fix"
  "lint:typed": "eslint --config eslint.typed.config.mjs ."

Omit lint:typed on a JavaScript project; preserve an equivalent existing
script name. Keep the type-aware tier separate from the fast lint command
and measure its runtime/memory on the actual runner before selecting its
CI scope. Preserve an existing typed gate. Do not add Git hooks.

## 5. Verify the copy survived

  node verify.mjs

Expected: three lines ending in ": ok", exit code 0. Anything else means
the copy is broken — fix it before going further. Delete verify.mjs
afterwards, or keep it and wire it into the test script; do not leave it
lying around unexplained.

## 6. Run the linter and MEASURE

  [PACKAGE_MANAGER] run lint

Report the count per newly introduced rule. Preserve existing severities;
do not downgrade an established protection or add ignores to hide violations.
For the new rules, set severities from the count:

- zero violations for a rule: leave it at "error"
- violations exist: drop that rule to "warn" and write the count in a
  comment next to it. That count is the baseline, and the migration is
  finished when it reaches zero and the rule goes back to "error"
- keep existing exceptions scoped and documented; do not add generic
  exclusions or increase ceilings to manufacture a passing result

## 7. Report

State: which rules were installed, which were skipped and why, the
violation count per rule, which rules are at "warn" with a baseline, the
list of files over the [MAX_LINES]-line budget sorted by size, and the
exact commands to run the linter.

## Rules for you, the agent

Do NOT fix any violation you found. Installing the gate and measuring what
it catches is the entire job. Refactoring is separate work with its own
review.

Do NOT raise [MAX_LINES] to make a file pass. Leave existing offenders
reported with the measured adoption baseline.

Do NOT enable a framework preset because it exists. Uncomment a block only
for a framework this project actually uses.
```

## Usage example

Imagine a Next.js TypeScript project with the `@/*` alias, the database
client in `src/db/index.ts` exported as `db`, components in `src/components/`
and routes in `src/app/`. Fill in:

- `[MAX_LINES]` → `350`
- `[PACKAGE_MANAGER]` → `npm`
- `[SOURCE_URL]` → the default raw URL, already filled in the prompt

The agent downloads the six files, reads `tsconfig.json` and discovers the
alias itself, points `modules` to `@/db`, `layers` to `/src/app/` and
`/src/components/`, runs `node verify.mjs` (three `ok`s), runs lint, and
returns something like: `quality/no-direct-console` has zero violations,
stays at `error`; `quality/no-direct-data-access` has two violations, drops
to `warn` with the count recorded; `quality/max-lines` has eleven files over
350 lines, listed largest first. It stops there — fixes nothing.

That eleven-file list is exactly the input for
[`09-file-size-refactor.md`](09-file-size-refactor.md).

## Tips

- If the agent rewrites the `.cjs` files instead of copying them, have it
  redo the work. The whole point is that these three rules always use the
  same tested code — a rule written on the fly fails silently.
- Run `node verify.mjs` before trusting any violation count. If the rules
  arrived broken, clean lint output means nothing.
- Install just `quality/max-lines` first if the project is large and you
  want one gate at a time. All three are independent.
- The full reasoning behind these choices — why warnings become errors,
  why architecture boundaries belong in lint — is in
  [`../tools/06-eslint-biome-quality-gates.md`](../tools/06-eslint-biome-quality-gates.md).

docs/prompts/09-file-size-refactor.md.text:
# Split the giant files revealed by the line ceiling

## Shortcut: just the link

After prompt 08 measures and gives you the list of files above the ceiling,
paste this line:

```
Read https://raw.githubusercontent.com/soumatheusgomes/vibe-coding-toolkit/main/docs/prompts/09-file-size-refactor.md
and execute the prompt in that file in this project. Use MAX_LINES=350,
BATCH_SIZE=3 and RULE_ID=quality/max-lines. Discover the lint, test and
typecheck commands by reading package.json yourself.
```

The rest of this document contains the same prompt in full.

## When to use

Use this prompt after the per-file size ceiling is installed and the linter
has identified the files exceeding it — usually right after
[`08-eslint-quality-gates-install.md`](08-eslint-quality-gates-install.md).
This is the second phase: 08 installs the ruler and measures; this prompt
tells the agent to take the files that did not fit and turn them into
smaller, isolated modules.

Do not use it for clearing lint warnings in general — that is
[`02-eslint-warning-burndown.md`](02-eslint-warning-burndown.md), which is
broader and works rule by rule. This prompt only concerns file size,
because splitting an 800-line file is different work from fixing 240
`complexity` warnings: every change here moves code between files, which
is where behavior changes hide.

## Why it works

The question that makes this work go wrong is always the same: *where to
cut*. An agent without guidance cuts where the line count dictates — takes
200 lines from the end, puts them in `utils.ts`, and produces two files
that only make sense when read together. The file passes lint and the code
gets worse.

That is why the prompt defines the split by responsibility, not line
number, using the same four seams the rule's own message suggests: business
logic becomes a domain service, repeated UI becomes a subcomponent, data
access becomes a repository, and a cluster of helpers becomes a domain
utility module. If none of these seams exists in the file, the instruction
is to say so and stop — inventing an abstraction just to satisfy the linter
trades a visible problem for an invisible one.

The second mechanism is pacing: **one file at a time, one commit per file**,
with tests and type checks between each. Splitting six files in one commit
means that when something breaks, you do not know which extraction caused
it. The third is preservation: the original file's public exports remain,
with the same names and signatures. Importers should not even know the
file was split.

Finally, the prompt requires the final count to come from rerunning the
command, never from mentally adding up what was done.

## How to adapt the placeholders

- **`[LINT_COMMAND]`** — the command that runs lint with full output per file
  and rule. Some CI wrappers summarize output; if yours does, invoke it
  directly.
- **`[TEST_COMMAND]`** — the test suite command.
- **`[TYPECHECK_COMMAND]`** — the type-checking command. For plain JavaScript,
  write `none` and the prompt skips this step.
- **`[MAX_LINES]`** — the ceiling configured in the rule. Toolkit default:
  `350`.
- **`[BATCH_SIZE]`** — how many files to split before stopping and showing
  you the result. Start with `3`. Increasing this before trusting the first
  three results is the fastest way to accumulate a diff nobody reviews.
- **`[RULE_ID]`** — the size rule's ID. If installed through prompt 08, it is
  `quality/max-lines`.

## The prompt

```
Split the files that exceed this project's per-file size budget into
smaller, focused modules. This is behavior-preserving refactoring, not a
rewrite and not a feature change.

## 0. Ground truth

Run [LINT_COMMAND] and list every file reported by [RULE_ID], with its
actual line count, sorted largest first. Use the real output from running
it now. Never a count from memory, from a previous message, or from a
summary — if the command's output is truncated by a wrapper, run the
linter directly until you have the full list.

Report that list before touching anything.

## 1. Pick the batch

Take the [BATCH_SIZE] largest files. Do not start on any others.

For each one, before editing, state:
  - what the file is responsible for today, in one sentence
  - the seams you found, and which one you will cut on
  - what its public exports are (the names other files import from it)

## 2. Where to cut

Cut on responsibility, never on line count. The four seams worth looking
for, in this order:

  - business logic mixed into a UI or route file -> a domain service or
    use-case module
  - a repeated block of UI -> a reusable sub-component
  - data access (queries, ORM calls, raw SQL) -> a repository or adapter
  - a cluster of helpers that only serve one concept -> a
    domain-specific utility module

If a file has no seam — it is one long, genuinely cohesive
implementation — say so, leave it alone, and move to the next file. Adding
an abstraction that exists only to satisfy the linter makes the codebase
worse than the long file did. Report it as "no natural seam" and let a
human decide.

Never split at an arbitrary line number to get under the budget. A file
named helpers.ts, utils.ts, misc.ts or common.ts holding whatever was
left over is a failure, not a result.

## 3. Preserve the interface

After the split, the original file's public exports must still exist,
with the same names and the same signatures. Prefer leaving the original
file as a thin module that re-exports from the new ones over editing
every import site across the codebase.

Rewriting import sites is allowed only when the original file is meant to
disappear entirely, and only when you say so explicitly before doing it.

## 4. One file at a time

For each file in the batch, in order:

  a. make the split
  b. run [TYPECHECK_COMMAND] (skip if it is "none")
  c. run [TEST_COMMAND]
  d. run [LINT_COMMAND] and confirm the file is no longer reported, and
     that no NEW violation appeared anywhere
  e. commit, with a message naming the file and the seam you cut on
  f. only then move to the next file

If b, c, or d fails, fix it before moving on. Do not proceed with a
failing check and do not batch the fixes at the end.

Watch for a specific trap in step d: extracting code frequently trades one
violation for another. A function pulled out of a long file can push its
new home over the budget, and an extraction can change a function's
inferred return type, which surfaces as a type error rather than a lint
error. Both are your problem, in the same commit.

## 5. Stop and report

After [BATCH_SIZE] files, stop. Do not continue into the next batch on
your own.

Report:
  - the files you split, and the seam used for each
  - the files you deliberately did NOT split, and why
  - the output of [LINT_COMMAND] run one final time: how many files are
    still over the budget, and their names
  - any violation of another rule that appeared as a side effect

Mark nothing as done that you did not verify by running the command again.

Codebase: [STACK/FRAMEWORK]. Budget: [MAX_LINES] lines. Rule: [RULE_ID].
```

## Usage example

Imagine prompt 08 just reported eleven files above 350 lines in a Next.js
app, the largest being a 780-line `src/app/dashboard/page.tsx`. Fill in:

- `[LINT_COMMAND]` → `npm run lint`
- `[TEST_COMMAND]` → `npm test`
- `[TYPECHECK_COMMAND]` → `npm run typecheck`
- `[MAX_LINES]` → `350`
- `[BATCH_SIZE]` → `3`
- `[RULE_ID]` → `quality/max-lines`

The agent lists the actual eleven files, takes the three largest, and
reports for `page.tsx`: current responsibility "builds the dashboard and
also calculates balance aggregates"; seams found "aggregate calculations
(business logic) and three repeated metric cards (UI)"; public exports
"default `DashboardPage`". It extracts aggregates to a domain module and
cards to a subcomponent, preserves `export default`, runs typecheck, tests
and lint, confirms no new warnings, and commits. Then it handles the second
file. In the third, it finds a 400-line parser that is one cohesive state
machine — reports "no natural seam", leaves it untouched, and stops. At
the end, it says eight files remain above the ceiling and lists them.

## Tips

- A low `[BATCH_SIZE]` is not excessive caution: it keeps the diff at a size
  a human actually reviews. Three files per round, one commit per file,
  gives six recovery points if something goes wrong.
- When the agent says "no natural seam", read the file before disagreeing.
  Sometimes it is right, and the right action is adding that specific file
  to the rule's `ignore` instead of chopping it up.
- Combine with [`03-multi-agent-code-review.md`](03-multi-agent-code-review.md)
  at the end of each batch — extraction is exactly the kind of change
  where a separate reviewer sees what the extractor misses.
- The pitfalls in step 4d have concrete code examples in
  [`../tools/06-eslint-biome-quality-gates.md`](../tools/06-eslint-biome-quality-gates.md)
  — worth reading before the first round.
