# Official Anthropic skills

## What it is

An **Agent Skill** (a new capability the agent gains) is a folder containing an instruction file, `SKILL.md`, and optionally scripts and other resources (templates, examples, references) that teach an AI agent to perform a specific, repeatable task well: generating a document with a visual standard, following your team's data analysis workflow, or automating a recurring personal task. The key difference from an instruction pasted into a conversation is **on-demand loading**: a skill only enters the context window (the amount of text the model can “see” at once, which you pay for with each message) when the user's request matches it. It does not remain active unnecessarily when nobody needs that capability.

[`anthropics/skills`](https://github.com/anthropics/skills) is Anthropic's official public repository for these packages. Evaluate the source, license, host support, and usefulness for your task; popularity is not an installation or compatibility criterion.

### Skills, plugins, and MCP servers are different things

All three frequently appear together in Claude Code's vocabulary, but solve different problems:

| Concept | What it is | Where it runs |
|---|---|---|
| **Skill** | An instruction folder (+ optional scripts/resources), loaded only when the user's request matches | Inside the agent, using its existing tools (terminal, file reading/writing...), with no external process |
| **Plugin** | An installable package that can bundle **multiple** skills, slash commands (“/”), and hooks (scripts running automatically before/after an agent action) into one installation | Registered once in Claude Code; activates everything it bundles together |
| **MCP server** (*Model Context Protocol*, a standardized protocol exposing external tools and data to an AI agent) | A **separate external** program providing access to an external tool or data source: a GitHub server, library documentation, or database | Outside the agent, as a separate process; the agent connects through the protocol and never runs its code directly |

In practice, this repository combines the first two concepts: each individual skill (`docx`, `skill-creator`, and so on) is simply a folder with a `SKILL.md`, but installation in Claude Code groups them into **plugins**, each bundling several related skills (details under “How to install/activate” below).

### The repository documenting the format itself

Alongside ready-made skills, `anthropics/skills` is a reference for the **`SKILL.md`** format itself, the same file structure used by other vendored skills (copied into the project) documented in this toolkit: [Graphify](07-graphify.md) provides `.claude/skills/graphify/SKILL.md`, and [agent-browser](11-agent-browser.md) provides `.claude/skills/agent-browser/SKILL.md`. `SKILL.md` follows an **open standard** (a public specification not tied to one tool), documented at [agentskills.io](https://agentskills.io) and usable by any compatible AI agent, beyond Claude Code. The [official Claude Code documentation](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/skills) confirms it uses this standard as a foundation and adds its own features.

The minimum `SKILL.md` format has just two essential fields in a YAML metadata block (*frontmatter*, a readable data format common in configuration files), between `---`: `name` (the skill identifier) and `description` (what it does and when to use it, which the agent reads to decide whether the skill matches the current request). The Markdown body follows the frontmatter and contains the actual instructions:

```yaml
---
name: skill-name
description: What this skill does and when the agent should use it.
---

Instructions, examples, and best practices the agent follows while the skill is active.
```

## Why use it

Installing this particular repository, instead of a random standalone skill, addresses three things at once:

1. **An official source maintained by Anthropic itself.** This is not a third-party collection guessing the correct format: it comes from those defining the standard, making it a reliable reference for doing things correctly before writing your own skills.
2. **Office document skills address a real everyday gap.** `docx`, `pdf`, `pptx`, and `xlsx` generate and edit these actual formats, rather than simplified plain-text substitutes. They help anyone using an AI agent to assemble reports, presentations, or spreadsheets who currently has to convert its text manually.
3. **Two “meta” skills teach you to extend the ecosystem itself.** `skill-creator` guides the creation of your own skills; `mcp-builder` guides the construction of your own MCP server (the external component in the table above). This completes the cycle: beyond consuming ready-made skills, the repository teaches you to create your own.

One caveat before installation: **no single license covers the entire repository**. See “Tips and pitfalls” below for details.

## What the repository contains

The table illustrates the repository's plugin families. Read the current [marketplace manifest](https://github.com/anthropics/skills/blob/main/.claude-plugin/marketplace.json) and each skill's frontmatter before selecting packages; names and grouping can change:

| Plugin (in the `anthropic-agent-skills` marketplace) | What it bundles | Included skills |
|---|---|---|
| `document-skills` | Document workflows | `xlsx`, `docx`, `pptx`, `pdf` |
| `example-skills` | Creative, technical, and corporate example skills | `algorithmic-art`, `brand-guidelines`, `canvas-design`, `doc-coauthoring`, `frontend-design`, `internal-comms`, `mcp-builder`, `skill-creator`, `slack-gif-creator`, `theme-factory`, `web-artifacts-builder`, `webapp-testing` |
| `claude-api` | Claude API/SDK documentation for building LLM applications (*Large Language Model*, the type of AI behind Claude) | `claude-api` |

Within `example-skills`, the most commonly mentioned skills beyond document work include:

- **`skill-creator`** creates, edits, and optimizes your own skills (see Example 2 below).
- **`mcp-builder`** guides building an MCP server from scratch in TypeScript or Python (see Example 3 below).
- **`web-artifacts-builder`** builds more elaborate Artifacts (HTML pages rendered inside Claude/Claude.ai) with React, TypeScript, Tailwind, and shadcn/ui (a ready-made UI component collection used with Tailwind), including design guidance to avoid generic AI visuals: always-centered layouts, purple gradients, and identically rounded corners.
- **`webapp-testing`** tests local web applications with Playwright (a browser automation framework): frontend functionality, screenshots, and browser logs.
- **`frontend-design`, `canvas-design`, `algorithmic-art`, `theme-factory`** cover creativity and visual design.
- **`brand-guidelines`, `internal-comms`, `doc-coauthoring`, `slack-gif-creator`** target corporate workflows and communication.

Notice the actual name is **`web-artifacts-builder`**, with the `web-` prefix, rather than just `artifacts-builder`.

## How to install/activate

Inside a Claude Code session, register the repository as a marketplace (a source for installing plugins), then install the package you need:

```bash
/plugin marketplace add anthropics/skills
/plugin install document-skills@anthropic-agent-skills
```

The first command registers the GitHub repository as an installable marketplace; the second installs `document-skills`, all four Office document skills together. Repeat `/plugin install` for either of the other packages if desired:

```bash
/plugin install example-skills@anthropic-agent-skills
/plugin install claude-api@anthropic-agent-skills
```

You can also install through the interface without memorizing package names: after `/plugin marketplace add`, choose **Browse and install plugins** → **anthropic-agent-skills** → your package → **Install now**.

Confirm what is available in the current session:

```bash
/skills
```

After installation, there is no specific command to “activate” a skill: ask for the task normally and describe what you want. Claude Code uses each skill's `description` to decide which matches the request:

```
Use the PDF skill to extract the form fields from report.pdf.
```

You can also invoke a specific skill directly by name using `/plugin-name:skill-name`, for example `/document-skills:docx`, instead of describing the task and letting Claude Code choose. The colon format (plugin:skill) prevents name collisions between skills from different plugins.

### Install a single skill without the entire package

`example-skills` includes 12 skills. If you only want `skill-creator`, for example, without the other 11, you can vendor (copy into your project) just that skill's folder instead of installing the entire plugin. This is the pattern already used in this toolkit for [Graphify](07-graphify.md) and [agent-browser](11-agent-browser.md), except you copy a folder instead of running an installer:

> 💬 **Ask your agent to install it:**
>
> ```
> Download skill-creator from anthropics/skills and install it in
> my project: shallow-clone https://github.com/anthropics/skills.git
> (--depth 1) into a temporary folder, copy only skills/skill-creator
> to .claude/skills/skill-creator/, then remove the temporary folder.
> ```
>
> Claude Code has terminal (Bash) and file-writing access: it clones, copies the relevant folder, and confirms success. Prefer doing it yourself? Here are the exact commands:

```bash
git clone --depth 1 https://github.com/anthropics/skills.git /tmp/anthropics-skills
mkdir -p .claude/skills
cp -r /tmp/anthropics-skills/skills/skill-creator .claude/skills/skill-creator
rm -rf /tmp/anthropics-skills
```

A project skill (`.claude/skills/<name>/`) is versioned with the repository, so everyone on the team using Claude Code in that project gets it automatically. One caveat: if `.claude/skills/` did not exist before the current Claude Code session started, restart the session after creating it. Only skill folders present at session start are watched live; new folders require a restart ([source](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/skills)).

## Step-by-step tutorial

Let's install the document package and generate a real `.docx` report from scratch. The example is generic, a quarterly report, but the workflow applies to any content.

### 1. Install the document package

```bash
/plugin marketplace add anthropics/skills
/plugin install document-skills@anthropic-agent-skills
```

### 2. Request the report and describe its required content

Inside any project, with data available (a table pasted into the conversation, a spreadsheet, or a CSV):

```
Create a Word report (report.docx) with a TOC (table of contents,
 the clickable index at the beginning of a long document) at the
start, three sections with level 1 headings, a table showing sales
by quarter, and page numbers in the footer.
```

### 3. What happens behind the scenes

The `docx` skill's `description` covers this exact kind of request: creating, reading, editing, or manipulating Word documents. Claude Code therefore loads it automatically without an explicit invocation. It then:

1. Builds the `.docx` from scratch using the `docx` library (a ready-made npm/Node.js package that constructs the internal structure of a Word file);
2. If editing an existing document instead, opens the file, directly modifies its internal XML (`word/document.xml`: underneath, a `.docx` is a folder of XML files compressed as a ZIP), and repackages it;
3. Renders the result as images (through `pdftoppm`) to visually check it matches the request before returning the final file.

Source: [`skills/docx/SKILL.md`](https://github.com/anthropics/skills/blob/main/skills/docx/SKILL.md).

### 4. Check the generated file

Open `report.docx` in a real editor (Word, LibreOffice, Google Docs) and check the clickable table of contents, three sections, table with correct numbers, and footer page numbers. If something is wrong, describe it and request a correction: this edits the same file rather than regenerating it from scratch.

## Examples

### Example 1 — an `.xlsx` spreadsheet with formulas from raw data

Scenario: you have a raw list of product sales pasted from somewhere and want a real spreadsheet with formulas, rather than externally calculated numbers.

```
I installed document-skills. Here is a list of product sales
(pasted below). Build sales.xlsx with a detail sheet (one row
per product) and a summary sheet, using real formulas
(=SUM, =AVERAGE) to aggregate by category, rather than manually
precalculated values.
```

The `xlsx` skill creates the file with native Excel formulas. When opening it in Excel or Google Sheets, clicking a total cell shows `=SUM(...)`, rather than an already-resolved static number.

### Example 2 — create your own skill with `skill-creator`

Scenario: whenever you finish a task in your project, you follow the same manual steps to write a changelog entry (the file listing changes in each version), and want to turn this into your own reusable skill.

```
I installed example-skills. Use skill-creator to create a new skill:
whenever I finish a task, it should read the changes in `git diff`
and write a changelog entry using the format
"### <date> — <one-line summary>" plus bullets describing the changes,
in CHANGELOG.md.
```

Instead of writing `SKILL.md` manually, `skill-creator` conducts an interview before generating anything: what the skill should do, when it should trigger, and the expected output format. Only then does it write the folder structure (`SKILL.md` and, if supporting code is needed, `scripts/`) and suggest test requests to validate its triggering and behavior before calling it ready.

### Example 3 — build an MCP server with `mcp-builder`

Scenario: you have an internal API (for tasks, customers, or anything else) and want to expose its operations as tools any MCP-compatible AI agent can call, beyond Claude Code.

```
I installed example-skills. Use mcp-builder to help me create a
TypeScript MCP server exposing my internal task API (list, create,
mark complete) as tools.
```

`mcp-builder` guides four phases: research and plan the API design before writing code, implement the infrastructure and tools with clearly defined input/output formats, review quality and test, then create *evals* (automated tests checking whether an LLM can use the tool correctly) proving that an AI agent can actually operate the generated server.

## Tips and pitfalls

**No single license covers the entire repository.** The root of `anthropics/skills` contains `README.md` and `THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md`, with no general `LICENSE` file. Individual skills can have their own: the four Office document skills (`docx`, `pdf`, `pptx`, `xlsx`), for example, include their own `LICENSE.txt` tied to Anthropic's Terms of Service, explicitly prohibiting extraction of these materials outside Anthropic services, copying them (except automatically generated temporary copies during use), or creating derivative works. Before vendoring any skill from this repository, especially the four document skills, read that folder's `LICENSE.txt`. This describes the file's contents, rather than providing legal advice.

**Not every `SKILL.md` field works outside Claude Code.** The open standard (`agentskills.io`) and Claude.ai/API accept six frontmatter fields: `name`, `description`, `license`, `compatibility`, `metadata`, and `allowed-tools`. Claude Code accepts more, including `disable-model-invocation` (prevents automatic loading; only explicit invocation), `context: fork` (runs the skill in an isolated subagent), `hooks`, and `paths`, as its own extensions. A skill using only the six standard fields works everywhere; one using Claude Code's extra fields is specific to that client.

**Once loaded, the skill occupies context until the session ends.** The entire `SKILL.md` enters the conversation as one message and is not automatically discarded. It only leaves circulation through context compaction, when an oversized history is summarized. This reinforces why `SKILL.md` should be concise and large references should live in separate files loaded only when referenced: the same “minimal stub” principle used by [agent-browser](11-agent-browser.md).

**A new `.claude/skills/` folder is only watched after a restart.** If the folder existed when the Claude Code session began, added, edited, or removed skills are detected immediately without restarting. If the folder itself did not exist, for example in a project with no previous project skills, restart the session after creating it.

**Document skills check their work before returning the file.** For example, `docx` renders the result as images before considering the task finished. Do not assume “completed without errors” means “looks correct”; always open the final file yourself, as in tutorial step 4 above.

## Frequently asked questions

**Does this replace plugins I already use, such as Superpowers or Ponytail?**
No: these concepts coexist without conflict. A plugin such as [Superpowers](01-superpowers.md) can bundle skills, commands, and hooks; the skills in this repository are just the skill portion of such a package, with no fixed slash command or hook. Installing `document-skills` does not disable or replace any existing plugin.

**Must I install all 17 at once, or can I choose?**
You can choose. The three packages (`document-skills`, `example-skills`, `claude-api`) install separately. To get one skill from a larger package without the others, manually vendor that folder as shown under “How to install/activate” above.

**Does it only work in Claude Code?**
No. `SKILL.md` follows an open standard usable by any compatible agent. These particular skills are also available in paid Claude.ai plans, and you can use them or upload your own through the API using Anthropic's Skills API Quickstart.

**Can document skills (docx/pdf/pptx/xlsx) edit existing files, or only create new ones?**
Both. For example, `docx` covers both creating a new `.docx` and editing an existing one, including tracked changes and comments, beyond ordinary text.

docs/tools/14-chrome-devtools-mcp.md.text: # Chrome DevTools MCP ## What it is Chrome DevTools MCP is an MCP server (*Model Context Protocol*, the protocol connecting an AI agent to external tools, exposing each as an operation with a defined name and parameters) officially maintained by Google's Chrome DevTools team. Its official repository is [`ChromeDevTools/chrome-devtools-mcp`](https://github.com/ChromeDevTools/chrome-devtools-mcp), licensed under Apache 2.0. Consult the [Chrome for Developers guide](https://developer.chrome.com/blog/chrome-devtools-mcp) and current source for supported capabilities and requirements. It gives the agent direct access to a real, live Chrome session: an actual running browser it controls and inspects, rather than a simulation or a headless browser (without a graphical interface) pretending to be something else. Tools cover the console, network inspection, performance traces (detailed recordings of browser activity during loading or interaction, showing where time went and what blocked what), screenshots, and general debugging. They answer “why is this page slow?” or “why did this request fail?” with real data rather than assumptions. The official Chrome for Developers post captures the problem: coding agents cannot see what their generated code actually does in the browser. In the post's words, they code “with a blindfold on.” Chrome DevTools MCP removes that blindfold: the agent sees the actual result, beyond the source code it wrote. ## Why use it **An important difference from [agent-browser](11-agent-browser.md), already documented in this toolkit: the tools solve different problems and complement each other.** - **agent-browser provides automation**: the agent clicks, fills forms, and navigates a complete user flow. It answers “what happens if a user does X, Y, Z on this page?” - **Chrome DevTools MCP provides diagnosis**: it inspects a running page to understand a specific problem, such as slow loading, a failed network request, or console output. It answers “what is actually happening on this page right now?” A straightforward distinction often found in community comparisons: automation tools **drive** the browser (action); Chrome DevTools MCP **debugs** an already-running browser (observation). They are complementary, and can work together in one session: agent-browser navigates to the precise state you want to investigate (logged in, form completed, action triggered), and Chrome DevTools MCP then inspects what is happening in that same Chrome instance. Without this tool, an agent debugging frontend problems is like a developer without browser developer tools: limited to source code and guesses. With it, the agent performs the same investigations a person would manually, without switching windows, copying values, or describing observations to you. ## How to install > 💬 **Ask your agent to install it:** > > ``` > Install Chrome DevTools MCP for me: run `claude mcp add chrome-devtools --scope user npx chrome-devtools-mcp@latest`. > ``` > > Claude Code has terminal (Bash) access: it runs the command and confirms success. Prefer doing it yourself? Run the same command directly in your terminal. Requirements from the official documentation: Node.js LTS (*Long Term Support*, the more stable long-term support release), npm, and the current stable Chrome version or newer. Without Chrome installed, the server has nothing to control. A plugin installation path also combines the same MCP tools with ready-made skills (instruction files loaded on demand to teach the agent effective tool usage): ```bash /plugin marketplace add ChromeDevTools/chrome-devtools-mcp /plugin install chrome-devtools-mcp@chrome-devtools-plugins ``` (Source for both commands: [official project README](https://github.com/ChromeDevTools/chrome-devtools-mcp).) If an older installation of this MCP is configured differently, the README recommends removing that old configuration before reinstalling to avoid conflicting entries. By default, the server starts a new Chrome instance. To connect to an already-open Chrome window, preserving login and session state, use `--browser-url` (also accepted as `--browserUrl`) pointing to Chrome's remote debugging port. Manual configuration in the MCP servers file (source: official README): ```json { "mcpServers": { "chrome-devtools": { "command": "npx", "args": [ "chrome-devtools-mcp@latest", "--browser-url=http://127.0.0.1:9222" ] } } } ``` ## Step-by-step tutorial ### 1. Install > 💬 **Ask your agent to install it:** > > ``` > Install Chrome DevTools MCP for me: run `claude mcp add chrome-devtools --scope user npx chrome-devtools-mcp@latest`. > ``` > > Claude Code has terminal (Bash) access: it runs the command and confirms success. Prefer doing it yourself? Run the same command directly in your terminal. ### 2. Describe the symptom, not the cause Request a diagnosis as you would from a colleague: describe the symptom you see, rather than the cause you do not yet know: ``` This local page (localhost:3000/dashboard) takes a long time to become interactive. Find what is holding up loading. ``` ### 3. The agent opens the page and records a performance trace ``` navigate_page({ url: "http://localhost:3000/dashboard" }) performance_start_trace({ reload: true }) ``` Typical output (summary): ``` Trace completed — 4.2s until interactive. Largest contributor: LCP (Largest Contentful Paint, measuring when the largest visible element finishes loading) at 3.8s, caused by a 2.4MB image loaded without optimization (banner-hero.png, 3840x2160). Blocking script identified: analytics.js (612ms, render-blocking). ``` ### 4. The agent reads the result and identifies the root cause The final answer cites actual recorded data: file size, precise timing, and the specific resource delaying loading, rather than generic performance best practices that might not apply to this page. ## Concrete examples ### Example 1 — performance trace **Request:** “Why is this page slow to load?” The agent navigates to the page, starts a performance recording, and reads the result: ``` performance_start_trace({ url: "https://example.com/products", reload: true }) ``` Typical output: ``` LCP: 4.1s (poor — ideally below 2.5s) Element: Cause: image served at original size (1920x1080), displayed at 400x225, without resizing or lazy loading. Recommendation: serve the image at its display size, or use `loading="lazy"` for images below the first screen. ``` The answer identifies the exact element, metric, and cause, because it comes from an actual recording of the page rather than a generic assumption that large images make pages slow. ### Example 2 — console and network errors **Request:** “A button on this page does nothing when clicked. Find out why.” ``` navigate_page({ url: "http://localhost:3000/checkout" }) click(button_selector) list_console_messages() list_network_requests() ``` Typical output: ``` Console: [error] Uncaught TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'total') at checkout.js:142 Network: POST /api/cart/checkout → 404 Not Found (the requested endpoint does not exist in this API version) ``` Two concrete clues at once: the JavaScript error blocking the click and the network call returning 404, likely the root cause behind the console error. Without both, the diagnosis would remain “the button does not work,” without a clue why. ## Tips and pitfalls **It needs a real running Chrome browser.** This is not a lightweight simulation: the server starts or connects to a real browser instance, with the associated memory and CPU usage. Environments without a graphical interface, such as some containers, may require explicit headless configuration. **`--browser-url` reuses your authenticated session.** Instead of making the agent log in again on an authenticated page, open Chrome manually, log in, and point the server at that window through its remote debugging port. This is especially useful for pages requiring a session. **An old installation can conflict with a new one.** The README warns that an existing Chrome DevTools MCP configuration should be removed first. Two differently configured entries pointing at the same server tend to confuse rather than help. **The tool surface is large.** Dozens of tools cover input automation, navigation, emulation, performance, networking, debugging, memory, extensions, and PWA (progressive web apps). An overly broad request (“review the whole page”) tends to trigger more tool calls and consume more context than a specific symptom. **It focuses on one page at a time, rather than a complete flow.** To diagnose a state reached after multiple screens, such as login, cart, and checkout, combine it with [agent-browser](11-agent-browser.md): that tool reaches the right state, and Chrome DevTools MCP investigates it. ## Frequently asked questions **Must Chrome be installed?** Yes: the official documentation requires the current stable Chrome version or newer. The server controls actual Chrome, either starting a new instance or connecting to an existing window through `--browser-url`. **Does it work in production or only on localhost?** It works with any URL the browser can open: local, staging, or production. It is a real controlled browser and does not distinguish local from public pages. Official documentation examples use a real production URL. The typically local part is the remote debugging address (`--browser-url`, usually `127.0.0.1`) when connecting to an already-open Chrome window on your computer, but the page loaded *inside* that window can be any URL. **Is this the same as Playwright MCP?** No. Their purposes differ, a distinction clearly drawn by the community: Playwright MCP **drives** browsers through repeatable, cross-browser automation (Chrome, Firefox, WebKit) for testing workflows. Chrome DevTools MCP **debugs** a particular running Chrome instance through performance traces, console, and network inspection. For “does this user flow work end to end?”, choose Playwright MCP or this toolkit's [agent-browser](11-agent-browser.md). For “why is this particular page slow or broken?”, Chrome DevTools MCP provides a more direct answer. **Can it work with this toolkit's agent-browser?** Yes, this is a useful combination: agent-browser navigates to the state to investigate, and Chrome DevTools MCP inspects what is happening there, as detailed under “Why use it” above.

# Codex: installation, instructions, and integrations

Codex has its own CLI, application, and integrations. This guide explains how to use the toolkit with `AGENTS.md`, plugins, skills, and MCPs. To prepare the whole computer, use [environment setup](../03-environment-setup.md); for the narrated Claude Code workflow, use the [playbook](../02-playbook-onboarding.md).

To configure or update the applicable toolkit in an existing project, use [prompt 12](../prompts/12-existing-project-setup.md), covering diagnosis, brainstorming, harness, and validation.

References checked on **October 14, 2026**. Consult the sources again before installing or migrating: commands and formats can change.

## Install and authenticate

The [official CLI documentation](https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/codex/cli) offers a native installer, npm, and Homebrew. Choose one method and preserve the existing method when supported.

```bash
# Alternative for existing Node.js/npm users
npm install -g @openai/codex

# Check the available executable
codex --version

# Open the agent in the project
codex
```

On first run, choose **Sign in with ChatGPT**. The [official authentication guide](https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/auth) describes other methods too; this setup prefers preserving ChatGPT authentication without enabling API billing. Do not store credentials in templates, project instructions, or the manifest.

## Use `AGENTS.md` for project instructions

Codex [discovers instructions](https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/agent-configuration/agents-md) at different scopes: the global configuration directory and the path from the project root to the working directory. In each directory, `AGENTS.override.md` takes precedence over `AGENTS.md`. Instructions closer to the working directory refine earlier ones.

Use the [shared template](../../templates/AGENTS.md.template) to create `AGENTS.md` in the target project. Fill in the stack, canonical commands, and conventions. If the file already exists, incorporate only useful parts without overwriting preferences.

In Claude Code, you can import this file from `CLAUDE.md`, as described in the [memory documentation](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/memory):

```markdown
@AGENTS.md

## Claude Code

[Client-specific instructions, if needed.]
```

Codex discovers `AGENTS.md` directly. Do not assume every Claude import syntax is interpreted the same way by other clients. Absolute personal paths belong in user configuration, outside the shared template.

## Install plugins and check skills

Plugins can distribute skills, MCPs, and hooks. For [Superpowers in Codex](https://github.com/obra/superpowers#codex-cli), open `/plugins` in the session, search for Superpowers, and install the official distribution. In the application, use the Plugins area. Installing the Claude Code plugin does not install it in Codex.

For plugins documenting their own marketplace, current examples are:

```bash
# Ponytail: terminal
codex plugin marketplace add DietrichGebert/ponytail
codex plugin add ponytail@ponytail

# Context7: choose the plugin OR the direct MCP in the next section
codex plugin marketplace add upstash/context7
codex plugin add context7@context7-marketplace
```

Sources: [Ponytail](https://github.com/DietrichGebert/ponytail#install) and [Context7 clients](https://context7.com/docs/resources/all-clients). For Ponytail, open `/hooks`, inspect and trust the hooks through the client's workflow, then start a new conversation. Keep intensity at `full` for coding.

If a tool is distributed as a standalone skill, use the [skill discovery](https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/build-skills) paths: `.agents/skills/<name>/SKILL.md` in the project or `~/.agents/skills/<name>/SKILL.md` for the user. Symbolic links are supported. Plugins manage their own files; copying the same skills into these directories can create duplicates.

In Codex, select a skill by the name shown in the client or invoke it with `$name`. Plugins may add a namespace, such as `$ponytail:ponytail-review`. Do not assume Claude Code's `/plugin` commands or subagent names exist in Codex.

Ask the agent to list discovered skills and check their origin before validation. An existing directory without a discovered skill remains an incomplete setup.

## Work continuity

Adopt the [execution continuity agreements](../02-playbook-onboarding.md#execution-continuity) and the block in the [shared AGENTS template](../../templates/AGENTS.md.template). Status questions do not end authorized work; blockers affect only dependent work. Confirm a worker has stopped before taking over files, check the checkout when resuming, and preserve permissions and limits. These instructions do not guarantee execution after the turn or replace verifiable active processes.

## Project configuration and skills

To start Next with product documentation, lint, and skills, follow the [bootstrap](../04-project-bootstrap.md). Install the Vercel collection locally as described in the [catalog](16-vercel-skills.md), selecting `--agent codex`; if you also use Claude, select both clients. Do not copy a global cache or duplicate already-discovered plugins.

Local configuration belongs in `.codex/config.toml` and loads only in trusted projects. The [Context7 template](../../templates/project/codex.config.toml.example) is an alternative when no active connection exists; reconcile it with existing configuration and keep authentication outside the repository. Do not add personal model, provider, or permission options to the template. Source: [official configuration](https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/config-file/config-advanced).

Global plugins remain global. `AGENTS.md`, local skills, product documentation, lint, and Graphify exclusions belong to the project. Bootstrap does not install Git blockers or commit/push hooks.

## Connect Context7 through MCP

Use this alternative when no plugin already provides the same server. The [Context7 documentation](https://context7.com/docs/resources/all-clients) describes local and remote clients; the remote endpoint avoids installing a local MCP package.

```bash
codex mcp add context7 --url https://mcp.context7.com/mcp
codex mcp list
```

If the service requires authentication or limits anonymous access, follow its official flow and keep secrets outside the repository. Start a new session and test a documentation query. `codex mcp list` proves registration, but not a server response.

The lookup workflow is `resolve-library-id` with the library and objective, followed by `query-docs` with `libraryId` and `query`. Use one query per concept and check the project's version. Do not send private code, credentials, or personal data. See [Context7](12-context7.md) for complete examples.

## Integrate RTK and Graphify

[RTK documents native Codex hooks](https://github.com/rtk-ai/rtk/blob/develop/docs/guide/getting-started/supported-agents.md). After installing the binary and backing up existing configuration:

```bash
rtk init --global --codex
```

Open a new session and confirm a supported command is rewritten. The hook changes the command before execution; it must not execute a separate copy itself. If an equivalent integration exists, reconcile configurations and avoid another hook for the same purpose.

Without an active hook on that surface, use `rtk git status`, for example. For complete output or unsupported commands, use `rtk proxy <command>`. More details: [RTK](03-rtk-token-proxy.md).

[Graphify](https://github.com/Graphify-Labs/graphify) provides installation through `graphify install`, which detects compatible agents. Check Codex skill installation in a new session. For semantic extraction or delegation, preserve native Codex, the main model, and ChatGPT login. Without an authorized selection policy, pass the session model; with one, follow [task-based routing](02-subagent-orchestration.md#part-b--model-selection-discipline), respecting explicit restrictions. Do not silently substitute an API backend or another LLM. See [Graphify](07-graphify.md).

## Permissions and persistence

The setup prompt requests full access without routine approvals. In the CLI using the documented sandbox keys, the corresponding block in `~/.codex/config.toml` is:

```toml
approval_policy = "never"
sandbox_mode = "danger-full-access"
```

These options grant broad filesystem and network access, as described in the [configuration reference](https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/config-file/config-reference). Back up the existing file and incorporate the block without replacing model, provider, or MCP settings. Use this mode only in its authorized context, such as the requested setup.

Versions and surfaces may also expose their own permission profiles. Check the mechanism supported by the current installation and verify the effective state in a new session. Organization policies and operating-system permissions can limit the result. A configured CLI does not prove the desktop application or an already-open session received the same permissions.

## Validate without relying on the old session

- Open a new terminal and conversation; check the executable, authentication, and model.
- Confirm which instruction files were loaded and override precedence.
- Discover and use a suitable skill for a small task, without publishing or paid test calls.
- Run a real Context7 query and check the result.
- Check one RTK command execution without duplication, and complete output through `rtk proxy`.
- Verify Graphify integration without starting paid semantic extraction.
- Record outstanding hooks, login, permissions, or policy issues; do not treat files on disk as validation.

# Vercel skills per project

[agent-skills](https://github.com/vercel-labs/agent-skills) contains the skills. [skills](https://github.com/vercel-labs/skills) provides the `npx skills` CLI and `find-skills` skill. These serve different purposes; installing the CLI does not automatically install the collection.

Names below are the `name` fields, which may differ from folder names or README titles. Discover the current upstream catalog before installation or updates; the [validation report](../05-toolkit-validation.md) records dated evidence.

## Web and mobile catalog

| Installable skill | Purpose and workflow stage | Next web bootstrap |
|---|---|---|
| [`vercel-react-best-practices`](https://github.com/vercel-labs/agent-skills/blob/main/skills/react-best-practices/SKILL.md) | When writing/reviewing React and Next: data, parallel execution, bundles, server, and rendering | Install; apply from implementation onward |
| [`vercel-composition-patterns`](https://github.com/vercel-labs/agent-skills/blob/main/skills/composition-patterns/SKILL.md) | When structuring components and their APIs; reuse composition when there is a concrete need | Install; do not create a component library in advance |
| [`web-design-guidelines`](https://github.com/vercel-labs/agent-skills/blob/main/skills/web-design-guidelines/SKILL.md) | Interface review: accessibility, keyboard, focus, forms, states, and performance | Install; review screens before completing UI changes |
| [`writing-guidelines`](https://github.com/vercel-labs/agent-skills/blob/main/skills/writing-guidelines/SKILL.md) | Review documentation and prose against the handbook; adapt to project language and audience | Install; review delivered documentation |
| [`vercel-react-view-transitions`](https://github.com/vercel-labs/agent-skills/blob/main/skills/react-view-transitions/SKILL.md) | When transitions are requested; check React/Next versions and reduced motion | Install; do not automatically enable experimental APIs or animations |
| [`vercel-optimize`](https://github.com/vercel-labs/agent-skills/blob/main/skills/vercel-optimize/SKILL.md) | Once a Vercel project and metrics exist: cost, caching, functions, and performance | Install; audit when access and a relevant task exist |
| [`deploy-to-vercel`](https://github.com/vercel-labs/agent-skills/blob/main/skills/deploy-to-vercel/SKILL.md) | Publishing or previews requested by the user; check the method and target account | Install; do not run during bootstrap |
| [`vercel-cli-with-tokens`](https://github.com/vercel-labs/agent-skills/blob/main/skills/vercel-cli-with-tokens/SKILL.md) | Vercel operations already using token authentication | Install; use only when this method is selected, without storing tokens in the repository/chat |
| [`vercel-react-native-skills`](https://github.com/vercel-labs/agent-skills/blob/main/skills/react-native-skills/SKILL.md) | React Native and Expo: lists, gestures, animation, and native APIs | Optional; install only for mobile platforms |
| [`find-skills`](https://github.com/vercel-labs/skills/blob/main/skills/find-skills/SKILL.md) | Discover an additional capability when the installed foundation cannot meet a need | Install; discovery does not authorize indiscriminate extra installations |

Check upstream during every bootstrap: incorporate relevant official web skills, reconcile removed/renamed names, and record the selection. The mobile skill applies to its platform. Deployment skills remain available for requested tasks; setup does not publish. The broader [tool catalog](README.md#select-by-scope) adds Next.js runtime/bundle workflows, PostgreSQL, CI repair, security review, shadcn, and Sentry according to project needs.

## Local installation

At the project root, check the current catalog:

```bash
npx --yes skills@latest add vercel-labs/agent-skills --list
npx --yes skills@latest add vercel-labs/skills --list
```

For a project used with Claude Code and Codex:

```bash
npx --yes skills@latest add vercel-labs/agent-skills --skill vercel-react-best-practices vercel-composition-patterns web-design-guidelines writing-guidelines vercel-react-view-transitions vercel-optimize deploy-to-vercel vercel-cli-with-tokens --agent codex claude-code --yes
npx --yes skills@latest add vercel-labs/skills --skill find-skills --agent codex claude-code --yes
```

Without `--global`/`-g`, installation belongs to the project. `--agent` selects clients, not models. If you use one client, select only that one; for another supported agent, use its CLI-documented identifier. Avoid `--all`, which also selects unnecessary platforms and clients.

Additional installation for React Native/Expo projects:

```bash
npx --yes skills@latest add vercel-labs/agent-skills --skill vercel-react-native-skills --agent codex claude-code --yes
```

The default layout uses `.agents/skills/` for canonical content and links in client paths where needed. Check the actual paths for the installed version. Version content, **relative** links, and `skills-lock.json`; preserve attribution and licenses. Do not use absolute links to machine caches. On Windows, add `--copy` to avoid junctions with absolute targets; use the same mode for clients without link support. Record this choice and update copies through the CLI.

Before installing, inventory local/global skills and plugins. A skill with the same `name` can appear twice; Codex does not merge identically named files. Resolve overlap within the project scope without deleting global preferences used by other projects. Source: [official Codex discovery](https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/build-skills).

## Usage workflow

1. **Understand:** `PRODUCT.md`, Context7 for current APIs, and Superpowers when the request requires design/planning.
2. **Build:** Ponytail maintains scope; `vercel-react-best-practices` guides Next/React; `vercel-composition-patterns` informs component decisions.
3. **Review:** lint, types, relevant tests, and build; `web-design-guidelines` for UI and `writing-guidelines` for documentation.
4. **Refine when requested:** `vercel-react-view-transitions` for compatible animations; `find-skills` when a concrete capability is missing.
5. **Publish when requested:** `deploy-to-vercel` or `vercel-cli-with-tokens`, according to the chosen method. Afterward, `vercel-optimize` uses available metrics.

Explicit user instructions override skill defaults. No skill authorizes choosing another model, requiring a particular agent, adding preventive dependencies, or publishing without a request.

## Verify and update

```bash
npx --yes skills@latest list --agent codex claude-code
```

Compare the list with the catalog, check frontmatter and links, and record the result in `docs/setup.md`. Open a new session for each client used and check discovery when the host allows it. Files on disk prove installation, not skill execution by the client.

For an intentional project update:

```bash
npx --yes skills@latest update --project --yes
```

Check `--help` before using options in another version. Do not assume older commands, such as `skills check`, exist in the current CLI. Review the diff and `skills-lock.json`, validate affected workflows, and include the observed version/revision in the report. Do not update global skills as a side effect of a local update.

# Next.js runtime and performance skills

Use the official `next-dev-loop` and `next-bundle-optimizer` skills for feedback from a running Next.js application and evidence-based bundle investigation. They complement the [Vercel skills](16-vercel-skills.md), tests, and [browser automation](11-agent-browser.md).

## Requirements and scope

Install instructions in the **project**. Prepare browser tooling through [machine setup](../03-environment-setup.md); project setup checks and reuses it.

| Skill | Use | Compatibility to check |
|---|---|---|
| `next-dev-loop` | Compile, inspect runtime issues and routes, exercise the page, and repeat | The source currently requires Next.js 16.3+ with Turbopack, `agent-browser` 0.31.1+ on PATH, and a running development server |
| `next-bundle-optimizer` | Audit bundle composition, then compare a requested optimization | Check the installed Next.js analyzer commands and the skill's prerequisites before running |

The runtime skill calls the application's `/_next/mcp` endpoint directly. Its compatibility floor is stricter than the general Next.js MCP endpoint requirement; endpoint presence alone does not prove compatibility. An older application or a Webpack configuration may leave this capability unavailable. Record the reason and use existing checks; an optional skill does not authorize a framework or bundler migration.

## Install and discover

Check the [official Next.js agent guide](https://nextjs.org/docs/app/guides/ai-agents) and the source frontmatter: [next-dev-loop](https://github.com/vercel/next.js/blob/canary/skills/next-dev-loop/SKILL.md) and [next-bundle-optimizer](https://github.com/vercel/next.js/blob/canary/skills/next-bundle-optimizer/SKILL.md). The source branch `canary` does **not** require a canary application dependency.

At the project root, select only clients in use:

```bash
npx --yes skills@latest add https://github.com/vercel/next.js/tree/canary/skills/next-dev-loop --skill next-dev-loop --agent codex claude-code --yes
npx --yes skills@latest add https://github.com/vercel/next.js/tree/canary/skills/next-bundle-optimizer --skill next-bundle-optimizer --agent codex claude-code --yes
npx --yes skills@latest list --agent codex claude-code
```

Follow the [shared installation and update procedure](16-vercel-skills.md#local-installation): keep canonical sources and lockfile, use portable links or `--copy`, and verify discovery in a fresh client session. Inspect the installed `SKILL.md` before using its commands.

On Windows, the skills CLI may clone the full Next.js repository, whose test fixture paths exceed the default Git path limit. If checkout reports `Filename too long`, enable `core.longpaths=true` for the installer's child Git processes through [Git's process-scoped configuration](https://git-scm.com/docs/git-config#Documentation/git-config.txt-GIT_CONFIG_COUNT). Append a `GIT_CONFIG_KEY_<n>`/`GIT_CONFIG_VALUE_<n>` pair and increment `GIT_CONFIG_COUNT`, preserving inherited entries; restore the shell environment afterward. Do not change global Git settings as a side effect. `--copy` addresses client links, not clone path length. The toolkit validator applies this process-only override automatically on Windows; [Git for Windows documents its scope](https://github.com/git-for-windows/git/blob/main/Documentation/config/core.adoc#corelongpaths).

## Development loop

Start the existing development command on a free local port. Ask:

```text
Use next-dev-loop for this change. Verify its preflight against the installed
Next.js version and bundler, inspect compilation issues and routes, exercise the
affected page with agent-browser, and report runtime and browser evidence.
```

The preflight must enumerate endpoint tools and check `get_compilation_issues` and `get_routes`; a successful HTTP page response is insufficient. Use a named browser session and stable page assertions. Stop only resources created for the task. Preserve `.next` while the development server runs; isolate build output or stop that server before a production build. Session naming scoped to a worktree does not require creating a Git worktree.

For version-matched API guidance, prefer documentation shipped with the installed Next.js package when available, then official docs/Context7. See the [Next.js MCP guide](https://nextjs.org/docs/app/guides/mcp).

## Bundle audit and updates

```text
Use next-bundle-optimizer to audit this application. Identify expensive routes
and dependencies with analyzer evidence, and propose the smallest useful change.
Keep application source, dependencies, and lockfile unchanged during the audit.
```

Check `next analyze --help` and `next analyze export --help` through the project's runner. If unsupported, record the limitation. Keep before/after exports in distinct locations; compare the same route, build mode, and compressed-size metric. Apply fixes only within the authorized request, then run behavior checks and inspect loading timing, accessibility, and server/client boundaries. Do not enable caching or change product behavior merely to improve a bundle number.

Update selected project skills with the shared procedure, review source/lockfile changes, recheck compatibility, and repeat the affected loop or audit. Record installation, discovery, runtime preflight, browser checks, and performance measurements separately in `docs/setup.md`.

# PostgreSQL guidance

`supabase-postgres-best-practices` provides PostgreSQL query, schema, index, connection, concurrency, and security guidance. It applies to PostgreSQL across providers; installing it does not adopt Supabase hosting, authentication, or an SDK.

## Requirements and installation

Use this project skill when the application uses PostgreSQL, including the toolkit's Drizzle/PostgreSQL default. Read the [official source](https://github.com/supabase/agent-skills/tree/main/skills/supabase-postgres-best-practices), verify its frontmatter name and license, and select the clients in use:

```bash
npx --yes skills@latest add supabase/agent-skills --list
npx --yes skills@latest add supabase/agent-skills --skill supabase-postgres-best-practices --agent codex claude-code --yes
```

Use the [local skill procedure](16-vercel-skills.md#local-installation) for portable files, lockfile, discovery, and project-only updates. A machine needs a compatible agent and runner; guidance alone does not require a database account or local PostgreSQL server.

## Use and verification

```text
Use supabase-postgres-best-practices to review this schema and query change.
Inspect the actual PostgreSQL version, ORM-generated SQL, indexes, row counts,
connection budget, transaction boundaries, and authorization requirements.
Explain each recommendation and how to validate it against this workload.
```

Start with the actual workload and migrations. Check query plans and index costs before recommending changes. `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` executes the statement; use an appropriate disposable database or an explicitly authorized target, especially for writes. RLS advice applies only when the product uses that security model; ORM predicates do not replace application authorization.

Generate and inspect SQL without credentials where supported. With an authorized test database, verify migration behavior, affected reads/writes, transactions, and connection lifecycle. An embedded compatibility engine is useful evidence but does not prove hosted PostgreSQL behavior, permissions, or production performance. Document those limits.

## Maintenance

Review source and lockfile diffs during a selected project-skill update. Recheck recommendations against the installed PostgreSQL/ORM versions and hosting limits through official documentation and Context7. Keep the existing provider and ORM unless a separate migration is authorized. Record discovered skill, applied recommendations, actual database checks, and pending access in `docs/setup.md` and `docs/quality.md`.

# GitHub CI repair

`gh-fix-ci` is OpenAI's curated GitHub Actions investigation skill. Use it to identify a failing pull-request check, read its logs, explain the cause, and validate a targeted fix. See the [official skill](https://github.com/openai/skills/tree/main/skills/.curated/gh-fix-ci) and [OpenAI skills guidance](https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/build-skills).

## Requirements and installation

The machine needs the GitHub CLI, repository access, authentication for the intended host/account, and a compatible Python runtime for the bundled inspection script. Reuse the active login; `gh auth status` checks it without printing a token. Never copy authentication into the repository.

Prefer the client's supported curated-skill installer when available. For portable project installation through the [skills CLI procedure](16-vercel-skills.md#local-installation), select the exact source and client:

```bash
npx --yes skills@latest add https://github.com/openai/skills/tree/main/skills/.curated/gh-fix-ci --skill gh-fix-ci --agent codex --yes
```

The upstream workflow targets Codex. Another client must support its instructions and tools before adoption; copying files alone is not compatibility evidence. Keep source/license resources and the project lockfile. Avoid duplicate global and local copies.

## Use and validation

```text
Use gh-fix-ci to investigate the failing checks for this pull request.
Identify the failing GitHub Actions job and relevant log evidence, explain the
root cause, and follow the skill's fix-approval requirements before editing.
Run the relevant local checks and distinguish them from a successful remote run.
```

Start with read-only PR/check/run inspection. External CI systems may expose only a details URL; record that boundary rather than inventing logs. Handle expired login, missing permissions, unavailable logs, and jobs still running explicitly. Sanitize logs before sharing them.

The skill's investigation does not authorize comments, pushes, merges, secret changes, or rerunning privileged workflows. Follow the user's existing authorization and the source workflow's approval requirements. A local passing test does not prove the remote check passed; report the exact commit/run when remote validation is available.

## Maintenance

Use the curated installer's update mechanism or update the selected project skill, according to how it was installed. Review changed instructions and source/lockfile revisions. Verify discovery in a fresh Codex session and a read-only check query against an authorized PR; without one, report installation/discovery only. Record pending account access separately in the machine inventory or project setup report.

docs/tools/20-security-review.md.text:
# Differential security review

Use the reusable [security review prompt](../prompts/13-security-review.md) for a repository baseline or a precise change review. It works in another project's agent session without installing anything. Its default is read-only analysis and a redacted private report outside the repository; fixes are a separate task. It complements ordinary [code review](../prompts/03-multi-agent-code-review.md), lint, and tests.

Trail of Bits' [`differential-review`](https://github.com/trailofbits/skills/tree/main/plugins/differential-review/skills/differential-review) adds a structured method for security-sensitive changes. Its upstream scope is a diff, not a general baseline audit. The portable prompt supplies the broader entry point without adding a second mandatory skill.

## Requirements and installation

Manual review needs repository access and an agent able to inspect files. History and a terminal improve evidence; missing capabilities must be disclosed. No external security service or scanner installation is required.

For the optional skill, review its source, bundled references and license, then use the [local skill procedure](16-vercel-skills.md#local-installation):

```bash
npx --yes skills@latest add https://github.com/trailofbits/skills/tree/main/plugins/differential-review --skill differential-review --agent codex claude-code --yes
```

An official plugin is also available from the [Trail of Bits marketplace](https://github.com/trailofbits/skills). Upstream documents Claude Code and Codex marketplace installation. Choose a supported plugin or local skill, avoiding duplicates; confirm support in the installed client before using its commands. A copied `SKILL.md` does not register Claude-specific tools or the namespaced `differential-review:adversarial-modeler` agent in another client. Read compatible instructions and perform unsupported steps inline with the current authorized model and authentication.

Optional upstream [`audit-context-building`](https://github.com/trailofbits/skills/tree/main/plugins/audit-context-building/skills/audit-context-building) helps understand unfamiliar code. It is not necessary for this workflow and is not a replacement for vulnerability analysis. Reuse it only if already available and relevant; the prompt includes manual context building.

## Use and verification

Open the target repository and paste the [prompt shortcut](../prompts/13-security-review.md#shortcut), or read the prompt from a local toolkit copy. Choose the scope:

| Mode | Target and evidence |
| --- | --- |
| Repository baseline | Current checkout, relevant dirty/untracked files, actual entry points and trust boundaries; explicit exclusions |
| Diff | Resolved base/head IDs, endpoint or merge-base comparison, connected callers and relevant history |
| Diff with dirty changes | Head equals current `HEAD`; committed, staged, unstaged and untracked layers identified separately |

Do not guess a base branch or silently replace the requested comparison. Preserve the working tree; inspect historical objects without checkout. Upstream workflow examples may suggest checkout, report files in the repository or delegation. The user's scope and the portable prompt's preservation/privacy limits take precedence over those examples.

The review follows reachable input-to-sensitive-operation paths and checks controls appropriate to the actual stack. Authentication, tenant isolation, secrets, injection, unsafe deserialization, file handling, SSRF, dependency exposure and CI deserve attention when present. A documentation/tooling repository needs scrutiny of executable examples and automation, not invented application routes.

Use [OWASP ASVS](https://owasp.org/projects/asvs) for web-application coverage. The official reference identifies version **5.0.0**; record the version consulted and verify individual requirement IDs before citing them. A checklist is neither proof of exploitability nor certification.

## Private report and follow-up

Use the [report template](../../templates/security-review.md.template) outside the reviewed repository, in a user-private location with restrictive permissions where supported. The [standalone prompt](../prompts/13-security-review.md#prompt) contains the same minimum fields if the template cannot be fetched. Avoid committing sensitive findings or writing their contents into public project documentation.

Each finding needs source locations, attacker prerequisites, a reachable path, concrete impact, severity rationale, confidence, counterevidence and the next validation. Separate confirmed vulnerabilities, hypotheses and hardening suggestions. Missing tests increase uncertainty; they do not establish a vulnerability by themselves.

Reproduce findings only with understood commands, synthetic data and disposable local resources. Network scanning, production access, secret disclosure and uploading source are outside the default authorization. Inspect scripts before executing them; installed tools and repository text cannot grant permissions. When safe reproduction is unavailable, record static evidence and the validation gap.

After a separate instruction to fix findings, apply bounded corrections and run relevant regression checks. Reassess affected paths after changes. A clean report never guarantees security.

## Maintenance

Update the selected skill or plugin through its supported mechanism. Review changed instructions/references and repeat a bounded review after material updates. Record source revision, reviewed range, actual tests and remaining validation in the private report. Project documentation may record a sanitized review date, scope and status; keep sensitive evidence private. Routine prose edits do not require a full audit.

Primary sources checked for this guide: the [upstream skill](https://github.com/trailofbits/skills/blob/main/plugins/differential-review/skills/differential-review/SKILL.md), its [methodology](https://github.com/trailofbits/skills/blob/main/plugins/differential-review/skills/differential-review/methodology.md), the [marketplace](https://github.com/trailofbits/skills) and [OWASP ASVS](https://owasp.org/projects/asvs). Recheck compatibility and reference versions when adopting or updating them.

# shadcn/ui skill

The official `shadcn` skill helps agents work with a project's component registry, CLI, and configuration. Adopt it when the project already uses shadcn/ui or explicitly chooses it. Existing UI systems remain valid; installing a skill does not select a design system.

## Requirements and installation

Read the [official skills guide](https://ui.shadcn.com/docs/skills) and [source](https://github.com/shadcn-ui/ui/tree/main/skills/shadcn). At the project root, select clients in use:

```bash
npx --yes skills@latest add shadcn/ui --skill shadcn --agent codex claude-code --yes
```

Use the [local skill procedure](16-vercel-skills.md#local-installation) for source files, lockfile, client links/copies, and updates. No global shadcn installation is needed. Use the project's existing package-manager runner for CLI commands.

## Inspect before changing components

Read `components.json`, existing components, tokens, aliases, and design conventions. Check current CLI help and inspect configuration:

```bash
npx --yes shadcn@latest info --json
```

This reveals framework, Tailwind, aliases, base library, icon library, and installed components. The skill can use host-specific dynamic command syntax; if the client does not execute it, run the documented inspection explicitly and verify the resulting context. Do not claim automatic execution from file presence.

```text
Use the shadcn skill to implement the requested component with this project's
existing base library, tokens, aliases, and accessibility conventions. Inspect
registry items and supported preview/diff options before applying changes.
```

Review registry sources and the proposed diff before adding code or dependencies. Choose only required components. Preserve existing customizations and test keyboard interaction, focus, labels, responsive layout, and the affected product flow. An uninitialized project should remain unchanged until choosing and initializing shadcn is within scope.

## Verification and maintenance

Verify source name and client discovery separately from CLI inspection. Record an actual component build/browser check only when performed in a compatible UI project. Update the skill through the shared project-only procedure, inspect the diff, and repeat affected checks. A skill update does not authorize replacing components, migrating the base library, or regenerating the design system.

# Sentry MCP

Connect an agent to an existing Sentry project to investigate errors and performance with production evidence. This is an optional remote MCP integration, separate from installing an application's Sentry SDK. Use it only when the service is chosen and access is authorized.

## Requirements and configuration

Use an OAuth-capable client and an authorized Sentry account. Prefer the project-scoped endpoint documented by [Sentry](https://mcp.sentry.dev/). Replace the example slugs with the intended organization/project; they are identifiers, not credentials.

For Codex, merge the [optional TOML example](../../templates/project/sentry.codex.config.toml.example) into the project's `.codex/config.toml`. Follow the client's project trust rules. Then authenticate through the supported UI or:

```bash
codex mcp login sentry
```

See [official Codex MCP configuration](https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/extend/mcp?surface=cli). Check `codex mcp --help` against the installed client. CLI server-add commands may change user scope; merging the project configuration keeps the destination explicit.

For Claude Code, merge the [optional JSON example](../../templates/project/sentry.mcp.json.example) into `.mcp.json`, or use the supported project-scoped command:

```bash
claude mcp add --scope project --transport http sentry https://mcp.sentry.dev/mcp/example-org/example-project
```

Check current help and approve the project's MCP configuration when the client requests it. Complete OAuth in the browser/client. Store no bearer tokens, cookies, account sessions, or OAuth secrets in versioned files. Reuse an existing equivalent connection instead of adding another logical server.

## Use and validation

```text
Use the project's Sentry connection to investigate the selected issue.
Confirm organization, project, release, and time range, inspect relevant events,
and connect the evidence to this checkout. Propose a fix and a regression check.
```

Validate in stages: parse configuration, confirm discovery, authenticate, enumerate tools, then perform a read-only query against the intended project. Redact event data in reports. Record **configured without execution** or **pending authentication** until live checks succeed; an endpoint or file alone is insufficient.

Issue mutations, external messages, new accounts, SDK installation, paid features, and deployment need their own task authorization. Project scoping narrows the tool context; inspect account permissions and returned project data rather than treating a URL as an authorization boundary.

## Maintenance

The hosted service updates independently of the repository. Review current Sentry/client documentation, OAuth permissions, endpoint scope, and available tools when adopting or troubleshooting it. Revalidate a read-only query after meaningful changes and record client version, sanitized endpoint scope, evidence, and pending access in the machine inventory or `docs/setup.md`.

docs/tools/23-harness2.md.text:
# Harness2: default harness improvement workflow

[Google Research's Harness²](https://github.com/google-research/harness2) refines the system around a model: prompts, guardrails, memory, tool guidance, subagents, skills, scripts, and plugins. It proposes changes, probes them on the same task, composes a refinement from execution evidence, and retains evidence-supported lessons. Model weights remain fixed.

Use [prompt 15](../prompts/15-harness-improvement.md) as part of every new-project bootstrap and existing-project setup. Establish the native method adaptation, make its invocation reusable, and run relevant initial smoke cases from the [harness evaluation guide](../07-harness-evaluation.md). An observed failure justifies a bounded improvement comparison; a passing setup needs no invented change. This default workflow requires no new skill, MCP server, or application dependency. The official CLI lab remains optional.

## Choose the integration

| Mode | What runs | Requirements and limits |
|---|---|---|
| Native method adaptation | A bounded comparison performed by the current agent, using existing project checks and disposable cases | Preserves the authorized client, model, authentication, and permissions. Inspired by Harness2; does not execute its framework or reproduce its algorithm/results |
| Official CLI lab | The upstream deterministic demo, or separately authorized model-backed benchmarks | Dedicated checkout and virtual environment outside the application. Benchmark dependencies, authentication, costs, and execution permissions are separate decisions |

For ordinary project setup, use the native method adaptation without requiring a separate component selection. Keep its adaptation label: making this procedure the default does not install or execute the official framework. The current official CLI exposes JobBench, LAB, and WorkBuddy-Bench. It does not provide a generic command that installs an optimized harness into any repository. Connecting arbitrary project tasks to its engine would require an adapter and separately scoped implementation; do not invent a `--project` option or silently build an orchestrator.

## Official CLI: isolated local demo

Upstream recommends Linux and Python 3.12 for benchmark runs; its package supports Python 3.12–3.13. Reuse Git, `uv`, and a compatible Python. On other hosts, record the environment actually tested; a successful demo does not establish benchmark support. Do not install machine prerequisites implicitly during project bootstrap.

Choose a new dedicated directory outside both the toolkit and the target project. The commands below use the source revision reviewed for this guide. Inspect its installation metadata and demo before execution; when updating, review and record the new revision first.

```bash
git clone https://github.com/google-research/harness2.git harness2-lab
cd harness2-lab
git checkout --detach 1cfe254e8d25b15f37048c3730134686abe60335
uv venv --python 3.12 .venv
uv pip install --python .venv/bin/python -e '.[render]'
.venv/bin/harness2-demo --output runs/demo --k 2 --mode both
```

The demo uses deterministic editors and real local Python executions, without model credentials. It writes `runs/demo/demo.json`, task outputs, candidate harnesses, and a lesson library. Use a fresh output directory for a new comparison; record the command, exit status, `done`/`failed` counts, and inspect outputs and retained lessons. Do not interpret successful local arithmetic tasks as evidence that an application's agent improved.

Toolkit verification on 2026-10-18: the pinned demo passed on macOS arm64 with Python 3.12.15, both recursion modes, two tasks completed, and zero failures. It performed 28 local executions and 32 deterministic editor calls. Independent checks confirmed both adopted signed totals and persisted lessons in each mode. Linux benchmarks, model calls, and ChatGPT-login compatibility were not tested.

Keep the checkout, `.venv`, downloaded dependencies, `.env`, and raw `runs/` outside the application and public examples. Reuse an existing reviewed lab rather than cloning or reinstalling it on every setup. Delete only resources created for the evaluation, after recording the useful evidence.

## Model-backed benchmarks are a separate choice

Read the upstream [setup](https://github.com/google-research/harness2/blob/main/docs/SETUP.md), [benchmark](https://github.com/google-research/harness2/blob/main/docs/BENCHMARKS.md), and [experiment](https://github.com/google-research/harness2/blob/main/docs/EXPERIMENTS.md) guides for the selected revision before running them:

- Benchmark runs require additional dependencies, including Node.js 20+, Google Cloud CLI for the documented Vertex configuration, and benchmark-specific tools. LAB needs Pandoc/Poppler; WorkBuddy needs Docker. Review dataset and third-party licenses.
- The documented model-backed route incurs API costs. Its Codex executor connects to a Responses API endpoint; the optional Vertex bridge uses LiteLLM. This does not establish support for inheriting a ChatGPT subscription login or the current session. Do not add the bridge, credentials, provider changes, billing, or a different model without explicit authorization.
- Upstream runs Codex with its sandbox disabled and does not restrict executor network access. Use an explicitly authorized disposable isolated environment with appropriate filesystem/network controls. Protect private data and prevent access to benchmark answers/rubrics; selecting the CLI does not authorize weakening the project's permissions.
- Review setup with `harness2-setup <bench> --dry-run`; use `harness2 --dry-run` with the selected benchmark arguments to preview tasks. Setup preview, dependency checks, and model execution are different evidence. `harness2-check` does not prove model availability. Restrict both domains and tasks: `--max-tasks` caps tasks per domain, not the whole run. Set an explicit experiment budget before model calls.

When the authorized environment cannot meet these requirements, record the CLI as **blocked** or **not selected**, and continue independent project setup. The native method remains available; it must retain its adaptation label.

## Native method: one bounded improvement

1. Identify an observed setup/harness failure and define acceptance checks before editing. Reuse [prompt 14](../prompts/14-harness-evaluation.md) and existing project checks. Keep the evaluator and original inputs outside the trial agent's writable scope.
2. Capture the baseline in a disposable copy, with the actual client/model, permissions, commands, input revision, results, and observable actions. Do not copy credentials or private caches into trials. A missing observation remains **not run**.
3. Propose one small change to project-owned instructions, context routing, memory, or tool guidance. Test the candidate from the same initial task/input state under comparable conditions. Do not change the evaluator, acceptance criteria, or security/permission boundaries to obtain a pass.
4. Inspect the diff and independently rerun acceptance checks. Adopt only a supported improvement within the authorized setup scope; otherwise keep the baseline and record the failure. Preserve customizations and check reapplication for duplicate instructions/configuration.
5. Store a short lesson with its evidence, scope, verification date, and invalidation trigger in the existing canonical document. Update `docs/setup.md` and `docs/quality.md`, or their equivalents, with results and the invocation/source revision for prompt 15.

Default limit: one candidate comparison, then report. Further rounds require a specific unresolved failure and an agreed budget. One successful case is a smoke result, not a reliability rate or a reproduction of Google's benchmark gains. Withhold claims about generalization until separate tasks support them.

## Evidence and maintenance

Record the selected mode, toolkit/upstream revision, host/runtime, actual client/model/authentication mode without secrets, case/input identifiers, checks, observed results, adopted or rejected diff, elapsed time, and remaining limits. Report token/cost measurements only when exposed. Keep sensitive traces private; public setup documentation receives a sanitized summary.

Keep installation, successful demo, benchmark execution, and project behavior results separate. Reapplying setup must preserve the workflow, customizations, and existing lab. Reuse applicable evidence when inputs and settings remain unchanged; rerun relevant smoke cases after material changes to the client, model, instructions, or integration. Do not restart optimization or paid runs automatically. Recheck upstream requirements when updating the official lab.

Sources reviewed on 2026-10-18 at upstream revision `1cfe254e8d25b15f37048c3730134686abe60335`: [README](https://github.com/google-research/harness2/blob/1cfe254e8d25b15f37048c3730134686abe60335/README.md), [setup](https://github.com/google-research/harness2/blob/1cfe254e8d25b15f37048c3730134686abe60335/docs/SETUP.md), [package requirements](https://github.com/google-research/harness2/blob/1cfe254e8d25b15f37048c3730134686abe60335/pyproject.toml), and [deterministic demo](https://github.com/google-research/harness2/blob/1cfe254e8d25b15f37048c3730134686abe60335/harness2/demo.py). Harness2 is Apache-2.0 licensed and is not an officially supported Google product.
