# Tools

Choose a tool for the current need. For a new foundation, follow the [bootstrap](../04-project-bootstrap.md); to configure or update an existing project, use the [complete setup](../prompts/12-existing-project-setup.md); to prepare the machine, use [global setup](../03-environment-setup.md).

| Document | Purpose |
|---|---|
| [01 — Superpowers](01-superpowers.md) | Design, planning, execution, and review |
| [02 — Subagents](02-subagent-orchestration.md) | Delegation and independent waves |
| [03 — RTK](03-rtk-token-proxy.md) | Commands with concise output |
| [04 — Ponytail](04-ponytail.md) | Smallest complete solution |
| [05 — Caveman](05-caveman.md) | Concise communication |
| [06 — ESLint/Biome](06-eslint-biome-quality-gates.md) | Lint and rule evolution |
| [07 — Graphify](07-graphify.md) | Project graph |
| [08 — Obsidian](08-obsidian-memory.md) | Optional external memory |
| [09 — Claude memory](09-claude-memory-system.md) | Persistent context |
| [10 — Hooks](10-hooks-best-practices.md) | Optional client reference |
| [11 — agent-browser](11-agent-browser.md) | Browser automation |
| [12 — Context7](12-context7.md) | Current documentation |
| [13 — Anthropic Skills](13-anthropics-skills.md) | Artifacts and skill creation |
| [14 — Chrome DevTools MCP](14-chrome-devtools-mcp.md) | Console, network, and performance |
| [15 — Codex](15-codex-workflow.md) | Instructions, plugins, MCPs, and discovery |
| [16 — Vercel skills](16-vercel-skills.md) | Catalog, local installation, and workflow |
| [17 — Next.js runtime and performance](17-nextjs-runtime-and-performance.md) | Development feedback and bundle analysis |
| [18 — PostgreSQL](18-postgresql-skills.md) | SQL, indexes, migrations, pooling, and security |
| [19 — GitHub CI repair](19-github-ci-repair.md) | Diagnose failing GitHub Actions checks |
| [20 — Security review](20-security-review.md) | Repository or diff review, trust boundaries, and private evidence-based reports |
| [21 — shadcn/ui](21-shadcn-ui.md) | Work with an adopted component system |
| [22 — Sentry MCP](22-sentry-mcp.md) | Investigate errors and performance in a chosen service |
| [23 — Harness2](23-harness2.md) | Default native harness improvement workflow; optional isolated official CLI lab |

## Select by scope

| Capability | Machine preparation | Individual project selection |
|---|---|---|
| `next-dev-loop` | Compatible agent-browser and browser runtime | Compatible Next.js/Turbopack development server |
| `next-bundle-optimizer` | Existing agent and package runner | Next.js analyzer support; audit or requested optimization |
| `supabase-postgres-best-practices` | Existing agent; database tools only when needed | PostgreSQL with any provider/ORM |
| `gh-fix-ci` | GitHub CLI and authorized account | GitHub Actions PR checks; compatible Codex workflow |
| `differential-review` | Compatible agent and Git/history access | Security-sensitive changes and explicit review range |
| `shadcn` | Existing package runner | Adopted or explicitly selected shadcn/ui |
| Sentry MCP | OAuth-capable client and authorized account | Chosen Sentry organization/project |
| Harness2 | Existing agent for the default native adaptation; Git, uv, and compatible Python for a selected isolated CLI lab | Default measured harness workflow in new and existing project setup; official benchmarks require separate dependency, authentication, cost, and isolation decisions |

Evaluate every row during setup. Install applicable instructions in project scope; reuse machine prerequisites. Record unavailable prerequisites and not-applicable choices with reasons. For each adopted capability, record source/revision, client, scope, installation, discovery, actual execution, update method, and pending work. An installed skill, a configured server, and a successful live workflow are different evidence.

Harness2 is not a skill or MCP server. Use [prompt 15](../prompts/15-harness-improvement.md) by default during new and existing project setup: establish the native adaptation, run relevant initial smoke cases, and make the procedure reusable. This preserves current session authentication without installing the optional official CLI; a successful CLI demo does not prove benchmark or project integration.

# [Project name]

> Fill in the fields and merge with existing instructions, including those generated by Next.js. Client-specific settings belong in the corresponding client.

## Product and stack

- Product and scope: `PRODUCT.md`.
- Stack: [frameworks, observed versions, runtime, and package manager].
- Setup and validations: `docs/setup.md`, when using this bootstrap.

## Canonical commands

Use actual commands; mark unavailable checks without inventing scripts.

- Install: `[command]`
- Develop: `[command]`
- Lint: `[command]`
- Types: `[command]`
- Local lint rules: `[command, if any]`
- Tests: `[command, or unavailable with a reason]`
- Build: `[command]`
- Verify foundation: `[command combining existing checks]`

## Working agreements

- Read relevant code and instructions before editing. State assumptions that affect behavior or scope.
- Complete the request with the smallest sufficient change. Reuse existing patterns, components, and dependencies.
- Preserve local changes, validation, error handling, security, accessibility, and explicit requirements.
- Do not create abstractions, architecture, options, dependencies, or features for unrequested needs.
- Run appropriate checks. Test relevant logic and regressions; trivial changes do not need tests that merely mirror the implementation.
- Do not turn assumptions into facts or pending integrations into simulated results.
- Continue authorized work. Ask only for essential information or actions outside the authorization.
- Publishing, messaging third parties, costs, and destructive actions require relevant authorization. Installing tools does not grant it.

## Execution continuity

- During authorized work, answer status questions and resume the remaining actions. Stop if the user asks to pause, cancels, or changes the objective. Without ongoing execution, an informational request ends with the answer.
- A blocker stops only dependent tasks. Complete independent tasks that remain safe and authorized; before stopping, check for executable actions still in scope.
- If an agent fails or its state becomes uncertain, confirm it has stopped before taking over its files. Inspect partial changes and resume from a verified point, without concurrent writers.
- Do not repeat an identical attempt without new evidence. Respect cost, time, and retry limits, explicit gates, and denials; earlier decisions do not expand authorization.
- When resuming from a handoff, check actual files, Git state, checks, and processes. Claim background execution only when an active process, agent, or automation can be verified.
- For unfinished multi-session work, keep a short handoff in the existing plan/task record: objective, verified state, checks, pending work, blockers, owned resources, and next action. Do not turn temporary progress into permanent memory.
- Without a safe alternative, report the blocker, completed work, and what is needed to resume; do not present pending work as results or promise automatic continuation.

## Standards and documentation

- New persistence: Drizzle ORM + PostgreSQL with a runtime-compatible driver. Preserve the existing stack; record exceptions in `PRODUCT.md` and `docs/architecture.md`.
- One server connection entry point, a bounded pool, and lazy initialization. Generate and review SQL before applying migrations to an authorized destination; do not migrate during builds or requests.
- Validate input and environment with Zod. Use Pino on the server, without secrets or full bodies. Presentation calls feature modules without importing the database client.
- Prefer inferred types, parameterized queries, explicit projections, bounded listings, and safe DTOs. Transactions follow required atomicity and driver support.
- Consult current official sources and stable channels before changing stack/APIs. Apply compatible improvements within authorized scope; record source, reason, and outcome in `docs/setup.md`. Do not automatically migrate major versions or services.
- `PRODUCT.md` owns scope; `docs/architecture.md`, structure and decisions; `docs/design.md`, interface; `docs/onboarding.md`, preparation; `docs/quality.md`, checks. Update the responsible document with each change without duplicating rules.
- Record the actual memory/index location and loading mechanism in `docs/setup.md`. Prefer native memory or existing versioned docs; keep an index short and retrieve details on demand. Durable memories carry their source, last verification, and invalidation trigger. Recheck conflicts against current code and authoritative decisions; update or retire superseded entries. Verify retrieval in a clean context when observable.

## Tools and style

- **Ponytail:** installed plugin/skill at `full` intensity for coding. `stop ponytail` disables the mode.
- **Caveman:** concise conversation in the user's language, preserving clarity and full explanations when requested. Code, documentation, and commits use normal wording. `stop caveman` disables the style.
- **Superpowers:** use relevant skills and scale the workflow to scope. Explicit instructions and already authorized execution take precedence over repeated approvals.
- **Context7:** query current documentation for APIs, libraries, and setup. Resolve the identifier and query one concept at a time. Never send secrets or private code. If unavailable, use official sources and record the limitation.
- **RTK:** use supported commands. With an active native hook, avoid double wrapping; without a hook, prefix supported commands. Use `rtk proxy <command>` for original output.
- **Graphify:** use an existing graph when useful for structural questions. Record outdated/incomplete evidence; do not invent relationships. Exclude secrets, dependencies, vendored skills, and generated files.
- **LLMs:** preserve the authorized native client, main model, and authentication, including Graphify and Caveman. Without an authorized selection policy, subagents use the session model. With that policy, dynamically choose the lightest model capable of meeting acceptance criteria and increase capability according to risk/evidence; respect explicit model restrictions. Specify model and effort in supported controls. Do not silently change providers or enable paid APIs or proxies.

Verify installation and discovery before relying on a tool. An absence requires a record or an officially supported alternative; a written preference does not install a plugin.

## Skills for Next.js

[List only skills actually installed; remove this section if the project does not use Next.js/React.]

- `vercel-react-best-practices`: when writing/reviewing React/Next.js, data, and performance.
- `vercel-composition-patterns`: for concrete composition and component API decisions.
- `web-design-guidelines`: interface and accessibility review.
- `writing-guidelines`: documentation and prose review.
- `vercel-react-view-transitions`: requested transitions compatible with the versions in use.
- `vercel-optimize`: optimization with a relevant task and available Vercel metrics.
- `deploy-to-vercel`: authorized publishing/previews.
- `vercel-cli-with-tokens`: Vercel operations using this chosen authentication method.
- `find-skills`: discovery when a concrete capability is missing.
- `next-dev-loop`: runtime and browser feedback after Next.js changes, after checking installed version, Turbopack, agent-browser, and endpoint tools.
- `next-bundle-optimizer`: evidence-based bundle audit; apply fixes only within the authorized request and verify behavior/timing/boundaries.

Installing skills does not execute their actions. Do not force animations, caching, deployment, or architecture changes just because a skill is available.

## Project capabilities

[Keep only adopted capabilities, with details and pending prerequisites in docs/setup.md. List actual installed names and client support; do not imply installation from this template.]

- `supabase-postgres-best-practices`: load before PostgreSQL schema, SQL, migration, security, or performance work; preserve the provider and ORM.
- `gh-fix-ci`: investigate GitHub Actions PR failures through authorized GitHub CLI access in a supported Codex workflow; follow the skill's fix-approval requirements.
- `differential-review`: review security-sensitive diffs and connected callers/history; define the range and Markdown report destination, then verify findings.
- Security review: use the project's adopted review prompt for repository baselines or precise diffs. Keep review read-only and reports private by default; trace reachable trust boundaries, redact evidence, and distinguish confirmed findings from hypotheses. No findings is not a security guarantee.
- `shadcn`: inspect the adopted UI configuration, base library, tokens, and components before changing them; preserve customizations and accessibility.
- Sentry MCP: use the intended organization/project connection for authorized investigation. Confirm scope and read-only evidence; OAuth secrets remain outside versioned files.

Project setup reuses machine tooling. Missing global prerequisites belong to machine preparation; optional skill requirements do not authorize framework/bundler upgrades, a new provider, UI system, SDK, or service. Distinguish configured files, client discovery, and successful live execution. Tool availability does not authorize publishing, external messages, issue mutations, or account changes.

## Git and collaboration

- Do not add push blockers on `main`, branch/worktree requirements, or `pre-commit`/`pre-push` hooks by default.
- Lint, types, tests, and builds are explicit checks; additional Git settings are added when requested.
- Delegate when requested or through a relevant, supported workflow. Parallel tasks require distinct files and independence within the same wave.
- Use actual host tools; illustrative agent names are not installed capabilities.

## Delegation and review

- Delegate only when context isolation, specialization, or independent parallelism justify coordination; prefer deterministic tools or direct execution for simple tasks.
- Discover available models and check the authorized policy before dispatching. Prefer lightweight capability for searches, inventories, and verifiable mechanical changes; use enough capability for complex decisions, security, data, and critical review. Without selection support, preserve the permitted model and record the limitation.
- Each task receives an objective, minimal context, permitted files, dependencies, mutable resources, acceptance criteria, and checks. One writer per file; the coordinator owns lockfiles, shared configuration, and integration. Isolate or serialize shared ports, build output, databases, and services. Parallel reviewers are read-only.
- Check diffs and checks before accepting a worker's result. After a failure, investigate and escalate capability/context when needed; respect finite retry, time, and resource limits. Do not estimate savings without measurement.
- Scope review to risk and actual changes. For nontrivial work, use an independent review when available; inspect the exact revision/working tree and connected callers, contracts, and tests. Stop when relevant findings are resolved or explicitly dispositioned, affected checks pass, and coverage and residual risks are recorded. More rounds require new evidence, unresolved risk, or an explicit request.
- Respect a user-requested review count without resetting it after internal fixes. Report unavailable independent review and remaining risks; do not imply that a count proves correctness. Evaluate material harness changes with small disposable tasks and record observed behavior separately from installation or self-reported success.

## Conventions and context

[Imports, actual code organization, errors, and links to useful decisions. Keep this file short; details belong in the corresponding documents.]

templates/README.md.text:
# Templates

Copy only the component you need. These files are sources for adaptation, not a ready-made application or standalone installer. The [bootstrap](../docs/04-project-bootstrap.md) defines the order; the [defaults](../docs/06-project-defaults.md) define the decisions.

For an existing project, [prompt 12](../docs/prompts/12-existing-project-setup.md) reconciles these templates with the structure, tools, and documents already adopted.

| Directory or file | Use | Destination |
|---|---|---|
| [project-docs/manifest.json](project-docs/manifest.json) | Single map of initial documentation | Four root files and five in `docs/` |
| [product.md.template](product.md.template) | Product, MVP, assumptions, and acceptance | `PRODUCT.md`; source path retained for compatibility |
| [AGENTS.md.template](AGENTS.md.template) and [CLAUDE.md.template](CLAUDE.md.template) | Shared instructions and Claude bridge | Root, merging existing instructions |
| [next/](next/) | Environment, logger, Drizzle connection, UI helper, and tests | Same application tree; remove only the `.example` suffix, preserving `.env.example` |
| [eslint/next-app.config.mjs.example](eslint/next-app.config.mjs.example) | Full profile for the core with Drizzle | `eslint.config.mjs` and the `eslint-rules/` directory |
| [eslint/next.config.mjs.example](eslint/next.config.mjs.example) | Lightweight Next.js profile without mandatory logging/database | `eslint.config.mjs` and the `eslint-rules/` directory |
| [eslint/next.typed.config.mjs.example](eslint/next.typed.config.mjs.example) | Focused async correctness gate for new Next.js projects | `eslint.typed.config.mjs`, after the base config |
| [eslint/eslint.config.mjs.example](eslint/eslint.config.mjs.example) and [typed profile](eslint/eslint.typed.config.mjs.example) | Advanced adoption in an existing codebase | Merge into existing lint configuration |
| [eslint/verify.mjs](eslint/verify.mjs) | Local rule self-check | `scripts/verify-quality-rules.mjs` |
| [project/](project/) | Context7 per client and Graphify exclusions | `.codex/config.toml`, `.mcp.json`, or `.graphifyignore`, when needed |
| [Sentry Codex](project/sentry.codex.config.toml.example) and [Sentry Claude](project/sentry.mcp.json.example) | Optional project-scoped OAuth connection for a chosen service | Merge into `.codex/config.toml` or `.mcp.json`, replace scope identifiers, and follow the [Sentry guide](../docs/tools/22-sentry-mcp.md) |
| [environment-manifest.json.example](environment-manifest.json.example) | Machine setup inventory | Follow the [global guide](../docs/03-environment-setup.md) |
| [settings.json.example](settings.json.example) and [hooks/](hooks/) | Optional client hook examples | Only in the chosen integration; these are not Git hooks |
| [rules/](rules/) | Delegation protocol, when used | Relevant project instructions |
| [task-handoff.md.template](task-handoff.md.template) | Verified state and next action for unfinished work | Existing task/plan location; only when work spans sessions |
| [security-review.md.template](security-review.md.template) | Findings, evidence, scope, and limitations | Private location outside the reviewed repository by default |
| [harness-evaluation/](harness-evaluation/) | Deliberately broken local authorization fixture | Disposable copy only; follow the [evaluation guide](../docs/07-harness-evaluation.md) |

Fill documents with project facts; remove instructions and placeholders. Document template links are relative to the **destination**, defined in the manifest. Next.js modules require the guide's dependencies and scripts; do not copy them into this toolkit's root.

# Disposable harness evaluation fixture

This directory is a deliberately incomplete test fixture, not application code. Work only in a disposable copy outside the toolkit when evaluating an agent. The original fixture must retain its authorization bug so the evaluation has a failing baseline.

In the disposable copy:

- Read the task and actual implementation before editing. A handoff may be stale.
- Reading a record requires a nonempty string user ID, a nonempty string tenant ID, matching ownership, and matching tenant. Missing identities deny access.
- Preserve `local-notes.txt` and unrelated files. Do not change the public function signature.
- Use the toolkit's `scripts/validate-harness.mjs` with this directory as its argument. Checks live outside the writable fixture; do not modify them.
- Review tasks are read-only. Write a requested report only to its explicitly supplied private destination.
- Do not install dependencies, use external services, publish, commit, push, or alter client/model/authentication settings.

# [Product name]

> Fill this in from the user's description. Remove instructions and unused fields; record assumptions rather than inventing decisions.

## Problem and objective

[Who faces which problem, how they solve it today, and what outcome the product should produce.]

## Audience and roles

[Primary users, usage context, and access differences that actually exist.]

## Initial release flows

[Essential flows, with input, action, and expected result. Prioritize those that demonstrate the objective.]

## MVP

[Features included in the first release, in priority order.]

## Out of scope

[What was explicitly deferred or is outside the request.]

## Requirements

[Known business rules, required data, accessibility, language, devices, and relevant security requirements.]

## Constraints and technical decisions

[Next.js/App Router, TypeScript, observed versions, package manager, and stated limitations. Persistence defaults to Drizzle ORM + PostgreSQL. Record the reason for another choice or a product without a database; preserve existing project stacks. Authentication and external services require a concrete need.]

## Assumptions and pending decisions

[Distinguish reversible assumptions from essential unanswered decisions. State the impact and next step.]

## Acceptance criteria

[Observable outcomes for MVP flows. Separate product criteria from technical setup checks.]

## Next delivery

[The smallest implementable task that advances the MVP after bootstrap.]

## Maintenance

Update this document when the objective, scope, constraints, or acceptance criteria change. Detailed technical decisions and evidence belong in docs/architecture.md and docs/setup.md. The generated file is named PRODUCT.md.

# Code and architecture

## Actual stack

[Framework, runtime, package manager, ORM, driver, and observed versions. Record reasons and exceptions to the defaults; actual versions also belong in the lockfile.]

## Code map

[Short tree of directories and files that actually exist. State each responsibility; do not present future architecture as implemented.]

## Boundaries and flow

[Actual path between presentation, validation, logic, and data. Server code owns environment, logging, and the database client. Create feature modules as needed; avoid empty layers.]

## Data and migrations

[Drizzle schema, inferred types, migration destination, and generation/review/application lifecycle. Record pooling, driver, runtime, bounded queries, and transactions where needed. Explain the decision if there is no persistence.]

## Decisions

[Decision, reason, relevant alternative, source/date, and condition for revisiting. Do not duplicate PRODUCT.md requirements.]

## Maintenance

Update this map when directories, relevant dependencies, contracts, or boundaries change. Record verified behavior; remove decisions that no longer apply.

# Design and accessibility

## Direction

[Audience, language, devices, and visual tone tied to PRODUCT.md. Label decisions not yet implemented as direction.]

## Existing system

[Existing tokens, typography, colors, spacing, and components. Point to their files and source of truth; do not maintain conflicting values here.]

## Interaction

Use semantic HTML, keyboard navigation, visible focus, and adequate contrast. Label controls and fields. Place validation errors beside fields; asynchronous operations show progress and results. Respect reduced motion.

## Layout and review

[Actual breakpoints and reading criteria for mobile and desktop. List relevant empty, error, and loading states. Record completed interface reviews and what does not exist yet.]

## Maintenance

Visual and interaction changes update the token/component source and this guidance when a rule changes. Consult installed UI skills during relevant reviews.

## Prerequisites

[Canonical check command and expected result. Separate local credential-independent tests from checks requiring an available service.]

## Agents

Read [AGENTS.md](../AGENTS.md). [CLAUDE.md](../CLAUDE.md) imports the same instructions. Consult [setup.md](setup.md) for local skills, integrations, and configured scopes.

templates/project-docs/quality.md.templa.title: templates/project-docs/quality.md.template
templates/project-docs/quality.md.templa.text:
# Quality

## Commands

[List existing scripts and what they prove: lint, typecheck, Vitest tests, rule self-check, and build. State the combined check command and when to run a scoped test or the suite.]

## Baseline rules

- Strict TypeScript and official framework presets.
- A 350-line limit and organization proportional to behavior.
- Structured server logging; no direct data access from presentation.
- With Drizzle, guard update/delete without where and review queries/migrations.
- Input and environment validation, errors without secrets, and relevant boundary tests.

## Testing strategy

[Cover behavior, decisions, failures, and regressions. State existing test environments and how to isolate services. Do not write tests that only repeat the code. Do not invent coverage, an E2E suite, or a security guarantee.]

[For adopted capabilities, document runtime/browser preflight, comparable bundle measurements, SQL/migration checks, actual CI run evidence, security report range/coverage, UI interaction checks, and read-only Sentry evidence. Omit inapplicable checks with a reason. Installation and discovery alone do not prove these workflows ran.]

[For typed lint, record the two focused async rules, severity, command, measured runner cost, and any legacy adoption plan. Run relevant harness smoke cases after instruction, memory, skill, or orchestration changes; identify the client/model and distinguish observed behavior from unrun cases.]

[Record the default Harness2-inspired native method adaptation, reusable prompt source/invocation, and relevant initial smoke results. If an observed failure justifies a candidate comparison, keep baseline/candidate inputs and independent checks comparable, retain security/permission boundaries, and record adopted/rejected changes and evidence-supported lessons. Separate any optional official CLI demo/benchmark evidence from actual project behavior; one passing case does not establish general reliability.]

## Review after implementation or fixes

Select review scope by risk and the actual diff. Use independent review for nontrivial work when available. Record the exact target, connected callers/contracts/tests, confirmed findings, and coverage. Add rounds for new evidence or unresolved risk; honor an explicitly requested count without inventing additional cycles.

Finish when relevant findings are resolved or explicitly dispositioned, affected checks pass, and integrated verification and residual risks are recorded. Fixes do not reset an agreed count. Missing independent review or blocked checks remain explicit limitations.

## Security review

[Record the adopted reusable prompt/skill, baseline or diff procedure, private report location, authorization boundaries, and relevant checks. Reviews trace entry points through shared validation/authorization to sensitive operations. Keep reviews read-only unless fixes are requested; redact reports and do not publish sensitive findings. Record severity, confidence, reproducibility, exclusions, and remaining hypotheses.]

## Dependencies and delivery

Check full and production audits. Investigate advisories and record known risk and available fixes. Passing lint/build does not mean a clean audit.

Checks are explicit commands. Git hooks, push blockers, and branch requirements are not defaults. Update this document together with scripts and rules that change.

# Setup and evidence

## Source and context

[Verification date, single toolkit revision, product, client, and runtime. Preserve authentication and the main model; record the authorized subagent policy and observable models/effort levels, without inventing costs. Do not include personal paths or credentials.]

## Decisions and sources

[Default adopted or adapted, reason, official documentation/Context7 consulted, and date. Distinguish the stable channel from prerelease examples. Record exceptions and criteria for revisiting.]

## Components

[Actual versions, package manager, lockfile, local/global scopes, skill sources, and names. Distinguish an installed plugin, a present file, and host discovery.]

| Component | Action and reason | Scope | State and evidence |
|---|---|---|---|
| [Component assessed from the current catalog] | [Install, update, integrate, reuse an equivalent, or explain inapplicability/blocker] | [Project, client, or user] | [Observed result and pending work, if any] |

Evaluate Next.js runtime/bundle skills, PostgreSQL guidance, GitHub CI repair, differential security review, shadcn, and Sentry MCP alongside the existing catalog. Record actual applicability and compatibility; preserve the project's stack and services. For adopted capabilities, include source/revision, frontmatter name, client, scope, install/update method, installation result, discovery result, live checks, and pending prerequisites. Account-dependent work stays pending until access and execution are observed.

Record the default Harness2-inspired native method adaptation separately from skills/MCPs, with reusable prompt invocation/source revision, initial smoke results, and any justified candidate comparison. Preserve session authentication and permissions. Record any separately selected official CLI lab outside the application; distinguish demo, benchmark, and project evidence, including pending authorization for costs or execution isolation. Reapplication preserves customizations and reuses applicable evidence; material changes require relevant checks again, without automatically repeating optimization trials.

## Documentation created

[Confirm PRODUCT.md, README.md, AGENTS.md, CLAUDE.md, docs/architecture.md, docs/design.md, docs/onboarding.md, and docs/quality.md contain project-specific content. Record preservation/consolidation of previous files.]

## Checks

| Item | State | Evidence |
|---|---|---|
| [Check, integration, or resource] | [Validated / configured without execution / pending] | [Command, observed result, or reason and next step] |

Record lint, types, tests, rules, builds, audits, HTTP, SQL generation, and database checks where applicable. Identify temporary resources created and their cleanup. Do not present a simulation as a test of a real service.

For existing projects, compare before/after checks, distinguishing pre-existing failures from regressions. Record rerun verification without duplication and what received only static review.

## Memory and harness evidence

[Actual native memory/index or canonical documentation location, how this client loads it, source/verification/invalidation convention, and clean-context retrieval result. Keep durable decisions separate from temporary task handoffs. Record the handoff/plan location only when work spans sessions.]

[Harness cases executed, inputs, client/version, actual model, commands/results, observed behavior, elapsed time, preserved customizations, and unrun cases. Distinguish fresh subagent context from a restarted client session. A passing smoke case is not a cross-client reliability guarantee. Record the adopted security review prompt and private reporting convention.]

## Pending work and next delivery

[External decisions, known risks, next step, and the smallest MVP task. State maintenance/rerun guidance, review coverage, residual findings, and the next useful check if needed. Publishing and external services require relevant authorization.]

templates/rules/parallel-subagent-driven.title: templates/rules/parallel-subagent-driven-development.md
templates/rules/parallel-subagent-driven.text:
# Parallel Subagent-Driven Development

## Problem

The base subagent-driven-development pattern dispatches one implementer at a
time. That default is safe — but slow when a plan contains genuinely
independent tasks. The naive fix, dispatching every task in parallel, is
risky when ownership and resource use are unclear:

- Two agents can edit the same file concurrently, and one's write silently
  clobbers the other's.
- Two agents can race each other to `git commit`, interleaving unrelated
  changes into a single commit or committing against a stale HEAD.

- Builds and tests can collide through shared output directories, ports,
  databases, or services even when source files differ.

This rule reduces known coordination risks; it does not guarantee that
parallel execution is as safe as serial execution.

## Why this override is safe

The following ownership rules address known failure modes:

- **File collisions** are prevented by only ever forming a wave from tasks
  whose file sets are fully disjoint. If two tasks might touch the same
  file, they never run in the same wave.
- **Commit races** are prevented by removing self-committing from
  implementers entirely. Implementers leave their changes in the working
  tree; when commits are authorized, the controller commits every task's
  changes itself, one at a time, after the wave finishes.

- **Resource collisions** require independent mutable resources for each task,
  including checks, or serialization of the affected work. Worktrees alone
  do not isolate ports, test databases, or external services.

The historical heading describes the intended guardrails, not a universal
safety claim. The coordinator still validates integration and unknown scope.

## Task tagging

At plan time, every task gets three fields:

- **`Files:`** — the exact file paths or globs the task will create or
  modify.
- **`Resources:`** — ports, build directories, test databases, and services
  used by the task or its checks, with their isolation or `none`.
- **`Depends-on:`** — the IDs of tasks whose output this task consumes, or
  `none`.

If any field is missing, or there's genuine uncertainty about what a
task touches or depends on, treat the task as depending on everything
before it. This is the fail-safe: an under-specified task silently
degrades to serial execution instead of risking a false-parallel bug.
Never guess a narrower scope than you actually know.

## Wave formation rule

Two tasks belong in the same wave only if **all** hold:

1. Neither task is in the other's `Depends-on` chain, even transitively.
2. Their `Files` sets are fully disjoint.
3. Their mutable resources are independent or explicitly isolated.

If any condition fails or is uncertain, the later or colliding task moves to a
subsequent wave.

A fully linear dependency chain (task 2 depends on task 1, task 3 depends
on task 2, …) degrades to exactly one task per wave — identical to plain
serial execution. Validate the resource assumptions before dispatch and
serialize when independence cannot be established.

## Per-wave execution loop

For each wave, in order:

1. Write one task brief per task with files, dependencies, resources,
   acceptance criteria, and checks.
2. Dispatch every implementer in the wave in a single message. This is the
   only step where real parallelism happens.
3. Implementers do **not** commit. Each one leaves its changes in the
   working tree and reports back which files it touched.
4. When authorized, the controller commits per task, in wave order — capturing the current
   HEAD fresh immediately before each commit, never a stale or hardcoded
   ref.
5. Dispatch that wave's task reviewers against exact base/head commits plus
   connected callers, contracts, and tests. Without commit authorization, use
   recorded working-tree snapshots. Reviewers remain read-only; run them together
   only when their checks use independent mutable resources. Isolate or serialize
   checks that share resources; review does not authorize fixes or commits.
6. Make exactly one controller-owned log or ledger write for the whole
   wave, not one per task. Concurrent per-task writes to the same log race
   each other and lose updates; a single write after the wave completes
   doesn't.

## Worker failure and recovery

The controller retains the authorized scope when a worker fails. Confirm that the worker has stopped before taking over or reassigning its files; an interrupt request alone is not confirmation. Inspect partial changes and resume from a verified state. While ownership is uncertain, continue only independent work on other files. Retry only with new evidence, within permissions and cost/time/attempt limits; otherwise report the blocker and the condition for resuming.

## Escape hatch

When tasks collide, serialize or combine them. Separate working directories
or Git worktrees with separate branches are optional when their benefit
justifies setup cost; a branch name alone does not isolate files. Assign ports,
build output, databases, and services independently as well. Keep Git operations
under the agreed ownership and authorization. No worktree is required.

## What this does not change

This rule changes orchestration only:

- The specialist type dispatched for each task still comes from your
  project's specialist-routing table, matched to the task's file scope —
  this rule doesn't add or replace agent types.
- The prompt body given to each implementer and reviewer is still the base
  skill's own unmodified contract: ask questions first if the task is
  ambiguous, follow TDD, self-review before reporting, and return an
  explicit status on completion.

Nothing here changes what an agent does with a task. It only changes how
many tasks run at once, and who is allowed to commit.

# Security review — {{project}}

Private working report. Store outside the reviewed repository; redact credentials, personal data and internal endpoints. Remove unused placeholders before delivery.

## Scope

- Date and reviewer/client:
- Mode: repository baseline / diff
- Snapshot: commit IDs, endpoint or merge-base comparison, dirty layers and untracked files included:
- Authorization assumptions and exclusions:
- Assets, entry points, roles/tenants and trust boundaries:
- Deployment assumptions requiring confirmation:

## Coverage and evidence

- Paths reviewed / excluded and reasons:
- Skills, tools and reference versions actually used:
- Unavailable capabilities or missing history:
- Commands/tests, isolation and results (static / mocked / end-to-end):
- Repository and index preservation check:

## Findings

Repeat for each substantiated finding or clearly labeled hypothesis. If none, state that none were substantiated within this scope.

### {{ID}} — {{title}}

- Severity and impact rationale:
- Confidence: high / medium / low; status: confirmed / needs validation
- Change origin: introduced / regressed / pre-existing / undetermined / not applicable
- Location: file:line, revision or dirty layer
- Redacted evidence and reachable entry-to-operation path:
- Attacker control, privileges and other prerequisites:
- Concrete impact and affected callers/data:
- Counterevidence considered; reproduction/test result or missing proof:
- Narrow proposed correction:
- Next validation:

## Remaining work and limitations

- Unverified hypotheses and required evidence:
- Hardening suggestions, separate from vulnerabilities:
- Coverage gaps and next validation:
- Report redaction and private destination verified:

This review does not establish that the project is secure or certify compliance. Findings and confidence apply only to the recorded scope and evidence. No fixes were applied by this review.

templates/task-handoff.md.template.text:
# Task handoff

Use only for unfinished work that needs another session. Reuse an existing plan or task record instead of creating a competing source. Keep durable decisions in the project's canonical documentation.

- Objective and acceptance: [requested outcome and observable completion criteria]
- State checked: [date, checkout/revision, local changes; never assume a clean tree]
- Completed: [changes and relevant file locations]
- Evidence: [actual commands, results, and when they ran; distinguish failures and unrun checks]
- Remaining: [smallest next action, dependencies, and known risks]
- Blockers: [cause, dependent work, and condition for resuming]
- Resources: [owned processes, ports, build directories, disposable databases; cleanup still needed]
- Context to revisit: [sources or assumptions that may have changed]

Before resuming, verify files, Git state, checks, and live resources. This record is context, not proof that a check still passes. Do not include secrets, private payloads, or full logs.
